The body mass index (BMI) of each mouse was calculated by dividing the body weight in grams by the square of the body length in centimeters, where body length was measured as the distance from the tip of the nose to the base of the tail.

For insulin tolerance testing, 301L-treated huR83C and control mice were fasted for 4 hours, weighed, and then received an intraperitoneal injection of 0.25 IU/kg sterile insulin (Sigma-Aldrich #I1882) diluted in PBS.
Blood glucose levels for the insulin tolerance test were measured at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 minutes after the insulin injection using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System.
Tissue sections were visualized using the Imager A2m microscope with an Axiocam 506 camera and ZEN 2.6 software from Carl Zeiss.
Statistical analyses were conducted using two-tailed unpaired T tests performed with the GraphPad Prism Program, version 10.2.2.
Data were presented as Mean values ± SEM, with individual data points for each animal displayed, and significance was denoted by * for p<0.05 and ** for p<0.005.
The animal study was performed once, with each animal infused with editing reagents independently to represent an independent outcome.
All experiments used huR83C mice homozygous for the pathogenic variant G6PC1-R83C, with mR83/mR83 (wild-type) and mR83/huR83C (heterozygote) mice included as controls in every experiment.
In the shorter 3-week study, untreated huR83C mice with a 3-week survival rate of 39% were included as controls.
Raw sequence reads are available on NCBI under the accession number PRJNA1164309.
The in vivo dosing protocol was optimized by Faith Musenge, Monique Otero, Edmond Wong, and Zach Howard. The lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation was developed by Raymond Yang and Sneha Gampa.
The off-target analysis for the CRISPR-based gene editing was described by Kenton Hetrick.
Blood glucose was measured at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 minutes after insulin injection using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System.
Permeabilized microsomes were prepared by incubating intact microsomes in sucrose buffer containing 0.2% sodium deoxycholate for 20 minutes on ice.

Phosphohydrolase reaction mixtures of 50 µl containing 50 mM sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 6.5), 2 mM EDTA, 10 mM G6P, and 100–200 µg of permeabilized microsomes were incubated at 30 °C for 10 minutes.

Background non-specific phosphatase activity was estimated by pre-incubating permeabilized microsomes in 20 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5) for 10 minutes at 37 °C to inactivate acid-labile G6Pase-α, with the resulting background (0.2 to 2 units) subtracted from all data points.

Enzyme histochemical analysis of G6Pase-α was performed on 10 µm thick cryopreserved OCT-embedded tissue sections incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes in a reaction buffer containing 40 mM Tris-maleate (pH 6.5), 10 mM G6P, 300 mM sucrose, and 3.6 mM lead nitrate.

Tissue sections were washed twice in 300 mM sucrose solution, then incubated for 2 minutes at room temperature in 0.09% ammonium sulfide solution to convert trapped lead phosphate to brown-colored lead sulfide.
Images of the tissue sections were acquired using an Imager A2m microscope with an Axiocam 506 camera and ZEN 2.6 software (Carl Zeiss).
Blood was collected by cardiac puncture from non-fasted, anesthetized mice and transferred into MiniCollect TUBE 0.8 ml CAT Serum Separator tubes (#450472, Greiner Bio-one).

Blood samples were allowed to coagulate for 20 minutes, then centrifuged for 10 minutes at 2000 × g, after which serum was transferred to a new microtube, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80 °C.
Blood samples were allowed to coagulate for 20 minutes, then centrifuged for 10 minutes at 2000 × g; the resulting serum was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80°C.

Serum cholesterol and uric acid were analyzed using Liquid Stable Reagents (#TR13421, #TR24321, ThermoFisher Scientific), the Cholesterol/Cholesteryl Ester Assay Kit (#ab65359, ABCAM), or the Uric Acid Assay Kit (#ab65344, ABCAM).
Serum L-Lactate was measured using the EnzyFluo™ L-Lactate Assay Kit (#EFLLC-100, BioAssay Systems), the Lactate Assay Kit (#K627-100, BioVision), or the L-Lactate Assay Kit (#ab65331, ABCAM).
Serum triglycerides were analyzed using the Serum Triglyceride Determination Kit (#TR0100, Sigma), the Triglyceride Assay Kit (#K622-100, BioVision), or the Triglyceride Assay Kit (#ab65336, ABCAM).

Serum AST and ALT activity were measured using the Enzy-Chrom™ Aspartate Transaminase Assay Kit (#EASTR-100, BioAssay Systems) and the EnzyChrom™ Alanine Transaminase Assay Kit (#EALT-100, BioAssay Systems), respectively.

Liver tissues from non-fasted mice were homogenized in 5% NP-40 solution at a 10:1 ratio (10 μl 5% NP-40 solution per 1 mg of tissue), deproteinized by incubation at 99°C for 5 minutes, and centrifuged at 17,000 × g for 15 minutes to remove insoluble materials.

Glycogen (#K646-100, BioVision), G6P (#K657-100, BioVision), glucose (#K686-100, BioVision; #ab102517, ABCAM), and lactate (#K607-100, BioVision; #ab65331, ABCAM) in deproteinized liver lysates were measured using the corresponding kits.
Calculations of glycogen in nmol/mg were based on a glycogen molar mass of 666.5777 g/mol.

Hepatic triglycerides were isolated by homogenizing liver tissues in 5% NP-40 solution at a 10:1 ratio (10 μl 5% NP-40 solution per 1 mg of tissue), heating and incubating at 85°C for 5 minutes, cooling to room temperature, repeating the heating/cooling step once, and centrifuging for 15 minutes at 17,000 × g.
Triglycerides in the supernatant of the processed liver samples were measured using the Triglyceride Assay Kit (#K622-100, BioVision) or the Triglyceride Assay Kit - Quantification (#ab65336, ABCAM).

H&E staining was performed on tissues fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin (#08379, Polysciences), and Oil Red O staining was performed on cryopreserved OCT (#4583; Sakura Finetek USA) embedded tissues processed according to standard procedures.
The study utilized primary hepatocytes for off-target studies, which were performed by T.L.
The study involved the design and optimization of a base-editor by M.S.P., L.-I.C., and G.L., with D.L. coordinating the animal study and NGS analysis.
L.S.S. designed the ONE-Seq panel and performed in-silico analysis, while C.B. nominated the Digenome-seq and validated rhAmpSeq assessments.
J.J.Q. designed and executed the off-target assay, and L.Y. designed and analyzed the off-target editing.

The study's 0.67% bystander editing rate cannot be verified without the raw sequencing files and the specific bioinformatics parameters from the CRISPResso2 batch analysis, which are currently missing from the manuscript.

The reported 0.67% bystander rate is confounded by undefined vehicle controls, making it impossible to distinguish the effect of the LNP delivery vehicle from the treatment itself without uncertainty quantification.
The study lacks the exact lipid formulation ratios required to replicate the LNP delivery system, preventing verification of whether the reported editing precision holds up under a second run.

The cell lysis procedure for the study utilized French press and sonication parameters that are specific enough to attempt a repeat, but the absence of raw sequencing data prevents full methodological verification.

The study's claim of 300-fold efficiency gains is methodologically compromised by the exclusion of low-quality sequencing reads, a filtering choice that obscures background noise and potentially inflates the apparent signal of the ionizable lipid formulation.
The study describes the design and testing of a novel HDR template vector that enables 'all-in-one' template plus gRNA sequences single vector HDR genome editing in Drosophila.
The study's methodology involves the identification and exclusion of undesired mutagenic insertional events of the HDR donor plasmid template vector into the genome.

The study utilized CRISPR gene-editing technology in Drosophila to introduce targeted breaks into the genome alongside a molecular template serving as a repair blueprint. The experimental design involved multiple genes, template designs, and editing strategies to identify the systematic integration of repair templates at unintended genomic locations.

The study utilized CRISPR/Cas9 based genome editing employing Homology Directed Repair (HDR) from template vector sequences to perform precise insertions, deletions, or modifications in Drosophila melanogaster germline genomes.

The researchers observed that the template vector employed for HDR repair unwantedly and commonly inserts into the Drosophila melanogaster genome at multiple genomic locations, with different HDR vectors, and with multiple genome editing designs.

To mitigate the bias of undesired vector integration, the study generated a novel HDR template vector that enables the identification and exclusion of Drosophila melanogaster animals containing these unwanted insertions.
The study utilized western blotting to analyze the expression of Drosophila TBPH and hTDP-43 proteins in homozygous animals from 22 individual genome-edited lines.
Genomic DNA sequencing was performed on the 18 lines where only hTDP-43 was expressed to confirm that the expected editing event had occurred.

A forward primer in the Drosophila TBPH gene and a reverse primer for the hTDP-43 gene were designed to amplify the region between these genes using genomic DNA from Drosophila lines expressing both proteins as a template.
The amplified ~10 kb product was sequenced to determine if it included genomic sequences flanking Drosophila TBPH and the entire pCR4 plasmid vector sequence.
Primers were designed to amplify the region between the lac promoter and pUC ori sequence of pCR4 to determine if the HDR donor vector sequence was present in all incorrectly edited animals.
The study used CRISPR Optimal Target Finder software to design two guide RNAs targeting the 3' and 5' UTR regions of the Drosophila TBPH gene to induce Cas9 dependent double-strand breaks.

A homology-directed repair template plasmid was generated containing approximately 1 kb of 5' and 3' sequences homologous to the Drosophila TBPH genomic region, an artificial replacement exon encoding human hTDP-43, and a DsRed selection cassette, which was cloned into the pCR4 plasmid vector.
The guide RNA encoding plasmids and the homology-directed repair replacement cassette were injected into Drosophila strains expressing Cas9 in the germline to facilitate genome editing.

Genome-edited Drosophila animals were identified by eye expression of DsRed, and the presence of the undesired vector backbone was detected via genomic DNA PCR using primers specific for the pCR4 vector sequence.

The study utilized CRISPR Optimal Target Finder to design two gRNAs and constructed an HDR donor plasmid containing homology arms, the VGAT sequence with an ALFA epitope tag, and an eye DsRed selection cassette cloned into the pHSG298 vector.

Fifteen genome-edited Drosophila animals were recovered with eye DsRed expression, and the presence of the ALFA tag was confirmed in all lines using PCR genotyping with primers specific for the ALFA tag and VGAT flanking regions outside the HDR homology arms.

The researchers tested for undesired pHSG298 vector sequence insertion and found that 10 lines (66.6%) incorporated pHSG298 sequences into the genome, while only 5 edited lines (33.3%) showed no evidence of a donor vector insertional event.

The experimental strategy involved using two gRNAs to enable two double-strand breaks between exons 1 and 2 of the VGAT gene, with the pHSG298 vector acting as a template containing an ALFA tag and a removable DsRed cassette flanked by approximately 1 kb long homology arms.

Agarose gel analysis of PCR products amplified using primers specific for the vector pHSG298 demonstrated that pHSG298 sequences could be amplified from genomic DNA derived from unwanted editing of VGAT Drosophila lines, but not from correctly edited VGAT Drosophila lines or controls.
The study utilized a DsRed piggyBAC selection cassette to identify successful editing events in Drosophila, with the intention to subsequently remove the cassette after edit identification.

The researchers designed a High-Fidelity DNA Repair (HDR) template cloning vector named pVID (Vector Insertion Detector) that expresses the ZsGreen1 fluorescent protein under the eye P3 promoter specifically when the vector backbone is incorporated into the genome.

For genome editing of the Synapsin gene to insert ALFA epitope tags, the study employed two guide RNAs designed using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder and a High-Fidelity DNA Repair donor plasmid containing homology arms, a Synapsin sequence with epitope tags, and an eye DsRed selection cassette cloned into the pVID vector.

The study designed two guide RNAs to target exon 12 of the Glutamate Receptor IIA (GluRIIA) gene and used a homology-directed repair (HDR) vector in pCR4 with homology arms to replace two amino acids in GluRIIA. Eye DsRed expression was used to select editing events, and twelve DsRed-expressing Drosophila lines were recovered and analyzed by PCR genomic amplification and sequencing.

DNA sequencing of the eleven incorrectly edited Drosophila lines revealed two peaks in the sequencing chromatogram, indicating the presence of both unmutated GluRIIA nucleotides and the desired modified nucleotides in the genome. PCR for pCR4 vector sequences from genomic DNA confirmed that all eleven incorrectly edited lines had pCR4 sequences inserted into their genome.

The CRISPR/Cas9 plus HDR editing strategy employed two guide RNAs to enable double-strand breaks in exon 12 of the GluRIIA gene, using a pCR4 plasmid containing the mutated GluRIIA exon 12 and a removable DsRed cassette flanked by approximately 1 kb long homology arms as the template. Agarose gel imaging of genomic DNA PCR amplification using primers specific for pCR4 identified the vector backbone sequence in incorrectly edited GluRIIA Drosophila lines but not in the correctly edited line or controls.

The study employed the pVID cloning vector as the backbone for homology-directed repair (HDR) templates, which included a ZsGreen selection cassette with a 3xP3 eye promoter, ZsGreen fluorescent protein coding sequence, and SV40 terminator to identify undesired vector integration events.

The CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing strategy for the Synapsin gene utilized two guide RNAs under the control of the dU6:3 promoter to create double-strand breaks between exons 1 and 2 and after exon 2, facilitating the in-frame insertion of seven ALFA tags in exon 2 and a DsRed cassette in intron 2.

Researchers performed PCR amplification for pVID vector sequences from genomic DNA derived from Drosophila lines to distinguish between correct edits (DsRed expression only) and undesired vector backbone insertions (co-expression of DsRed and ZsGreen).

A second CRISPR/Cas9 HDR genome editing procedure using the pVID vector was applied to the GluRIIC gene, which encodes an obligate Glutamate receptor, to test the vector's utility in a different genomic context.

The study utilized Drosophila germline genome editing with five fully independent HDR procedures, employing gRNA sequences designed using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder based on conventional on-target and off-target selection criteria.
The HDR repair templates utilized a conventional design featuring approximately 1 kb flanking homology arms together with the sequence to be inserted or edited, including mutated PAM sequences.
The germline Cas9 expressing animals employed in the study were the widely used nos-cas9 attp2 BL 78782 and nos-cas9 attp40 BL 78781 injection stocks.
The study used specific vector backbones including pCR4, pHSG298, and pVID (ZsGreen) for the HDR donor constructs.
The HDR donor vectors included an eye expression DsRed selection cassette to identify editing events, which could be 'scarlessly' removed after successful transgene or genome edit identification.
The study expresses Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells under the nos promoter to enable homology-directed repair (HDR) to occur.

The study routinely uses two selection cassettes: a positive selection dsRed cassette to indicate an editing event has occurred and a negative selection ZsGreen cassette to eliminate events where the HDR template vector has inserted into the genome.
Homology arms, desired edits, and selection cassettes were PCR amplified using Platinum SuperFi II high-fidelity DNA polymerase (Invitrogen) and assembled via HiFi DNA Assembly (Invitrogen).
All guide RNAs (gRNAs) were selected using the CRISPR Optimal Target Finder software.

The hTDP-43 HDR construct was inserted into pCR4 via Topo cloning, flanked by approximately 1 kb homology arms, and targeted by two gRNAs in pCDF3 vectors aimed at the neighbouring genes cpes and bgcn.

The ALFA-VGAT tagged HDR construct was inserted into pHSG298 via restriction digestion and ligation, flanked by approximately 1 kb homology arms, and targeted by two gRNAs in pCFD4 vectors aimed at the intronic region between VGAT exon 1 and exon 2.

The 7ALFA-Synapsin HDR construct in the pVID vector included 7 copies of the ALFA tag and an excisable dsRed selection cassette, flanked by two 600-700bp homology arms, with the full sequences synthesized and cloned by Genscript.

The GluRIIC HDR construct in the pVID vector included a Myc tag followed by an excisable dsRed selection cassette, flanked by two 600-700 bp homology arms, with the full sequences synthesized and cloned by Genscript.

The pVID HDR vector was generated by inserting a Drosophila eye negative selection cassette composed of a 3xP3 promoter, a ZsGreen fluorescent protein, and a SV40 terminator upstream of a dU6:3 gRNA promoter, with a multiple cloning site introduced downstream for gRNA and HDR template insertion.

Transgenic Drosophila melanogaster lines were generated by injecting embryos expressing Cas9 under the germ cell specific nos promoter with the HDR construct and gRNA expressing vectors, performed by Genetivision (Stafford, TX, USA) or FlyORF (Zürich, Switzerland).

The study purified Drosophila genomic DNA using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen) and performed PCR with specific primers targeting the lac promoter and pUC ori in pCR4 or pHSG298 plasmid sequences, expecting bands of 817 bp and 1001 bp respectively.
To detect pVID vector sequences, the study performed PCR using primers covering the region between the zsGreen CDS and the dU6:3 promoter, with a resulting band expected to be 813 bp long.

Fluorescence screening to identify undesired pVID genomic integration was performed using a fluorescence stereomicroscope (MC165F Leica) equipped with a GFP and dsRed filter, with images captured by a fluorescence CCD camera (DFC3000G, Leica).
The study utilized exclusively the nos promoter to highly express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells, a methodological choice that could affect vector template integration results.
Protein expression of hTDP-43, Drosophila TBPH, and tubulin was analyzed using Western blot with the Blue Precision Plus molecular weight marker from Bio-Rad.
Genomic DNA PCR products were visualized on agarose gels using the SmartLadder molecular weight marker from Eurogentec to identify DNA amplicon size.
The pVID HDR template vector was used to identify Drosophila genome edited lines with undesired vector integration events via ZsGreen expression.

Twenty adult Drosophila heads were lysed in RIPA lysis buffer containing 140 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100, 0.5 mM EGTA, 10 mM Tris-Cl pH 8, and 0.1% SDS, followed by centrifugation at 12000 x g for 1 minute.

Protein concentration was measured using a Micro BCA Protein Assay kit from Thermo Scientific, and 30 µg of protein was loaded into a 4-12% Tris-Glycine gel from Invitrogen after mixing with 4x Laemmli buffer and heating at 85° C for 2 minutes.
Protein bands were dry transferred to a PVDF membrane using the iblot transfer system from Invitrogen and blocked for 1 hour in 5% milk blocking solution.

The PVDF membrane was incubated at 4°C overnight with primary antibodies including anti-hTDP-43 (H00023435-M01, Novus Biologicals) at 1:500, anti-TBPH (custom made, Pierce) at 1:500, and anti-α-tubulin (T6199, Sigma) at 1:10,000.

Secondary antibodies, specifically goat anti-rabbit (111-035-003, Jackson ImmunoResearch) and goat anti-mouse (115-035-003, Jackson ImmunoResearch), were diluted in blocking solution at 1:10,000 and incubated for 1 hour.

Imaging was enabled by adding WesternBright Sirius chemiluminescent substrate from Advansta, and membranes were stripped for 10 minutes at 37°C using Restore Western Blot Stripping Buffer from Thermo Scientific before re-blocking.
Genomic DNA from Drosophila lines was purified using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit from Qiagen.

PCR was performed using Platinum SuperFi II proofreading DNA polymerase from Invitrogen with a reverse primer in the 5' end of the hTDP-43 gene (TTCTCATCCTCGGTCACGCG) and a forward primer in the 3' end of the TBPH gene (GGAACACCGGTTGGTCGAAC).

The PCR product was purified using the GeneJET Gel Extraction Kit from Thermo Scientific and the MinElute Reaction cleanup kit from Qiagen, then cloned into a pCR8 vector using the pCR8/GW/TOPO TA Cloning Kit from Invitrogen.

The study's reproducibility is compromised by the omission of the specific ionizable lipid identity and the exact lipid-to-RNP weight ratio, which are critical formulation parameters required to establish initial mixing conditions and rule out lipid-membrane interaction artifacts.

The experimental design lacks a solvent-only control formulation, a methodological omission that prevents the isolation of bystander editing effects from artifacts caused by the lipid's interaction with the cell membrane.

The study's inferential power is compromised by the absence of reported sample sizes (n) per group and test statistics, which are required to validate the efficacy claims independent of the authors' background.

The experimental design relied on n=3 biological replicates per group with two analytical replicates each, a sample size parameter that is too low to detect anything but massive effects and renders the 40% efficiency point estimate statistically indistinguishable from zero.

The analysis lacked covariate adjustment for baseline mutation rates, a methodological omission that leaves the undefined control formulation as the primary threat to validity by preventing the attribution of observed changes to the gene-editing technology rather than the container.

The statistical power is limited by the use of n=3 biological replicates per group, which leaves the study unpowered to detect anything but massive effects and prevents proper covariate adjustment for the undefined LNP formulation.

The absence of raw sequencing reads prevents verification of the reported 40% efficiency point estimate and 95% confidence intervals, as well as confirmation that the n=3 biological replicates were analyzed with correct statistical tests and uncorrected multiple comparisons.

The analysis pipeline relies on CRISPResso2 batch parameters set to a window size of 20 (-w 20), a window center offset of -10 (-wc-10), and a quality threshold greater than 30 (Q>30), which are the specific methodological choices required to replicate the software analysis if the underlying data were available.

The reported aggregate off-target metrics are unverifiable because the study lacks the raw sequencing reads and specific guide design parameters necessary for an independent analyst to re-run the CRISPResso2 pipeline and confirm that the precision results are not artifacts of the analysis settings.

The low-quality read filtering parameter of Q>30 may be artificially suppressing the detection of off-target events, potentially inflating the apparent safety profile of the 0.67% bystander rate, which is currently unsupported by confidence intervals or full distribution reporting.

The methodological choice to report a 40% editing efficiency as a point estimate without a confidence interval or per-cell distribution data prevents the quantification of risk and the distinction between a uniform biological effect and a small fraction of highly edited cells.

The replication process is hindered by the unavailability of raw FASTQ files and exact SM102 ratio controls in a public repository, forcing independent labs to compare aggregate metrics against undefined baselines rather than running an identical pipeline with the original filtering steps.
