documents: The study utilizes the ionizable lipid SM102 and the synthetic lipid DMG-PEG 2000 to formulate lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) for the encapsulation of adenine base editor and prime editor ribonucleoproteins (RNPs).
The LNP formulations are produced via microfluidic mixing to encapsulate the ribonucleoproteins (RNPs).
Cell-penetrating peptides are used either covalently fused to the protein or as excipients to enhance the efficiency of ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery.
The CRISPR/Cas9 system utilizes a Cas9 nuclease targeted by a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) and a guide RNA binding to a 20-bp-long DNA protospacer.
Homology-directed repair with a donor DNA template exhibits low efficiency compared to non-homologous end joining, particularly in post-mitotic cells such as neurons.

Base and prime editors fuse a DNA effector domain to a partially inactivated Cas9 domain (Cas9 nickase) to avoid double-stranded DNA breaks, maintaining high editing efficiency in post-mitotic cell types.
The potential off-target effects of prime editors have not yet been carefully explored or documented.

The net size of guide RNA constructs along with base or prime editors exceeds the packaging limits of commonly used viral vectors such as lentiviruses and adeno-associated viruses, often requiring splitting into two viral vectors.

Transient delivery methods for CRISPR/Cas9 include virus-like particle delivery, mRNA lipid-nanoparticle delivery, and direct ribonucleoprotein delivery as naked RNP or lipoplex with cationic lipid reagents such as Lipofectamine 2000.

The study utilizes purified ABE and PE RNPs encapsulated in lipid nanoparticle LNPs, which were formulated using cell-penetrating peptides and commercially available ionizable cationic lipids with acid dissociation constants (pKa) greater than 6.

Protein purification protocols include Ni-NTA, size exclusion chromatography (SEC), TALON chromatography, and 1D4 chromatography, with purity assessed via SDS-PAGE, western blot, and absorbance spectra showing the removal of contaminating nucleic acids.

Size exclusion chromatography of ABE and PE proteins was performed relative to standards including blue dextran (2,000 kDa), thyroglobulin (670 kDa), γ-globulin (158 kDa), ovalbumin (44 kDa), myoglobin (17 kDa), and vitamin B12 (1.35 kDa).
Thermal stability of ABE and PE proteins was characterized using differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) in PBS containing 10% (w/v) sucrose, with averaged profiles from n=3 replicates.

In vitro activity assays for ABE and PE were conducted using urea-PAGE gels imaged for fluorescein and SYBR Gold, with specific controls including no substrate, substrate-only, no epegRNA, and no dNTP conditions.

Cre recombinase was purified to homogeneity using nickel metal-affinity chromatography (Ni-NTA) followed by size exclusion chromatography (SEC), with purity confirmed by SDS-PAGE and anti-Cre western blot.
ABE8e was purified using affinity chromatography on TALON metal and 1D4 affinity columns, followed by SEC, with purity assessed via SDS-PAGE and anti-Cas9 western blot.
PE2 was purified using a protocol similar to ABE8e, with an additional heparin chromatography step after 1D4 immunoaffinity to separate impurities.
SEC effectively removed contaminating nucleic acids and aggregates from ABE8e that remained after immunoaffinity chromatography.
ABE8e RNP stability was enhanced by refolding the single guide RNA (sgRNA) through heating and slow cooling, and further stabilized by the addition of 10% (w/v) sucrose.

PE2 RNP complex stability with engineered prime-editing guide RNA (epegRNA) was higher than PE2 protein alone, but heat refolding of epegRNA did not provide additional stability benefits, and sucrose was not required for solubility.
All sgRNAs and epegRNAs used in the study were heat refolded for consistency.
Enzymatic activity of ABE8e RNP was verified using an in vitro deamination assay, while PE2 RNP activity was verified using an in vitro reverse-transcriptase extension assay.
Cre recombinase delivery was assessed in HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cells, where Cre excises a floxed GFP-STOP sequence to enable red fluorescent protein (RFP) expression.
Lipofectamine 3000 was used as a positive control for Cre delivery in HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cells, achieving up to 40% cell conversion.
Unmodified Cre recombinase induced up to 4.4% colour switching from GFP to RFP in HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cells, indicating baseline membrane crossing ability.
TAT- and ANTP-fused Cre proteins increased delivery efficiency to up to 28% and 45% respectively in HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cells, whereas CPP5-fused Cre did not enhance delivery.
Non-covalent complexation of Cre with the CPP peptide 6×His-CM18-PTD4 increased Cre delivery to approximately 6% and synergistically enhanced the delivery efficiency of CPP-fused Cre proteins.

In ROSA mT/mG mice, Cre recombinase excises tdTomato and stop signals to enable enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) expression, which was monitored in primary fibroblasts and via subretinal injection.
In ROSA mT/mG fibroblasts, only the ANTP-fused Cre peptide modestly improved delivery efficiency compared to untagged Cre or Lipofectamine 3000 delivery.
Subretinal injection of AAV1-CMV-Cre and eVLPs packaging Cre protein into ROSA mT/mG mice mediated efficient tdTomato to eGFP conversion primarily in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

The ROSA mT/mG Cre-reporter mouse model constitutively expresses tdTomato and prevents eGFP expression until Cre-mediated excision of the stop signal occurs. Subretinal delivery of Cre recombinase was performed using AAV2/1-CMV-Cre, VSV-G pseudotyped Cre eVLP, or direct protein delivery with Lipofectamine 3000, 6x His-CM18-PTD4 peptide, CPP5-fused Cre, TAT-fused Cre, or ANTP-fused Cre, with outcomes measured by two-photon excitation microscopy one week post-delivery.

In vitro quantification of Cre-mediated GFP to RFP conversion used a protein concentration of 1 µM, which corresponds to 41.9 µg ml⁻¹, with three biological replicates and two analytical replicates each. The enhancement of conversion was quantified with increasing concentrations of 6x His-CM18-PTD4 peptide at a fixed protein concentration of 0.5 µM.

A fluorescent rd12 reporter cell line was created by retrovirally transducing NIH/3T3 cells with a construct containing a fragment of Rpe65 rd12 cDNA with an in-frame nonsense mutation flanked by mCherry and eGFP. In unedited cells, the stop codon permits only mCherry expression, while successful base or prime editing results in mCherry-eGFP fusion protein expression.

Adenine base editing was verified using ABE8e with a previously validated rd12 sgRNA, achieving 22% editing efficiency by next-generation sequencing and 32% by flow cytometry. The addition of 10% w/v sucrose to the RNP mixture boosted ABE8e delivery, and the non-covalent 6x His-CM18-PTD4 peptide further enhanced this delivery by 1.5-fold.

Prime editing (PE) activity was not observed with 2% sucrose but was detected with 10% sucrose. The 6x His-CM18-PTD4 peptide improved PE2 RNP delivery efficiency by approximately 1.6-fold, although overall efficiencies remained low.

Subretinal injection of ABE8e RNP using a low-NaCl, high-sucrose formulation restored the scotopic dark-adapted flash electroretinography (ERG) b-wave in rd12 mice, with the non-covalent 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide promoting rescue more effectively than fused CPPs.

Genomic DNA and transcript sequencing from RPE samples of treated mice revealed up to 2% on-target genomic editing and up to 7% on-target base editing in cDNA, with editing outcomes distributed approximately equally between precise edits and edits containing at least one bystander adenine deamination.
Purified RNP delivery resulted in more precise ABE editing compared to eVLP packaging of the same ABE8e, which caused multiple deaminated adenines.

Binding of sgRNA to ABE shifts the net zeta potential from +4.4 mV to -7.6 mV, enabling efficient capture by cationic lipids for lipoplex formation or lipid nanoparticle encapsulation via microfluidics.

In vitro delivery of ABE RNP via a Lipofectamine 3000 lipoplex was efficient in the rd12 reporter cell line at concentrations as low as 20 nM (4.5 µg ml⁻¹), restoring RPE65 expression and improving editing efficiency and precision compared to plasmid delivery.

The in vitro optimal formulation of 50 pmol (11.2 µg) ABE8e RNP per µl of Lipofectamine 3000 (5.6 µg RNP per eye) failed to restore ERG responses in rd12 mice, likely due to toxicity from the high dose of Lipofectamine 3000 (50% by volume, 0.5 µl per eye).

Using a 5-fold lower dose of Lipofectamine 3000 with the same amount of ABE RNP resulted in substantially higher rescue efficiency in rd12 mice, indicating that minimizing toxicity is required for effective in vivo lipid-mediated RNP delivery.

ABE RNP LNPs containing ionizable lipid SM102 and 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 have a diameter of 228 nm and a polydispersity index of 0.072, while formulations with CL4H6 and DODMA have diameters of 235 nm and 249 nm, respectively.
In vitro delivery of ABE RNP to rd12 reporter cells used a concentration of 20 nM (4.5 μg ml⁻¹) with incubation times ranging from 1 to 48 hours.

In vivo treatment of rd12 mice involved a subretinal injection of 1 μl ABE RNP LNP per eye, with RNP concentrations of approximately 2.3 μM (515 ng per eye) for SM102/CL4H6 formulations and 1.8 μM (403 ng per eye) for DODMA formulations.
The optimized ABE RNP LNP formulation for cryo-electron microscopy and in vivo testing contains ionizable lipid SM102 and 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000.

Subretinal injection of ABE RNP LNP with SM102 and 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 into 3-4-week-old juvenile rd12 mice resulted in an average of 0.30% precise correction of Rpe65 genomic DNA and 1.25% precise correction of Rpe65 transcripts two weeks post-injection.
ABE protein was detectable in the neural retina up to 24 hours and in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) up to 48 hours after subretinal injection of the optimized ABE RNP LNP into wild-type mice.

ABE and PE RNP LNPs were formulated using a prototypical lipid mixture of ionizable lipid, 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DSPC), cholesterol, and 1,2-dimyristoyl-rac-glycero-3-methoxypolyethylene glycol-2000 (DMG-PEG 2000) at a molar ratio of 50:10:38.5:1.5.

Ionizable lipids with a pKa above 6.0 were selected to prevent ABE inactivation, specifically 8-[(2-hydroxyethyl)[6-oxo-6(undecyloxy)hexyl]amino]-octanoic acid,1-octylnonyl ester (SM102) with pKa 6.68, 9-octadecenoic acid, 1,1'-[7-[4-(dipropylamino) butyl]-7-hydroxy-1,13-tridecanediyl] ester (CL4H6) with pKa 6.25, and 1,2-dioleyloxy-3-dimethylaminopropane (DODMA) with pKa 6.59.
The ABE RNP LNPs exhibited a hydrodynamic diameter between 200 and 250 nm as measured by dynamic light scattering.

Encapsulation of ABE RNP within LNPs was verified by immunoprecipitation with 1D4 resin and subsequent anti-Cas9 western blot analysis, where ABE RNP LNPs were detected in the non-bound fraction while free ABE RNPs were bound by the resin.
A B6-30 resin directed against the N terminus of rhodopsin served as a non-binding control and did not bind ABE, confirming the epitope specificity of the 1D4 resin binding.

ABE RNP LNPs containing SM102 elicited nearly total conversion of rd12 reporter cells at a concentration of 20 nM ABE RNP (4.5 μg ml⁻¹), whereas lipoplex with Lipofectamine 3000 peaked at approximately 50% cell conversion.

The rd12 reporter construct expresses mCherry and eGFP under the CMV promoter with an intervening Rpe65 rd12 genomic sequence containing the c.130 C > T (p.R44X) mutation, where successful base editing restores the reading frame for co-expression.

In vitro delivery efficiency was assessed with ABE in the presence of 2% (w/v) sucrose, 10% (w/v) sucrose, or 0.5 μM ABE with 10% (w/v) sucrose and 6× His-CM18-PTD4 peptide, where 1 μM corresponds to 224 μg ml⁻¹.

LNPs containing 2.5% DSPC and 1-stearoyl-2-oleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (SOPS) remained stable for at least 28 days at -80 °C and at least 14 days at 4 °C. The ABE concentration in the LNP preparation was 2 μM (0.45 mg ml⁻¹, 450 ng per eye), which is at least 10-fold lower than the 20–36 μM (4.5–8.1 mg ml⁻¹, 4.5–8.1 μg per eye) concentrations used for RNPs formulated with sucrose or Lipofectamine 3000.

LNPs without DMG-PEG 2000 exhibited the highest particle size and were not active in vitro, while LNPs with 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 achieved nearly 100% cell conversion at 5 nM (1.1 μg ml⁻¹) ABE RNP. The optimal lipid:RNA weight ratio was at least 40:1, and the ABE RNP was fully encapsulated at this ratio with 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000, as confirmed by 1D4 immunoassay and size-exclusion chromatography (SEC).

Cryoelectron microscopy (cryoEM) confirmed that optimized RNP LNPs had intact and uniform particles with an approximate diameter of 100 nm. Targeted proteomics showed that Cas9 and TadA* deaminase peptides were detected at the same level, indicating intact, full-length ABE8e protein within the LNPs.

Next-generation sequencing revealed that RNP LNPs mediated up to 40% on-target editing and lower bystander editing compared with plasmids, with off-target activity minimal at ≤0.3% edited alleles concurrent with almost 60% on-target adenine editing. In vivo, SM102 LNP-RNP with 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 resulted in a maximal ERG b-wave rescue of 368 μV, compared with 265 μV for LNPs with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000.

PE2 RNP encapsulation was partially successful with 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000, showing unencapsulated PE2 protein and larger particle size, but increasing DMG-PEG 2000 to 2.5% eliminated unencapsulated PE2 and enabled robust delivery. CryoEM images of optimized PE RNP LNP revealed homogeneous, well-defined particles, and the PE2 RNP LNPs achieved ERG b-wave amplitudes exceeding 300 μV in rd12 mice.

Targeted proteomics indicated that Cas9 and the reverse transcriptase (MMLVRT) were not detected at equimolar concentrations within PE2 RNP LNPs, suggesting necessary improvements in LNP formulation and PE2 purification. Next-generation sequencing showed exceptional purity of editing outcomes for RNP-mediated prime editing, with no unwanted editing or off-target editing detected in cells treated with PE RNP LNP.

PE2 RNP LNP particle-size distributions were measured for formulations containing 1.5% DMG-PEG 2000 with ionizable lipids SM102 (diameter 270 nm, PdI 0.068), CL4H6 (diameter 298 nm, PdI 0.024), or DODMA (diameter 176 nm, PdI 0.096), and for formulations containing 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 with ionizable lipid SM102 (diameter 194 nm, PdI 0.040).

Delivery of PE2 RNP LNP to rd12 reporter cells was analyzed using a concentration of 20 nM, which corresponds to 6 µg ml⁻¹, with experiments performed as two biological replicates with two analytical replicates each.
Cryoelectron-microscopy imaging of PE2 RNP LNP containing ionizable lipid SM102 and 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 was conducted with two biological replicates and two analytical replicates per condition.

The LNP-mediated delivery of RNPs requires fully quantitative characterization of encapsulation efficiency before advancing to good manufacturing practice production for non-human-primate and human trials.
Pigmented Gt(ROSA)26Sor tm4 (ACTB-tdTomato, EGFP)Luo (ROSA mT/mG) mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory (JAX 007676) for the study.

The lipid content in the LNP formulation exceeds the weight of the ribonucleoprotein complex by approximately eight times, which poses potential translational challenges in non-human primates or humans.
Smaller LNPs, typically below 100 nm in diameter, are more readily internalized by cells due to more efficient endocytosis, a characteristic that may enhance uptake and retention in the RPE.
A gap exists in the data regarding the correlation between functional Rpe65 mRNA levels and the zygosity of corrected alleles of Rpe65 in rd12 mice, requiring additional experiments to resolve.
Homozygous RPE65-P2A-CreERT2 knock-in mice expressing RPE65 at levels of 1-5% of wild-type counterparts exhibited ERG responses nearly indistinguishable from wild-type mice.
The study utilized the ABE8e and PE2 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) variants to correct the rd12 mutation in vitro and in vivo, with ABE8e N108Q used to improve precision.
The PE2 editing strategy was used without the introduction of a second guide RNA that programmes a nick on the unedited strand, which characterizes the PE3 strategy.
Subretinal injection of ABE RNP LNPs into wild-type mice was followed by anti-Cas9 western blot analysis of RPE/choroid/sclera and neural retina lysates to determine degradation kinetics.
Genomic DNA and transcripts were analyzed via next-generation sequencing to document Rpe65-editing outcomes following treatment with ABE RNP LNP or PE RNP LNP.

High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was used to quantify 11-cisretinal in whole eyes from dark-adapted untreated rd12 mice, ABE-RNP-LNP-treated rd12 mice, PE-RNP-LNP-treated rd12 mice, and wild-type mice.
RPE flatmounts of rd12 mice were stained for RPE65 (green), counterstained with ZO-1 (magenta) and DAPI (blue), with a scale bar of 50 μm.

Pigmented Gt(ROSA)26Sor tm4 (ACTB-tdTomato, EGFP)Luo (ROSA mT/mG) mice (JAX 007676) were crossed with BALB/cJ albino mice (JAX 000651) to establish the albino ROSA mT/mG line, while C57BL/6J (JAX 000664) and rd12 (JAX 005379) mouse lines were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory and housed at the University of California, Irvine on a normal mouse chow diet with a 12 h/12 h light/dark cycle.
N-terminal Cre recombinase fusion proteins were produced from recombinant plasmids based on pTAT-Cre (Addgene 35619), with pCPP5-Cre and pN-Cre inserts synthesized by GeneWiz and cloned into pET-28b.

The antennapedia (ANTP) DNA sequence was generated by annealing ANTP-Or_F and ANTP-Or_R primers at a 1:1 molar ratio for a total DNA concentration of 80 μM in 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 62.5 mM NaCl, and 10 mM EDTA, using a thermocycler protocol of 2 min at 95 °C followed by gradual cooling to 25 °C over 45 min.

The pANTP-Cre plasmid was constructed by replacing the TAT sequence with ANTP between the Ncol and Ndel cloning sites, and all plasmids were propagated in Escherichia coli NEB-5α cells (New England Biolabs C2987H).
A positive control Cre eVLP was produced by subcloning Cre (Addgene 123133) into pCMV-MMLVgag-3xNES-ABE7.10-NG (Addgene 181753) via USER cloning (NEB).

Genes encoding ABE7.10, ABE8e, and PE2 constructs were subcloned into pRha rhamnose-inducible expression vectors via USER cloning (NEB), and the 1D4 peptide with a preceding tobacco etch virus (TEV) protease recognition site was introduced using PCR site-directed mutagenesis and KLD cloning (NEB M0554S).

Cell-penetrating peptide sequences were introduced into ABE using PAGE-purified single-strand oligonucleotides (Sigma-Aldrich) annealed at a final concentration of 25 μM in 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, and 5 mM MgCl2 by heating at 95 °C for 5 min and slow cooling.

Assembled duplexes were ligated at a 100-fold excess into protein expression vectors linearized with FastDigest Ndel (Thermo Fisher FD0584), transformed into NEB-5α cells, and plated onto LB-agar plates containing 25 μg ml-1 kanamycin.

Cre recombinase expression plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli BL21star (DE3) (Thermo Fisher, C601003) and grown in Terrific Broth (TB; Thermo Fisher, 22711-022) with 50 μg ml⁻¹ kanamycin (Goldbio, K-120-SL25) overnight at 37 °C.

Cre recombinase protein expression was induced with 0.5 mM isopropyl β-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG; Goldbio, I2481C25) when the optical density at 600 nm reached 0.5, followed by incubation at 20 °C for 16 hours.

Cre recombinase cell pellets were resuspended in Cre-lysis buffer (50 mM Na phosphate pH 7.4, 1 M NaCl, 1 cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitor cocktail tablet (MilliporeSigma, COEDTAF-RO) per 50 ml) and lysed by sonication (125-W pulses, 5 s on/5 s off for 10 min) or French press (3 passes at up to 15,000 psi).

Cre recombinase purification utilized Ni-Sepharose High Performance beads (Cytiva, 17526801) with a Cre-wash buffer (25 mM Na phosphate pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl) and elution via a gradient of Cre-elution buffer (25 mM Na phosphate pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 500 mM imidazole).

Pure Cre recombinase fractions were purified using size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva, 28990944) or HiLoad 16/600 Superdex 200 pg column (Cytiva, 28989335) with P500G buffer (20 mM sodium phosphate, pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 20% v/v glycerol).

ABE and PE expression plasmids were transformed into Escherichia coli BL21star (DE3) cells (Thermo Fisher, C601003) and grown in Terrific Broth with kanamycin until the optical density at 600 nm reached 1.5.
ABE and PE protein expression was induced with 0.8% (w/v) rhamnose (Goldbio, R-105-250) after cooling the culture in an ice-water slurry, followed by expression at 17 °C for 16-24 hours.

Proteins were expressed at 17 °C with mixing at 190 r.p.m. for 16-24 h, and cells were collected by centrifugation at 5,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C before storage at -80 °C. All protein purification steps were conducted in a cold room (~4-8 °C) or on ice.

Thawed cells from a 1.5-L culture were homogenized with a 40 ml Dounce homogenizer in lysis buffer (100 mM Bis-Tris propane, pH 8.0, 1 M NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol, 5 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP), 1 cOmplete Ultra EDTA-Free protease inhibitor tablet per 40 ml of buffer). The cells were lysed by sonication with a Qsonica Q125 sonicator (125 W) with a 1/8-inch microtip at 100% amplitude for a total of 20 min (intermittent pulses: 5 s on, 5 s off).

The lysate was clarified two times at 4 °C by centrifugation at 48,500 g for 10 min. ABE was captured on a 3-ml TALON metal-affinity resin (Takara Bio, 635502), washed with 100 ml of lysis buffer without inhibitors and 10 ml of wash buffer (100 mM Bis-Tris propane, pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 20% (v/v) glycerol, 1 mM TCEP), and eluted with wash buffer supplemented with 150 mM imidazole.

ABE was purified by immunoaffinity chromatography using a 1D4 resin (Sepharose CL-4B resin; Cytiva, 17043001) with immobilized 5-10 mg ml⁻¹ 1D4 antibody purified in house. The 4 ml 1D4 resin was packed in a DWK Life Sciences Kimble Kontes FlexColumn, equilibrated with wash buffer, and loaded by gravity flow.

The 1D4 column was washed with at least 40 ml of wash buffer at 0.5 ml min⁻¹, and ABE was eluted with 1 mg ml⁻¹ 1D4 peptide in the wash buffer at ~1 ml h⁻¹. Fractions containing ABE were pooled, concentrated, and purified by size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column or a Superdex 200 16/60 Prep Grade column using ABE storage buffer (10 mM 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazine ethanesulfonic acid (HEPES), pH 7.0, 500 mM NaCl, 20% glycerol).

Fractions containing pure ABE were concentrated using Amicon Ultra centrifugal filters with 30-kDa molecular weight cut-off membranes (Merck, UFC903024), sterilized by passage through 0.22-µm filters, quantified using UV absorption at 280 nm, divided into aliquots, and snap frozen in a chilled metal block for storage at -80 °C.

Cells expressing PE were lysed using a single pass through the French press and subsequent sonication for 10 min. Metal affinity and immunoaffinity steps for PE were identical to those for ABE, except that the wash buffer contained 400 mM NaCl.

After immunoaffinity chromatography, PE was subjected to heparin-affinity chromatography (HiTrap Heparin HP 5 ml; Cytiva, 17040703) at 0.5 ml min⁻¹. The heparin column was equilibrated with wash buffer containing 400 mM NaCl, washed with at least 50 ml of wash buffer until the UV baseline was stable, and bound proteins were eluted with a 200-ml NaCl gradient (0.4 M-1.0 M).

Purest PE fractions were selected for size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 16/60 Prep Grade column with PE-storage buffer (10 mM HEPES, pH 7.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5% (v/v) glycerol) as the eluent. Pure PE was concentrated, filtered, quantified using UV absorption at 280 nm, distributed into aliquots, and snap frozen for storage at -80 °C.
The eluent composition for protein purification was pH 7.0, 500 mM NaCl, and 5% (v/v) glycerol. Purified PE was quantified using UV absorption at 280 nm and stored at -80 °C.

Protein purity was assessed using SDS-PAGE with hand-cast Tris-glycine-SDS discontinuous gels containing 4% acrylamide in the stacking gel (pH 6.8) and 10% acrylamide in the resolving gel (pH 8.8) with a 2.7% crosslinker (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide ratio of 37.5:1; Bio-Rad, 1610158). Samples were mixed with 4x-concentrated Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad, 1610747) and 50 mM dithiothreitol (DTT; MilliporeSigma, D9779), denatured at 70 °C for 10 min, and centrifuged before application.

Protein concentration was quantified using a Nanodrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer by measuring absorbance at 280 nm. Contaminating nucleic acids were monitored by the ratio of absorbance at 260 nm to 280 nm, with a ratio <0.60 indicating protein free from nucleic acids and a typical value of 0.55 for purified ABE and PE.
Extinction coefficients for the ABE and PE constructs were estimated using the ProtParam tool available at https://web.expasy.org/protparam/.

Synthetic 60-bp-long DNA oligonucleotides (Sigma) labelled with fluorescein on the strand undergoing deamination were annealed at a 1:1 ratio in 10 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, and 1 mM EDTA by incubation at 95 °C for 5 min followed by slow cooling to 20 °C.

End-modified sgRNA and epegRNA were ordered from IDT Technologies with 2'-O-methyl groups on the first three and last three nucleotides, and the first and last three phosphodiester bonds replaced with phosphorothioate bonds. The guide RNAs were dissolved in nuclease-free water at 37 °C for 15 min at 500 r.p.m. and folded by incubation at ~75 °C for 5 min followed by slow cooling.

Prepared nucleic acids were quantified using UV absorption spectroscopy at 260 nm, where an A260 nm value of 1.0 corresponded to a DNA concentration of 50 μg ml⁻¹ or an RNA concentration of 40 μg ml⁻¹. DNA was stored at -20 °C and RNA at -80 °C.

HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cells (CS cell line, GenTarget SC018-Bsd), NIH/3T3 rd12 cells, and rd12 reporter cells were maintained in DMEM/F12 medium with GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher 10565018) or DMEM with glutamine (Thermo Fisher 11965092), supplemented with 10% FBS (Genesee Scientific 25-514H) and 100 U ml⁻¹ penicillin-streptomycin (Thermo Fisher 15140122) at 37 °C and 5% CO₂.

Primary fibroblasts were isolated from P0-P3 ROSA mT/mG mouse skin by digesting with a 1:1 mixture of 0.25% trypsin without EDTA (Thermo Fisher 15050065) and 5 U ml⁻¹ dispase (STEMCELL Technologies 07913) for 1 hour at 37 °C, followed by digestion with 0.25% collagenase I (Thermo Fisher 17018029) in serum-free DMEM/F12 for 1 hour at 37 °C.

Isolated primary fibroblasts were filtered through a 70-μm strainer, washed with DMEM/F12 containing 15% FBS and 100 U ml⁻¹ penicillin-streptomycin, and passaged every 3-4 days using 0.05% trypsin-EDTA (Thermo Fisher 25300054), with a 40-μm strainer used after the first passage to remove aggregates.

For protein delivery experiments, cells were seeded 24 hours prior to the experiment in 24-, 48-, and 96-well plates to reach 50-70% confluency, corresponding to approximately 100,000, 50,000, and 25,000 cells per well for the CS cell line and NIH/3T3 rd12 cells, and 50,000, 24,000, and 10,000 cells per well for rd12 reporter cells and primary fibroblasts.

ABE ribonucleoprotein was assembled by incubating ABE with a 1.5-fold molar excess of sgRNA in a reaction buffer containing 20 mM Bis-Tris propane (pH 7.5), 100 mM KCl, 2.5 mM MgSO4, 2 mM DTT, and 5% (v/v) glycerol for 15 minutes at room temperature.

ABE ribonucleoprotein assemblies above 4 μM included 10% (w/v) sucrose, while ABE was diluted to 1 μM with reaction buffer, preheated at 37 °C, and added to 15 ng of DNA substrate (0.02 μM final) for deamination reactions of 10–60 minutes for ABE8e.

The 20-μl ABE deamination reactions were quenched by adding 30 μl of water preheated to 95 °C and incubating for 2 minutes at 95 °C, followed by treatment with 1 μl of RNase A (20 mg ml−1) and 1 μl of proteinase K (20 mg ml−1) for 15 minutes at room temperature.

DNA products from the ABE assay were purified using an Oligo Clean and Concentrator kit (Zymo Research, D4061) and nicked with 5 units of Endonuclease V (EndoV, NEB) for 2–3 hours at 37 °C before quenching with 1× TriTrack DNA-loading dye (Thermo Fisher, R1161) and incubation at 95 °C for 2 minutes.

Cleavage products from the ABE assay were analyzed by denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis using 15% acrylamide gels (acrylamide:bis-acrylamide ratio 19:1, Bio-Rad, 1610144) in Tris-borate-EDTA buffer (Bio-Rad, 1610770) with 7 M urea, maintained at at least 42 °C.

Gel imaging for the ABE assay was performed using a ChemiDoc MP system (Bio-Rad), with fluorescein detection done immediately after electrophoresis and SYBR Gold (Thermo Fisher, S11494) detection done after 30 minutes of staining with 1× dye in 1× TBE.

The in vitro reverse-transcriptase elongation assay for PE was conducted in the ABE reaction buffer supplemented with 0.5 mM deoxyribonucleotides (dNTP), using PE2 ribonucleoprotein assembled with a 1.1-fold molar excess of epegRNA targeting the rd12 locus without added sucrose for 15 minutes at room temperature.

PE2 assay reactions were preheated at 37 °C, 45 ng of fluorescein-labelled substrate was added to a final volume of 15 μl, and after 15 minutes, reactions were quenched with 1 μl each of proteinase K (20 mg ml−1) and RNase A (20 mg ml−1), denatured at 95 °C for 2 minutes, and supplemented with 6× TriTrack loading dye.

For the differential scanning fluorimetry assay, ABE and PE proteins were complexed with a 1.5-fold molar excess of guide RNA in phosphate-buffered saline at room temperature for 15 minutes to obtain 10 μM ribonucleoprotein, with ABE ribonucleoprotein containing an additional 10% (w/v) sucrose.

Differential scanning fluorimetry samples were diluted with phosphate-buffered saline to 1 μM, SYPRO Orange probe was added to a final concentration of 5×, and 10 μl aliquots were placed into a 384-well plate (Applied Biosystems, 4483319) sealed with optical foil (Applied Biosystems, 4360954).

After a 15-minute incubation, differential scanning fluorimetry plates were centrifuged at 1,000 g for 1 minute at room temperature and installed in a pre-equilibrated Bio-Rad CFX384 thermocycler to measure fluorescence in Förster resonance energy transfer mode every 0.2 °C from 20 °C to 95 °C.

Cre recombinase was prepared at final concentrations of 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, or 1.00 μM (4.2, 10.5, 21.0, 31.4, or 41.9 μg ml⁻¹) in 250 μl of OptiMEM medium (Thermo Fisher, 31985070) for cell-based assays.
For non-covalent complexation, 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide (Genscript) was added to Cre recombinase and incubated for 15 minutes at room temperature before delivery to cells.
Cell imaging was performed using a Keyence BZ-X810 microscope with GFP and Texas Red optical filters after exchanging the medium to FluoroBrite DMEM (Thermo Fisher, A1896701).

Flow cytometry analysis used a Novocyte Quanteon (Agilent) flow cytometer equipped with Pacific Blue (445/45 nm), FITC (530/30 nm), and PE (586/20 nm) optical filters, with cells resuspended in FACS buffer containing 1 μg ml⁻¹ DAPI (Thermo Fisher, 62248).

Subretinal injections utilized Cre proteins diluted to 10 μM in OptiMEM, optionally with 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide in 10-fold excess, or a lipoplex of Cre with Lipofectamine 3000 at 2% by volume (419 ng Cre and 0.02 μl Lipofectamine 3000 per eye).
Positive controls for subretinal injections included AAV2/1-Cre (Addgene, 105537-AAV1; 1.8 × 10¹⁰ vg) or VSV-G pseudotyped eVLP-Cre concentrated by ultracentrifugation.

Mice were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal cocktail of 20 mg ml⁻¹ ketamine and 1.60 mg ml⁻¹ xylazine (100 mg kg⁻¹ ketamine and 8 mg kg⁻¹ xylazine) and pupils were dilated with 1% tropicamide (Akorn, 17478-102-12) and 10% phenylephrine (MWI Animal Health, 054243).

Subretinal surgery used a 34-gauge blunt-end needle (World Precision Instruments, NF34BL-2) connected to an RPE-KIT (World Precision Instruments, RPE-KIT) with SilFlex tubing (World Precision Instruments, SILFLEX-2) and a UMP3 UltraMicroPump (World Precision Instruments, UMP3-4) to deliver 1 μl per eye.
Two-photon imaging utilized a Ti:sapphire laser (Coherent, Vision S) tuned to 950 nm, with detection bandwidths of 490-545 nm for GFP and 590-680 nm for tdTomato, using a 1.0 NA×20 Leica objective.

The rd12 reporter construct consists of 198 bp of mouse Rpe65 cDNA flanked by 5'-mCherry and 3'-eGFP, inserted into the pcDNA3.1/(Zeo)+ backbone via BamHI and XhoI restriction sites, and subsequently subcloned into pMXs-IRES-blasticidin.

The rd12 reporter cell line was generated by transducing NIH/3T3 cells with retrovirus from Phoenix-Eco cells transfected with pMXs-mCherry-rd12-eGFP-IRES-blasticidin, followed by selection with 5 µg ml⁻¹ blasticidin (Thermo Scientific, R25001) for 10 days.
Clones were screened for expression and editability via co-transfection with pCMV-NG-SpCas9-ABE7.10max and pSPgRNA-rd12-A6, and no additional characterization was performed on the sorted cells.

ABE RNP was assembled by incubating up to 20 μM ABE with a 1.1-fold excess of sgRNA (rd12-A6-sgRNA highly modified, supplied by IDT) in OptiMEM medium supplemented with 10% (w/v) sucrose for at least 15 minutes at room temperature. The 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide was diluted to 400 μM with water and added to the ABE RNP for an additional 15-minute incubation.

For Lipofectamine 3000 lipoplex assembly, 0.5 μl (48-well) or 0.2 μl (96-well) of Lipofectamine 3000 was diluted with OptiMEM containing 10% (w/v) sucrose to 12.5 μl or 5 μl per well, respectively, and mixed with ABE RNPs diluted to the same volumes in OptiMEM with 10% (w/v) sucrose, followed by a 15-minute incubation at room temperature.
Plasmid DNA transfections were performed in 48-well plates using 160 ng pCMV-NG-SpCas9-ABE, 80 ng pSPgRNA-rd12-A6, and 0.75 μl Lipofectamine 3000 per well following the manufacturer's protocol.

For PCR analysis, one-tenth of the NIH/3T3 cell suspension expressing Rpe65 rd12 cDNA was lysed with 10 mM Tris pH 7.5, 0.05% SDS, and 0.02 mg ml⁻¹ proteinase K for 1 hour at 37°C, followed by proteinase K inactivation at 85°C for 45 minutes.

For western blotting, the remaining NIH/3T3 cells were lysed in 1× RIPA buffer (Cell Signaling Technology, 9806) with 1× cOmplete Ultra EDTA-free protease inhibitors (Roche) for 1 hour on a rotator in a cold room, then centrifuged at 17,000–21,400 g for 20 minutes at 4°C.
Protein concentration in the extracts was measured using the BCA assay (Thermo Fisher, 23252).
Complementary DNA was synthesized from RNA using the High Capacity RNA-to-cDNA kit (Thermo Fisher, 4387406).
The input for the first of two PCR reactions (PCR1) was 0.5-1 µl of isolated genomic DNA or cDNA.
Genomic loci were amplified in PCR1 using Phusion Plus polymerase (Thermo Fisher, F631S) with primers listed in Supplementary Table 2 (marked as HTS_fwd and HTS_rev).
PCR1 was performed with the following parameters: 98 °C for 30 s; 30 cycles at 98 °C for 10 s, 60 °C for 20 s and 72 °C for 30 s; 72 °C for 5 min.
One microlitre of PCR1 product was used as input for PCR2 to install Illumina barcodes.
PCR2 was conducted for 9 cycles of amplification using a Phusion HS II kit (Life Technologies).
Following PCR2, samples were pooled and gel purified in a 1% agarose gel using a Qiaquick Gel Extraction kit (Qiagen).
Library concentration was quantified using the Qubit High-Sensitivity Assay kit (Thermo Fisher).
Samples were sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq instrument using paired-end reads (read 1: 200-280 cycles, read 2: 0 cycles) with an Illumina MiSeq 300 v. 2 kit (Illumina).
Sequencing reads were demultiplexed using the MiSeq Reporter software (Illumina) and analysed using CRISPResso2.
The CRISPResso2 analysis used batch analysis mode, with one batch for each unique amplicon and sgRNA combination analysed.
Sequencing reads were filtered according to a minimum average quality score of Q>30 before analysis.
The quantification window parameters used for the analysis were -w 20 -wc-10.
Prism 10 (GraphPad) was used to generate dot plots and bar plots.
The supernatant was pre-cleared with Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo Fisher, 10003D) by rotation at 4 °C for 15 min to remove immunoglobulin contaminants from blood before loading on the gel.
Mouse eyes were enucleated and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde in PBS for 20 min at room temperature, then washed three times in PBS for 5 min each.
For RPE flatmounts, the anterior segment and retina were removed from the posterior eyecup under a dissecting microscope, and four radial cuts were made towards the optic nerve to flatten the eyecup.
Samples were permeabilized and blocked in 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich, T8532) with 3% normal goat serum in PBS for 30 min.

Samples were incubated with mouse anti-RPE65 antibody (1:100; in house) and rabbit anti-ZO-1 polyclonal antibody (1:100; Invitrogen, 61-7300) in PBS, 0.1% Triton X-100 and 3% normal goat serum overnight at 4 °C.

After washing three times in PBS for 5 min each, samples were incubated with Alexa Fluor 555-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG (1:200; Thermo Fisher, A11032) and Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG (1:200; Thermo Fisher) in PBS, 0.1% Triton X-100 and 3% normal goat serum for 2 h at room temperature in the dark.
Flatmounts were incubated in DAPI (1 μg ml⁻¹; Thermo Fisher, 62248) in PBS for 10 min after secondary antibody removal and subsequent washing.
Samples were mounted with VECTASHIELD HardSet Antifade Mounting Medium (Vector Labs, H-1400-10) and imaged on a Keyence BZ-X810 All-in-One fluorescence microscope.

Western blotting used mouse anti-RPE65 antibody (produced in house) or mouse anti-SpCas9 (clone 7A9, Biolegend, 844302) diluted 1:1,000 in 5% non-fat dry milk in PBS (Bio-Rad, 1610780) with 0.1% Tween 20 (MilliporeSigma, P9416).

Lysates containing 7-10 μg total protein were separated by SDS-PAGE, transferred to a polyvinylidene fluoride membrane (MilliporeSigma, IPVH00010), blocked for 1 hour with 5% non-fat dry milk in PBST, and incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C.

After four 5-minute washes with PBST, blots were incubated for 1 hour at room temperature with horseradish peroxidase-linked horse anti-mouse antibody (Vector Laboratories, PI-2000-1) diluted 1:2,500 in 5% non-fat dry milk in PBST.
Signals were detected with SuperSignal West Pico Plus Chemiluminescent substrate (Thermo Fisher, 34577), followed by stripping with 0.2 M glycine pH 2.2, 0.1% SDS, and 1% Tween 20.

Stripped membranes were re-probed for 1 hour at room temperature with rabbit anti-β-actin polyclonal antibody (1:2,000; Cell Signaling Technology, 4970S) and goat anti-rabbit IgG with HRP (1:2,500; Cell Signaling Technology, 7074S).
ABE was diluted into OptiMEM with 10% or 25% (w/v) sucrose, or into ABE storage buffer with 390 mM NaCl final concentration without added sucrose.

ABE was added to guide RNA dissolved in water and incubated for 15 minutes at room temperature to form RNPs, which were then combined with 5-fold molar excess of 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide diluted to 1 mM or undiluted Lipofectamine 3000.
RNPs were incubated with delivery reagents for at least 15 minutes at room temperature before subretinal injection into rd12 mice.
Mouse posterior eyecups were immersed in RLT Plus (Qiagen), and cells were detached by gentle pipetting before processing with the AllPrep DNA/RNA Micro kit (Qiagen, 80284).

Protein lysates were prepared by homogenizing posterior eyecups in 40 μl ice-cold RIPA buffer with protease inhibitors using a motorized tissue grinder (Fisher Scientific, K749540-0000), incubating on ice for 20 minutes, and centrifuging for 20 minutes at 21,000 g at 4 °C.
The resulting supernatant was pre-cleared with Dynabeads Protein G (Thermo Fisher, 10003D) by rotation at 4 °C for 15 minutes to remove immunoglobulin contaminants.
Pupil dynamics were verified and absolute pupil diameters were calculated using Adobe Premiere Rush programme version 10.0.1 from Adobe Systems.
Mice eyes were homogenized in 1 ml of 10 mM sodium phosphate buffer (pH 8.0) containing 50% (v/v) methanol (Sigma-Aldrich, 34860-1L-R) and 100 mM hydroxylamine (pH 8.0) (Sigma-Aldrich, 159417-100G).
After 15 min incubation at room temperature, 2 ml of 3 M NaCl was added to the homogenized mouse eye sample, which was then extracted twice with 3 ml ethyl acetate (Fisher Scientific, E195-4).
The combined organic phase from the mouse eye extraction was dried in vacuo and reconstituted in 250 µl hexane, with 100 µl of the resulting extract used for HPLC separation.
Retinoids were separated on a Zorbax Sil column (5 µm, 4.6 mm × 250 mm; Agilent Technologies) connected to an Agilent Infinity 1260 HPLC system with a diode-array detector.
HPLC separation used a mobile phase of 0.6% ethyl acetate in hexane (Fisher Scientific, H302-4) at 1.4 ml/min for 17 min, followed by a step increase to 10% ethyl acetate in hexane for 25 min.
Retinoids were detected by monitoring absorbances at 325 nm and 360 nm using Agilent ChemStation software.

ABE and PE RNPs were assembled by mixing 10 μM purified ABE or PE with synthetic sgRNA or epegRNA at a 1:1.1 molar ratio in specific buffers containing 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 500 mM NaCl, and 20% or 5% glycerol for ABE or PE respectively.

The final buffer composition for RNP assembly was 2.8 mM HEPES (pH 7.0), 140 mM NaCl, 10% (w/v) sucrose, and 5.6% (v/v) glycerol for ABE, or 1.4% (v/v) glycerol for PE, after diluting proteins supplemented with 10% (w/v) sucrose from a 50% (w/v) stock.

RNPs were incubated at room temperature for at least 15 minutes and then diluted to 0.711 μM in 50 mM Tris-acetate buffer (pH 6.0) with 10% (w/v) sucrose to achieve a final NaCl concentration of 10 mM before encapsulation.

LNP encapsulation utilized ionizable cationic lipids CL4H6 (Cayman Chemical, 37279), SM102 (Broadpharm, BP-25499), or DODMA (Avanti Polar Lipids, 890899) with pKa values of 6.25, 6.68, and 6.59 respectively, combined with co-lipids DSPC (Avanti Polar Lipids, 850365), cholesterol (Avanti Polar Lipids, 700100), and DMG-PEG 2000 (Avanti Polar Lipids, 880151).

The standard molar lipid composition was 50/10/38.5/1.5 for ionizable lipid/DSPC/cholesterol/DMG-PEG 2000, with DMG-PEG 2000 optimized from 1.5 to 10 mole% by decreasing cholesterol concentration accordingly.

Alternative formulations included 2.5 mole% SOPS (18:0-18:1 PS, Avanti Polar Lipids, 840039C) with 7.5 mole% DSPC, and lipids were dissolved in ethanol and combined with pre-formed RNP at a 1:3 ethanol:aqueous volume ratio and a total lipid:guide RNA weight ratio of 40:1.
Mice were dark adapted for 1 week and anaesthetized with isoflurane inhalation before electroretinography (ERG) recording.

Mice pupils were dilated with 1% tropicamide ophthalmic solution (Akorn, 17478-102-12) and 10% phenylephrine ophthalmic solution (MWI Animal Health, 054243), followed by hypromellose (Akorn, 9050-1) for hydration.

The mouse was placed on a heated Diagnosys Celeris rodent-ERG device, with ocular stimulator electrodes on the corneas, a reference electrode subdermally between the ears, and a ground electrode in the rear leg.
Eyes were stimulated with a green-light flash stimulus (peak emission 544 nm, bandwidth ~160 nm) of -0.3 log (cd s m^-2) light intensity.
The responses for 10 stimuli with an inter-stimulus interval of 10 s were averaged, and a- and b-wave amplitudes were acquired from the averaged ERG waveform.
Data were analysed with Espion V6 software (Diagnosys).
For the RNP LNP optimization study, eyes that received LNP and had no ERG response after treatment were excluded from the analyses.
The pupillary light reflex (PLR) was characterized in mice (n=5 for each group) using the A2000 computerized pupillometer (Neuroptics).
Mice were dark adapted for 6 h before recordings in a dark room.
The light profile consisted of four white-light stimuli (1.2 log, 10^1.2 W m^-2), each for 500 ms.

Mice were kept under isoflurane anaesthesia during the PLR testing routine, carried out under scotopic conditions with no background illumination from the pupillometer, using infrared cameras as the primary light source.
The maximum size of the pupil after dark adaptation was quantified at 2 min after anaesthesia to establish baseline size.
The pupil response was expressed as percent constriction of the pupil compared to baseline.
Captured digital movies of pupil responses were recorded using Active Presenter software (v.9.1.3, Atomi Systems).
Videos were decomposed into individual frames using Adobe Premiere Rush programme (v.10.0.1, Adobe Systems) for manual verification of pupil dynamics and calculation of absolute pupil diameters.

Replication is blocked by the absence of the distribution of edited alleles across individual cells, as the study only reported aggregate editing efficiency, preventing verification of whether functional rescue stems from a small fraction of highly edited photoreceptors or broad, low-level editing.

Assessment of formulation-driven variance is impossible without access to the raw, unadjusted ERG traces and the specific lipid-to-RNP ratio used in the control arms, which are critical missing parameters for reproducing the experimental conditions.

The statistical analysis is characterized by a sample size of n = 12 per group and an uncorrected effect size of d = 0.8 (95% CI 0.1 to 1.5), parameters that must be replicated exactly to evaluate the precision of the reported results.

The SM102 study methods section omits the exact ionizable lipid and PEG ratios for the vehicle control arm, leaving the formulation undefined and blocking any calculation of effect size or interpretation of the Kruskal-Wallis p-values.

Cryo-EM imaging was only reported for the 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 SM102 formulation, leaving the particle size distribution and aggregation kinetics for the 1.5% variant and the vehicle control entirely uncharacterized.
The humanized mouse model huR83C carries the pathogenic G6PC1-R83C variant and lacks blood glucose control due to a deficiency in the G6PC1 gene encoding glucose-6-phosphatase-α.
BEAM-301 is a formulation of lipid nanoparticles containing a newly engineered adenine base editor designed to correct the G6PC1-R83C variant in liver cells.

Replication of the metabolic correction requires achieving approximately 10% base correction of the G6PC1-R83C variant, as this threshold is sufficient to restore blood glucose control and improve metabolic abnormalities.

The huR83C mouse model was generated by inserting the entire human G6PC1-R83C (G6PC1-c.247C > T) coding sequence into exon 1 of the mouse G6pc gene, which knocked out native mouse G6pc expression while placing human G6PC1-R83C expression under the control of the mouse G6pc promoter/enhancer.
The human G6PC1-R83C variant corresponds to the specific mutation G6PC1-c.247C > T/p.R83C, which accounts for 32% of sequenced alleles in Caucasian GSD-Ia patients.

A previous homology directed repair (HDR) strategy utilized AAV to deliver editing reagents to neonatal G6pcR83C mice, while a non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) strategy utilized lipid nanoparticles (LNP) to deliver editing DNA oligonucleotides to 2- to 4-week-old G6pc-R83C mice.

The in vivo experiment used 10-12 week-old heterozygous (mR83/huR83C) mice that were not fasted, treated via systemic administration of BEAM-301, and analyzed one week later using next-generation sequencing (NGS).

The target site sequence analysis focused on the conversion of the p.R83C (G6PC1-c.247C> T) variant to wild-type p.R83 (G6PC1-c.247C), alongside the p.Y85H bystander variant and p.R83 synonymous variant.
Off-target validation was performed in primary human hepatocytes using a 2-stage approach involving the nomination of candidate sites and their validation in treated cells.
Candidate off-target sites were nominated using two complementary biochemical assays: oligonucleotide enrichment and sequencing (ONE-seq) and Digenome-seq.

A total of 591 unique candidate sites were selected for evaluation, comprising sites from ONE-seq or Digenome-seq experiments, in silico low-mismatch sites, the 1 on-target site, and 20 negative control sites.

The base-editing strategy for correcting the G6PC1-R83C variant utilizes a guide RNA designed with an saCas9 'NNGRRT' protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) and a base-editor harboring an saCas9 nickase domain and a TadA deaminase domain engineered to maximize editing of the target adenine at position 16.
The investigational therapy BEAM-301 consists of a guide RNA and messenger RNA encoding the base-editor co-formulated into a lipid nanoparticle (LNP).

BEAM-301 was administered systemically via tail vein injection at doses ranging from 0.1 to 3.0 mg/kg to 10-12-week-old heterozygous (mR83/huR83C) mice, with base-editing efficiency analyzed via next-generation sequencing (NGS) in isolated liver slices at 7 days post-dose.

In heterozygous mice administered BEAM-301 at 1.5 mg/kg, an average of 40.3% of sequencing reads encoded wild-type G6Pase-α, while 5.5% contained the nonsynonymous bystander edit resulting in the Y85H allele, 0.3% contained a synonymous bystander edit, and 0.7% exhibited indels.

The functional impact of the nonsynonymous Y85H bystander edit was evaluated using transient expression assays in COS1 cells, where the G6Pase-α-Y85H variant lacked detectable phosphohydrolase activity.

The study utilized a humanized mouse model (huR83C) carrying two alleles with the human G6PC1-R83C variant knocked-in at the G6pc locus, alongside wild-type (mR83) and heterozygous (mR83/huR83C) controls.

Liver microsomal G6Pase-α activity in 3-week-old wild-type, heterozygous, and homozygous huR83C mice averaged 330.4 ± 36.3, 176.2 ± 13.7, and 2.2 ± 0.3 units, respectively, while kidney microsomal G6Pase-α activity averaged 607.2 ± 49.2, 267.8 ± 18.2, and 2.6 ± 0.4 units.
The lower level of quantitation for the microsomal G6Pase-α assay is 2 units, which indicates that the huR83C mice have null hepatic and renal G6pc loci.

The therapeutic candidate BEAM-301 consists of messenger RNA encoding the adenine base editor (ABE) and guide RNA targeting the G6PC1-R83C variant, encapsulated in a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation.
BEAM-301 was delivered via a single systemic administration at a high dose (301H, 1.5 mg/kg) or a low dose (301L, 0.75 mg/kg) to newborn mice within 48 hours post-birth or at 3 weeks of age.
Outcomes for the treated mice were monitored for 53 weeks of age, with no decline in hepatic G6Pase-α activity observed over this period.
Untreated huR83C mice exhibited a 3-week survival rate of 39%, with only 16 of 42 mice surviving to age 3 weeks.
Newborn huR83C mice were treated with a high dose of BEAM301 (301H) at 1.5 mg/kg, and the phenotype of the resulting NB-301H mice was evaluated at age 3 weeks.
Statistical analysis for the comparison of body weight, liver weight, and kidney weight ratios was performed using a two-tailed unpaired T test.
The study utilized specific sample sizes for biochemical assays, including n=24 for control blood glucose, n=16 for huR83C-3W blood glucose, and n=6 for NB-301H-3W blood glucose.
Serum cholesterol levels were measured with sample sizes of n=16 for control-3W, n=7 for huR83C-3W, and n=6 for NB-301H-3W mice.

Primary human hepatocytes from 3 donors were treated with BEAM-301 at or near saturation of on-target editing, and the rhAmpSeq method was used to amplify candidate off-target sites in parallel in treated and untreated donor-matched cells for NGS processing.
Newborn huR83C mice were treated by systemic administration of BEAM-301 at a dose level of 1.5 mg/kg (301H), and metabolic correction was assessed at 3 weeks of age.

In the remaining six treated huR83C mice, liver microsomal G6Pase-alpha activities averaged 163.8 ± 48.5 units, which was statistically equivalent to heterozygous control mice that had 176.2 ± 13.7 units.
Hepatic G6Pase-alpha activity in the treated huR83C mice ranged from 33 to 289 units and revealed a positive correlation with base-editing efficiency (R83C > R83), with a maximum rate of ~60%.

The 301H-treated huR83C mice survived 24 hours of fasting challenges with fasting blood glucose levels indistinguishable from control mice, whereas untreated huR83C mice exhibited marked hypoglycemia within 60 to 75 minutes of fasting.

Histochemical enzyme analysis showed that in NB-301H-dosed huR83C mice expressing wild-type levels of hepatic G6Pase-alpha activity, the distribution pattern was similar to mR83/huR83C control mice, while mice expressing lower levels had a focal pattern of expression associated with the vasculature.
The study measured glucose, triglyceride, lactate, glycogen, and G6P levels in control (n=16), huR83C-3W (n=8), and NB-301H-3W (n=6) mice.
Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining was performed on liver and kidney sections to assess the restoration of liver G6Pase-alpha activity.
The kidney-to-body weight (KW/BW) value decreased from 5.2 ± 0.2% in untreated huR83C mice to 2.4 ± 0.1% in edited mice, compared to 1.30 ± 0.02% in control mice.
In 3-week-old NB-301H-dosed mice, liver-to-body weight (LW/BW) values were inversely correlated with the level of restored hepatic G6Pase-alpha activity.
In NB-dosed mice, hepatic levels of glycogen, triglyceride, and G6P were inversely correlated with the level of restored hepatic G6Pase-alpha activity.

Untreated huR83C mice exhibited hypoglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia, and hyperuricemia, while serum lactate concentrations were not significantly elevated in 3-week-old untreated huR83C mice.
In 3-week-old untreated huR83C mice, hepatic glucose levels were markedly reduced, while hepatic levels of triglyceride, glycogen, lactate, and G6P were increased compared to controls.
NB-dosed mice displayed normal hepatic levels of triglyceride, lactate, and glycogen, but hepatic glucose levels remained reduced and hepatic G6P levels remained elevated compared to controls.

Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of 3-week-old untreated huR83C mice revealed a diffuse mosaic pattern of hepatocytes and marked glycogen accumulation in renal tubular epithelial cells, resulting in glomerular enlargement and compression.
Oil Red O staining confirmed increased neutral fat accumulation in the liver of 3-week-old huR83C mice, with little to no fat accumulation observed in the kidney.

H&E and Oil Red O staining of NB-dosed huR83C mice confirmed a marked reduction in hepatic glycogen and neutral fat levels, which inversely correlated with the extent of restored hepatic G6Pase-α activity.

Homozygous (huR83C) mice edited at birth with BEAM-301 exhibited large variation in both editing efficiency and the level of restored hepatic G6Pase-α activity, contrasting with the tight range of editing rates observed in BEAM-301-treated adult heterozygous (mR83/huR83C) mice.
The 53-week persistence study infused newborn (NB) huR83C mice with a high dose (301H) and 3-week-old (3W) huR83C mice with a 50% lower dose (301L) of BEAM-301 editing reagents.
The high dose (301H) of BEAM-301 was administered at a concentration of 1.5 mg/kg to newborn (NB) and 3-week-old (3W) huR83C mice.
The low-dose BEAM-301 regimen (301L) was administered at a specific dose of 0.75 mg/kg.
The 8-week survival rate for the 18 huR83C mice treated as newborns with the 301L dose was 50%, while the survival rate for the 21 huR83C mice treated at age 3 weeks with the 301L dose was 86%.

The liver microsomal G6Pase-α activity in 8-week-old control mice averaged 238.9 ± 17.6 units, in surviving NB-dosed huR83C mice (n=9) it averaged 24.5 ± 5.1 units, and in 3W-dosed huR83C mice (n=8) it averaged 31.3 ± 7.3 units.
All 8-week-old edited huR83C mice in the study were able to sustain 24 hours of fasting.

The 8-week-old 301L-dosed huR83C mice exhibited normal hepatic triglyceride levels, reduced hepatic glucose levels, and elevated hepatic levels of glycogen, G6P, and lactate compared to littermate controls.
The NB-dosed huR83C mice displayed increased levels of serum cholesterol, whereas the 3W-dosed huR83C mice displayed a normal blood/serum metabolite profile at age 8 weeks.
Liver microsomal G6Pase-α activity in 8-week-old wildtype mice measured 258.9 ± 14.3 units and in heterozygous mice measured 174.7 ± 7.0 units.
Liver microsomal G6Pase-α activity in 3W-dosed huR83C mice averaged 150.8 ± 27.4 units, while NB-dosed mice averaged 65.0 ± 22.8 units.
Liver microsomal G6Pase-α activities in NB-dosed mice ranged from 5 to 173 units with a base-editing efficiency range of 0.8% to 35% as analyzed via NGS.
Liver microsomal G6Pase-α activities in 3W-dosed mice ranged from 30 to 294 units with a base-editing efficiency range of 2.9% to 36.6%.
Kidney microsomal G6Pase-α activity in NB-dosed huR83C mice was 4.5 ± 0.44 units and in 3W-dosed huR83C mice was 3.3 ± 0.51 units.
Kidney microsomal G6Pase-α activity in 8-week-old wild-types was 520.8 ± 55.5 units and in heterozygotes was 270.2 ± 18.8 units.
All 301H-dosed huR83C mice displayed normal blood/serum levels of glucose, cholesterol, triglyceride, lactic acid, and uric acid.
At age 8 weeks, hepatic levels of glucose and lactate were completely normalized in 3W-dosed huR83C mice but not in NB-dosed huR83C mice.
Liver microsomal G6Pase-α activity in 53-week-old wild-type and NB-dosed huR83C mice averaged 211.4 ± 6.1 and 87.1 ± 19.9 units, respectively.
Analysis of liver isolates from 53-week-old NB-dosed huR83C mice revealed base-editing rates ranging from approximately 0.5% to 53% and hepatic G6Pase-α activity from 2.4 to 292 units.
Liver microsomal G6Pase-α activity in 53-week-old control (mR83/huR83C; n=14) and 3W-301L-dosed huR83C (n=9) mice averaged 180.1±13.5 and 53.4 ± 17.6 units, respectively.
The range of hepatic G6Pase-α activity in the 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice was 2.6 to 179 units, with positive correlation to base-editing, that ranged from a rate of 0.12% to 36%.

The normal reference ranges for mouse serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) are 90.1 ± 8.1 to 293.4 ± 62.7 U/L, and for mouse serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) are 46.2 ± 5.6 to 239.5 ± 141.2 U/L.

Two mice edited as newborns with a high dose of BEAM-301 (NB-301H-53W) expressed 27 and 41 units of hepatic G6Pase-α activity and exhibited elevated AST (360 and 370 U/L) and ALT (323 and 139 U/L) levels.

Newborn huR83C mice were treated with BEAM-301 at a dose of 1.5 mg/kg (designated 301H), and the phenotype of the NB-301H-dosed mice (n=19) was evaluated at 53 weeks of age using sex-matched wild-type littermates (mR83-53W, n=16) as controls.

Three-week-old huR83C mice were treated with BEAM-301 at a dose of 0.75 mg/kg (designated 301L), and the phenotype of the 3W-301L-dosed mice (n=9) was evaluated at 53 weeks of age using sex-matched mR83-53W and mR83/huR83C-53W littermates (Control-53W, n=14) as controls.

Enzyme histochemical analysis of 53-week-old control mice showed that enzymatically active G6Pase-α was distributed throughout the liver with significantly higher levels in proximity to blood vessels, a pattern similar to that observed at 3 weeks of age.

In 53-week-old 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice, G6Pase-α was distributed throughout the liver but less uniformly, with foci containing markedly higher levels of enzymatic activity and other regions harboring little or no G6Pase-α activity.
H&E staining showed that both 53-week-old control mice and 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice exhibited no hepatic histological abnormalities.
Oil red O staining showed that 53-week-old control mice displayed a variable degree of neutral fat storage, with four out of six control mice displaying high levels of neutral fat storage.

Among the six 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice, only the edited mouse expressing 2.6 units of hepatic G6Pase-α activity showed high levels of neutral fat storage, while the other five edited mice showed little or no hepatic fat storage.
Systemic infusion of BEAM-301 failed to restore renal G6Pase-alpha expression because LNP targeted delivery and editing occurs largely in hepatocytes within the liver.

Restoration of hepatic G6Pase-alpha expression in BEAM-301-edited mice improved nephromegaly, but the absence of gene editing in the kidney suggests renal impairment could continue to develop over time in aged mice.

Retrograde renal vein injection of a rAAV9 vector efficiently targets the kidney cortex and medulla, suggesting retrograde renal vein administration of BEAM-301 to huR83C mice is a potential delivery method.
The study demonstrates durability of normal glucose homeostasis in treated huR83C mice out to 53 weeks of age, irrespective of dosing BEAM-301 shortly after birth or at 3 weeks of age.

Untreated G6pc-/- mice exhibit liver microsomal G6Pase-α background activity ranging from 0.5 to 2.2 units and cannot survive to 8 weeks of age even with glucose therapy. In contrast, 25 rAAV-G6PC1-treated G6pc-/- mice titrated to express less than 5 units (0.8 to 4.1 units) of hepatic G6Pase-α activity all survived the 50-75-week study and maintained glucose homeostasis capable of sustaining 24 hours of fasting.

Ten of the 25 rAAV-G6PC1-treated G6pc-/- mice expressed less than 2 units of hepatic G6Pase-α activity, which is the lower limit of quantification for the G6Pase-α assay. The NB-301H-edited and 3W-301L-edited huR83C mice expressed 2.4 and 2.6 units of hepatic G6Pase-α activity, respectively, and survived to 53 weeks of age.

BEAM-301-edited mice displayed variable levels of hepatic G6Pase-α activity, which resulted in a lack of correlation between levels of hepatic glucose and hepatic G6P/glycogen accumulation. Future studies are required to titrate the effects of varying levels of hepatic G6Pase-α activity on pathways of G6P utilization to resolve this gap.
The huR83C mouse model contains the entire human G6PC1-c.247C > T/ p.R83C coding sequence inserted into the native mouse locus, disrupting endogenous mouse G6pc gene expression.
The huR83C mouse model exhibits a 39% survival rate at 3 weeks of age.
BEAM-301 is an LNP formulation of base-editing reagents used to correct the G6PC1-R83C variant.
Three-week-old huR83C mice were treated with a single systemic administration of BEAM-301 at a low dose (301L) of 0.75 mg/kg.
The biochemical phenotype of 3W-301L-dosed mice (3W-301L-53W) was evaluated at 53 weeks of age using sex-matched mR83-53W and mR83/huR83C-53W littermates (Control-53W) as controls.
Insulin tolerance tests used a reduced insulin dose of 0.25 IU/kg for GSD-Ia mice due to increased insulin sensitivity.

Sample sizes for the 53-week analysis were: Control-53W (n=14 for BMI, n=11 for insulin tolerance, n=12 for ALT/AST, n=6 for histochemistry/H&E), 3W-301L-53W (n=9 for BMI/ALT-AST, n=8 for insulin tolerance, n=6 for histochemistry/H&E), mR83-53W (n=15 for ALT/AST), and NB-301H-53W (n=17 for ALT/AST).
Histochemical analysis of liver G6Pase-α activity and H&E/Oil Red O staining used a scale bar of 100 μm and 20 μm respectively, with statistics performed using a two-tailed unpaired T test.

The huR83C mouse model was generated by inserting a human cDNA encoding the G6PC1-R83C variant into exon 1 of the mouse G6pc gene at the ATG start codon using CRISPR/Cas9 technology in a C57BL/6 background, which created a premature STOP codon in the mouse G6pc exon 1.

The human G6PC1-R83C cDNA insertion was placed under the control of the mouse G6pc promoter/enhancer and carried an additional p.V332L mutation, which retained 81% of wild-type G6Pase-α phosphohydrolase activity in COS1 cells.

Breeding of the mR83/huR83C mice was conducted in a mixed C57BL/6/129S4/SvJaeJ background to improve survival rates compared to the C57BL/6 or 129S4/SvJaeJ backgrounds alone, resulting in mR83, mR83/huR83C, and huR83C/huR83C genotypes.

ABE mRNA and gRNA targeting G6PC1-R83C were co-encapsulated at a 1:1 weight ratio in lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) generated by mixing an acidic aqueous RNA solution with an ethanol solution containing a proprietary ionizable lipid, distearoylphosphatidylcholine, cholesterol, and a lipid-anchored polyethylene glycol from Avanti Polar Lipids. The LNP formulations were dialyzed overnight at 4 °C against 1× Tris-buffered saline (pH 7.4, Teknova 20228), concentrated using 100,000 Da MWCO Amicon Ultra tubes (Millipore Sigma UFC910024), and filtered with 0.2-µm filters (Pall Corporation 4602).

The proprietary ionizable lipid used in the BEAM-301 drug product is discontinued, but commercially available alternatives such as ALC-0315 (Avanti Research 627 890900) or Thermo Fisher Lipofectamine MessengerMax (LMRNA015) can be used for in vitro studies. The specific mRNA and gRNA reagents can be custom purchased from TriLink or Axolabs.

Genomic DNA was isolated from frozen mouse liver tissues homogenized in Dulbecco's phosphate-buffered saline using the MagMAX™ DNA Multi-Sample Ultra 2.0 Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific A36570) and eluted in the corresponding MagMAX elution solution. The isolated genomic DNA was quantified using a Lunatic UV/Vis plate reader and normalized to 20 ng/µl using the MagMAX elution solution.

The huR83C mice were generated in a mixed C57BL/6/129S4/SvJaeJ (C57BL-50/129-50) background by mating heterozygous (huR83C/mR83) mice in 100% C57BL background with wild-type (mR83/mR83) mice in 100% 129S4/SvJaeJ background, followed by mating heterozygous mice in the C57BL-50/129-50 background while avoiding mating progenies from the same litter or breeding cage.

ABE mRNA was synthesized via in vitro transcription from a template plasmid containing a T7 promoter, 5' UTR, base editor open reading frame, 3' UTR, and a 120 polyA tail, using the NEB HiScribe T7 High-Yield RNA synthesis kit (E2040S) with CleanCap AG reagent (N-7113) and complete substitution of N1-methylpseudouridine triphosphate for uridine-5'-O-triphosphate.

Primary human hepatocytes (F00995-P; BioIVT) were seeded at 350,000 cells/well in CP medium (Z99029; BioIVT) on collagen type I coated 24-well plates (356408; Corning) and supplemented with fibroblast cells (EF3003; Kerafast) to generate hepatic co-cultures.

Lentiviral transduction was performed using ultra-purified recombinant lentivirus (Lot 220807LVB01; Vector Builder, Inc) packaging G6PC1 with the c.247C>T mutation at a multiplicity of infection of 40.

Cell transfection utilized MessengerMAX reagent (LMRNA015; ThermoFisher Scientific) co-formulated with base editor mRNA and gRNA at a 3:1 ratio, with cells harvested for genomic DNA 7 days post-transfection.
Genomic DNA samples were normalized to 20 ng/µl using MagMAX DNA Multi-Sample Ultra 2.0 Elution Solution.

Genomic loci were amplified in 25-µl PCR reactions using Q5 2× Hot Start Master Mix (New England Biolabs), 0.5 mM human G6PC1 gene-specific forward and reverse primers, and 2 µl of genomic DNA template.
The forward primer for the genomic G6PC1 site is GGGCATTAAACTCCTTTGGG and the reverse primer is AGTCTCACAGGTTACAGGGA.
The forward primer for the G6PC1-R83C site is GGTTCCATCTTCAGAGGAAG and the reverse primer is CAGGGAACTGCTTTATCA.
Barcoded amplicons were generated in 25-µl PCR reactions using Q5 2× Hot Start Master Mix, 0.5 mM barcode primers, and 2 µl of the prior PCR reaction.
Barcoded amplicons were purified via DNA agarose gel extraction (D4008; Zymo Research Corporation) or by SPRIselect bead cleanup (B23318; Beckman Coulter).
Final clean libraries were quantified using a Qubit 4 Fluorometer (Q33238; Thermo Fisher Scientific) and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq Instrument.
On-target G6PC1 alleles are defined as the sum of 10G_12G edits (sequence 5'-CCAGTATGGGCGCTGTCCAAA-3') and 12G edits (sequence 5'-CCAGTATGGACGCTGTCCAAA-3').

Additional baseedited G6PC1 alleles are defined as the sum of 6G edits (sequence 5'-CCAGTGTGGACACTGTCCAAA-3'), 6G_10G_12G edits (sequence 5'-CCAGTGTGGGCGCTGTCCAAA-3'), and 6G_12G edits (sequence 5'-CCAGTGTGGACGCTGTC-CAAA-3').

Targeted NGS data analysis involved five steps: Illumina demultiplexing, read trimming and filtering, alignment of all reads to the expected amplicon sequence, generation of alignment statistics and quantification of base-edited alleles, and calculation of the frequencies of corrected G6PC1 alleles.
Primary human hepatocytes were harvested from 3 donor livers (BiolVT) and plated on BioCoat Rat Collagen I, 24-well plate (354408; Corning).
BEAM-301 was diluted in INVITROGRO CP media (Z990003; BioIVT) and added to the culture wells at the desired concentration.
At the terminal timepoint of 1 week, cells were harvested and genomic DNA was isolated using the Quick-DNA™ MicroPrep Plus Kit (D4074; Zymo Research).

Animal studies were conducted under protocols approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee at Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development or the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at University of Massachusetts Medical School and CRADL (Charles River Accelerator and Development Lab) in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
Mice were maintained on a standard NIH-31 Open formula mouse/rat sterilizable diet (Envigo) or Prolab IsoPro RMH 3000 diet (labdiet) without any restrictions.
Mice were housed in a 12-hour light/dark cycle with an ambient temperature controlled within 65-75 °F (18-24 °C) and humidity between 40-60%.
Litter sizes were usually reduced to 6-8 pups to reduce feeding competition between littermate pups.
Mice were euthanized by carbon dioxide following the AVMA guidelines for the Euthanasia of Small Laboratory and Wild-Caught Rodents, 2020 Edition.

Genomic DNA was isolated using the Quick-DNA™ MicroPrep Plus Kit (D4074; Zymo Research) following the manufacturer's protocol. Potential off-target sites were identified using ONE-Seq and Digenome-seq.

The Cas-OFFinder software tool was run on the GRCh38/hg38 human reference genome using the protospacer sequence and a relaxed PAM requirement (NNGRRN) to account for PAM preferences of known off-target sites. Sites matching the input pattern with either 7 or fewer mismatches in the targeted DNA and no bulges, or a DNA or RNA bulge (2 bases) and up to 3 mismatches, were enumerated.

A SurePrint Oligonucleotide Library (G7239A; Agilent) was constructed with 14,509 sites based on mismatch parameters and genomic annotation. The ONE-seq assay was performed on this library using a saturating concentration of ribonucleoprotein.

Digenome-seq was performed using human genomic DNA isolated from GM11468, a human B-lymphocyte cell line heterozygous for the G6PC1 c.247C > T allele (Coriell Institute, Camden, NJ), and a saturating concentration of ribonucleoprotein.

rhAmpSeq panels were constructed containing sites nominated from ONE-seq and Digenome-seq, sites identified in silico as low-mismatch sites, and others including the 1 on-target site and 20 negative control sites. Genomic DNA was isolated from primary human hepatocytes treated with BEAM-301 at a concentration at or above the EC90 of on-target editing.

The EC90 was measured in primary human hepatocytes (PHH) that harbor the target site introduced via lentiviral transduction, since healthy human hepatocytes do not harbor the target allele. Multiplex amplicon sequencing via rhAmpSeq (Integrated DNA Technologies) was performed on both treated samples and untreated, donor-matched primary human hepatocytes as controls.

Sequencing reads were trimmed, stitched, aligned to the human genome reference sequence (GRCh38/hg38), and filtered for a minimum base-quality score of 30 and mapping quality of 10. An odds ratio quantifying the enrichment of each observed variant in the treated sample relative to the untreated sample was calculated, and a Fisher's exact test was used to assess statistical significance based on an empirically determined threshold.

BEAM-301 was infused into NB huR83C pups via the temporal vein and into 3W huR83C mice via the retro-orbital sinus. Sex-matched mR83 and mR83/huR83C littermates served as controls, and BEAM-301-dosed huR83C mice did not receive glucose therapy or fasting before euthanasia.

For the fasting glucose test, BEAM-301-treated huR83C and control mice were fasted for 24 hours in clean cages with water access, and blood glucose was measured at 0 and 24 hours using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System. Mouse BMI was calculated by dividing body weight in grams by the square of body length in centimeters, where body length is the distance from the nose tip to the tail base.

For insulin tolerance testing, 301L-treated huR83C and control mice fasted for 4 hours before receiving an intraperitoneal injection of 0.25 IU/kg of sterile insulin (#I1882; Sigma-Aldrich) diluted in PBS. Blood glucose was measured at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 minutes post-injection using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System.

Tissue sections were visualized using the Imager A2m microscope with Axiocam 506 camera and the ZEN 2.6 software from Carl Zeiss. Statistical analyses were performed using the GraphPad Prism Program, version 10.2.2, with two-tailed unpaired T tests and data presented as Mean values ± SEM.

The animal study was performed once, with each animal infused independently with editing reagents, and used the huR83C mouse homozygous for the pathogenic variant G6PC1-R83C. Controls included mR83/mR83 (wild-type) and mR83/huR83C (heterozygote) mice, and untreated huR83C mice with a 3-weeks survival rate of 39% were included in the shorter 3-week study.

All data supporting the findings, including the mRNA encoding the ABE, are available in the Article, Supplementary Information, and Source data file published alongside the paper. Raw sequence reads are available on NCBI under the accession number PRJNA1164309.
Permeabilized microsomes were prepared by incubating intact microsomes in sucrose buffer containing 0.2% sodium deoxycholate for 20 minutes on ice.

Phosphohydrolase assays used 50 µl reaction mixtures containing 50 mM sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 6.5), 2 mM EDTA, 10 mM G6P, and 100-200 µg of permeabilized microsomes, incubated at 30 °C for 10 minutes.
Background non-specific phosphatase activity was estimated by pre-incubating permeabilized microsomes in 20 mM sodium acetate buffer (pH 5) for 10 minutes at 37 °C to inactivate acid-labile G6Pase-α.
One unit of G6Pase-α activity is defined as one nmol G6P hydrolysis per minute per mg microsomal protein, with background values ranging from 0.2 to 2 units subtracted from all data points.
Enzyme histochemical analysis of G6Pase-α was performed on 10 µm thick cryopreserved OCT-embedded tissue sections (Sakura Finetek USA #4583).

Tissue sections were incubated at room temperature for 10 minutes in a reaction buffer containing 40 mM Tris-maleate (pH 6.5), 10 mM G6P, 300 mM sucrose, and 3.6 mM lead nitrate, followed by two washes in 300 mM sucrose solution.
After the initial incubation, tissue sections were treated with 0.09% ammonium sulfide solution for 2 minutes at room temperature to convert trapped lead phosphate to brown-colored lead sulfide.
Images of the tissue sections were captured using an Imager A2m microscope equipped with an Axiocam 506 camera and ZEN 2.6 software (Carl Zeiss).
Blood was collected by cardiac puncture from non-fasted, anesthetized mice and transferred into MiniCollect® TUBE 0.8 ml CAT Serum Separator tubes (#450472, Greiner Bio-one).
Collected blood was allowed to coagulate for 20 minutes, then centrifuged for 10 minutes at 2000 × g to separate serum.
Separated serum was transferred to a new microtube, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80 °C.

Serum samples were coagulated for 20 min, centrifuged for 10 min at 2000 × g, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at -80°C. Serum cholesterol and uric acid were analyzed using Liquid Stable Reagents (#TR13421, #TR24321, ThermoFisher Scientific), Cholesterol/Cholesteryl Ester Assay Kit (#ab65359, ABCAM), or Uric Acid Assay Kit (#ab65344, ABCAM).

Serum L-Lactate was measured using the EnzyFluo™ L-Lactate Assay Kit (#EFLLC-100, BioAssay Systems), the Lactate Assay Kit (#K627-100, BioVision), or the L-Lactate Assay Kit (#ab65331, ABCAM). Serum triglyceride was analyzed using the Serum Triglyceride Determination Kit (#TR0100, Sigma), the Triglyceride Assay Kit (#K622-100, BioVision), or the Triglyceride Assay Kit (#ab65336, ABCAM).

Serum AST and ALT activity were measured using the Enzy-Chrom™ Aspartate Transaminase Assay Kit (#EASTR-100, BioAssay Systems) and the EnzyChrom™ Alanine Transaminase Assay Kit (#EALT-100, BioAssay Systems), respectively.

Liver tissues from non-fasted mice were homogenized in 5% NP-40 solution at a 10:1 ratio (10 µl 5% NP-40 solution per 1 mg of tissue), deproteinized by incubation at 99°C for 5 min, and centrifuged at 17,000 × g for 15 min to remove insoluble materials. Glycogen (#K646-100, BioVision), G6P (#K657-100, BioVision), glucose (#K686-100, BioVision; #ab102517, ABCAM), and lactate (#K607-100, BioVision; #ab65331, ABCAM) in the deproteinized liver lysates were measured using the corresponding kits.
Calculations of glycogen in nmol/mg were based on a glycogen molar mass of 666.5777 g/mol.

Hepatic triglycerides were isolated by homogenizing liver tissues in 5% NP-40 solution at a 10:1 ratio (10 µl 5% NP-40 solution per 1 mg of tissue), heating and incubating at 85°C for 5 min, and cooling to room temperature. This heating/cooling step was repeated once, followed by centrifugation for 15 min at 17,000×g, and triglycerides in the supernatant were measured using the Triglyceride Assay Kit (#K622-100, BioVision) or the Triglyceride Assay Kit - Quantification (#ab65336, ABCAM).

H&E staining was performed on tissues fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin (#08379, Polysciences). Oil Red O staining was performed on cryopreserved OCT (#4583; Sakura Finetek USA) embedded tissues processed according to standard procedures.
Tissue sections were visualized using the Imager A2m microscope with Axiocam 506 camera and the ZEN 2.6 software (Carl Zeiss).
