Raymond Yang and Sneha Gampa performed the lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation, and Faith Musenge, Monique Otero, Edmond Wong, and Zach Howard optimized the in vivo dosing protocol, which are specific procedural steps required for replication.
Kenton Hetrick described the off-target analysis methodology, a specific technical component necessary for replicating the safety and specificity assessment of the gene editing approach.

The Kruskal-Wallis test analysis is statistically insufficient for replication because it lacks the specific effect size and 95% confidence interval, and the study design fails to define the vehicle control formulation or apply covariate adjustment for baseline mutation rates.

The reported mean bystander editing rate of 0.67% and the 1.25% correction rate are uninterpretable for precision assessment because the 95% confidence intervals are omitted from the dataset with n=12 per group.

Replication of the LNP delivery efficacy claims is blocked by the absence of defined vehicle controls and missing uncertainty quantification, which prevents the distinction between the biological mechanism and the effects of the undefined container.
The study fails to specify the software version used for initial demultiplexing, a gap that blocks exact replication of the data processing pipeline.

The CRISPResso2 batch analysis parameters are defined as a quantification window of -w 20 -wc-10 and a minimum quality score of Q>30, but the exclusion of low-quality reads may obscure noise relevant to replication.

The LNP lipid-to-RNP weight ratio is fixed at eight-to-one, but the absence of a solvent-only control means the 40% on-target editing rate cannot be decoupled from the formulation's internalization efficiency.

The study describes an undesired event in Drosophila melanogaster germline genome editing where the template vector used for Homology Directed Repair (HDR) unwantedly inserts into the genome. This deviation occurs at multiple genomic locations, with different HDR vectors, and with multiple genome editing designs.
The authors generated a novel HDR template vector designed to enable the identification and exclusion of animals with undesired vector template genomic insertions.
All relevant data for the study is available within the manuscript and Supporting Information files.
The study was supported by Swiss National Science Foundation grant numbers CRSII3_154455, 31003A_179587, and 320030-232324.

The HDR template plasmid used for Drosophila germline injection contains homology arms flanking the desired edited sequence and an eye expression DsRed selectable cassette to facilitate the identification of edited animals.
The homology arms in the Drosophila HDR template plasmid are approximately 1 kb long.
The study describes a novel and versatile HDR template vector designed to enable 'all-in-one' template plus gRNA sequences single vector HDR genome editing in Drosophila.

The HDR template plasmid contains approximately 1 kb of 5' and 3' sequences homologous to the genomic region surrounding the Drosophila TBPH gene, an artificial replacement exon encoding human hTDP-43, and a DsRed selection cassette, all cloned into the pCR4 plasmid vector.

Two gRNAs targeting sequences in the TBPH neighbouring genes, bgcn and cpes, were designed to induce Cas9 dependent double-strand breaks and were synthesized and inserted into the pCFD3 plasmid for expression in germline cells.

Incorrectly edited hTDP-43 Drosophila lines exhibit the entire HDR template vector sequence inserted into the genome, flanked by sequences matching homology arm 2, which can be detected by genomic DNA PCR using a forward primer in the TBPH 3' end and a reverse primer in the hTDP-43 5' end.

The presence of the undesired pCR4 vector backbone in the genome of incorrectly edited hTDP-43 Drosophila lines can be confirmed by genomic DNA amplification using primers specific for the template pCR4 vector, which are not present in correctly edited lines or controls.

The study identified 18 of 22 Drosophila lines expressing only hTDP-43 and 4 of 22 lines expressing both Drosophila TBPH and hTDP-43, with the latter confirmed by the presence of the entire pCR4 plasmid vector sequence inserted into the genome proximal to Drosophila TBPH and the bgcn gene.

The pCR4 vector insertion occurred at the site of a double-strand break designed by one of the gRNAs, where the PAM sequence on both sides of the insertion was modified to match the edited PAM sequence of the template donor plasmid.

PCR amplification using primers targeting the region between the lac promoter and pUC ori sequence of pCR4 detected pCR4 sequences in 100% (4 out of 4) of incorrectly edited animals but not in background control or correctly edited animals.
The undesired pCR4 template vector insertion was stably inherited across multiple generations, consistent with germline genome insertion.

The HDR donor plasmid pHSG298 was constructed using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder for gRNA design and contains homology arms, the VGAT sequence with an ALFA epitope tag, and an eye DsRed selection cassette.

Genotyping was performed using PCR primers specific for the ALFA tag and VGAT flanking regions outside the HDR homology arms to confirm the presence of the ALFA tag insertion in the 15 recovered genome edited Drosophila lines.

PCR amplification using primers specific for the vector pHSG298 confirmed the incorporation of pHSG298 sequences in 10 of 15 edited Drosophila lines (66.6%), while 5 lines (33.3%) showed no evidence of donor vector insertional events.

The CRISPR/Cas9 plus HDR strategy utilizes two gRNAs to create double-strand breaks between exons 1 and 2 of the VGAT gene, with the pHSG298 vector providing ~1 kb long homology arms flanking the ALFA tag and a removable DsRed cassette.

The Glutamate Receptor IIA (GluRIIA) gene is homozygous viable even in protein null mutants, unlike TBPH and VGAT which are recessive lethal when mutated. The HDR vector used for GluRIIA editing was pCR4, containing homology arms designed to replace two amino acids in exon 12.

Two gRNAs were designed to target exon 12 of the GluRIIA gene, and eye DsRed expression was used to select editing events. Twelve DsRed expressing Drosophila lines were recovered and analyzed by PCR genomic amplification and sequencing, with only one line containing the correct edit confirmed by DNA sequencing.

Eleven incorrectly edited Drosophila lines displayed two peaks in the sequencing chromatogram, indicating the presence of both unmutated GluRIIA nucleotides and the desired modified nucleotides. PCR for pCR4 vector sequences from genomic DNA confirmed that all 11 incorrectly edited lines had pCR4 sequences inserted into their genome.

The pCR4 plasmid template contained the mutated GluRIIA exon 12 and a removable DsRed cassette flanked by approximately 1 kb long homology arms. Agarose gel imaging of genomic DNA PCR amplification using primers specific for pCR4 identified the vector backbone sequence in incorrectly edited GluRIIA Drosophila lines but not in the correctly edited line or controls.

The pVID vector expresses the ZsGreen1 fluorescent protein under the eye P3 promoter only if the vector backbone is incorporated into the genome, allowing for negative selection of vector insertional mutagenic events.

The genome editing experiment on Synapsin used two gRNAs designed with CRISPR Optimal Target Finder and an HDR donor plasmid containing homology arms, a Synapsin sequence with ALFA epitope tags, an eye DsRed selection cassette, and the pVID cloning vector.

The pVID cloning vector contains an Ampicillin resistance gene, a Drosophila U6:3 promoter for gRNA expression, a multiple cloning site (MCS) for the HDR template sequence, and a ZsGreen selection cassette comprising a 3xP3 eye promoter, ZsGreen fluorescent protein coding sequence, and SV40 terminator.

For Synapsin gene editing, the HDR template sequence includes the desired edit and a DsRed cassette selection flanked by two homology arms, plus two gRNAs under the control of the dU6:3 promoter, designed to create double-strand breaks between exons 1 and 2 and after exon 2.

The GluRIIC gene edit utilized an HDR template containing the desired insertion and an eye DsRed selection cassette, resulting in 5 of 6 recovered lines expressing both DsRed and ZsGreen eye expression and 1 of 6 lines expressing only DsRed.

PCR for pVID vector sequences from genomic DNA confirmed that all 8 ZsGreen expressing Synapsin lines and all 5 ZsGreen expressing GluRIIC lines had template vector insertion, while the 8 DsRed-only Synapsin lines and the 1 DsRed-only GluRIIC line showed no evidence of vector template sequences.
The study utilizes a positive selection dsRed cassette and a negative selection ZsGreen cassette to identify and eliminate events where the HDR template vector has inserted into the genome.
Cas9 is expressed in Drosophila germ cells under the nos promoter to enable HDR, with a noted risk that very high levels of Cas9 expression can be toxic.
The precise sequence of the HDR vector does not influence genome integration, as insertion was observed with pCR4, pHSG298, and pVID vectors.
All reagents used in the study are described in Table 2.
The study utilized germline Cas9 expressing animals with the injection stocks nos-cas9 attp2 BL 78782 and nos-cas9 attp40 BL 78781.
The HDR repair templates employed conventional designs with approximately 1 kb flanking homology arms, specifically ranging from 602 bp to 1328 bp as detailed in Table 1.
The gRNA sequences for the hTDP43 HGE, GluRIIA mutation, ALFA-vGat, and ALFA-Synapsin edits are provided in Table 1 with specific off-target counts, GC content, and efficiency scores.

The vector backbones used for the HDR templates were pCR4, pHSG298, and pVID (ZsGreen), with pVID allowing for the exclusion of undesired mutagenic HDR vector insertion events via a DsRed selection cassette.

The cutting distances from the edit site for the gRNAs ranged from 5 bp to 1895 bp, and the gRNA sequences were designed using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder based on conventional on-target and off-target selection criteria.

An average of 54% of the edited lines generated in the five independent HDR procedures had undesired vector insertion, with specific aberrant insertion rates of 18%, 91%, 67%, and 50% for the respective experimental conditions.
The VGAT exon 1-2 intronic HDR edit includes an ALFA tag and a DsRed selection cassette, flanked by approximately 1 kb homology arms, with gRNA sequences listed in Table 1.
The GluRIIA exon 12 HDR construct is assembled in pCR4 via Topo cloning, targeting the beginning of exon 12 and the intergenic region between GluRIIA and GluRIIB, with gRNA sequences in Table 1.
The GluRIIA HDR edit inserts a version of exon 12 followed by the endogenous 3'UTR and a DsRed selection cassette, surrounded by approximately 1 kb homology arms.
The 7ALFA-Synapsin HDR construct in pVID targets the intronic regions between Synapsin exon 1-2 and exon 2-3, with gRNA sequences in Table 1.
The 7ALFA-Synapsin edit includes 7 copies of the ALFA tag and an excisable dsRed selection cassette, flanked by two 600-700 bp homology arms.
The 7ALFA-Synapsin construct places two gRNAs with scaffold sequences interspaced by a tRNA sequence upstream of the edit, synthesized and cloned into pVID by Genscript.
The GluRIIC HDR construct in pVID targets the middle of exon 10 and the intronic region between exon 2 and 3, with gRNA sequences in Table 1.
The GluRIIC HDR edit includes a Myc tag followed by an excisable dsRed selection cassette, flanked by two 600-700 bp homology arms.
The GluRIIC construct places two gRNAs with scaffold sequences interspaced by a tRNA sequence upstream of the edit, synthesized and cloned into pVID by Genscript.

The pVID vector contains a Drosophila eye negative selection cassette with a 3xP3 promoter, ZsGreen fluorescent protein, and SV40 terminator upstream of a dU6:3 gRNA promoter and a multiple cloning site.
The pVID vector full sequence is available via Genbank accession PV446458 and Addgene deposit number 236635.
Transgenic Drosophila melanogaster lines were generated by injecting embryos expressing Cas9 under the nos promoter with the HDR construct and gRNA vectors, performed by Genetivision or FlyORF.

Homology arms, desired edits, and selection cassettes were PCR amplified using Platinum SuperFi II high-fidelity DNA polymerase (Invitrogen) and assembled via HiFi DNA Assembly (Invitrogen). All guide RNAs were selected using the CRISPR Optimal Target Finder tool.

The study utilized the following antibodies: Mouse anti-hTDP-43 (Novus Biologicals, H00023435-M01), Rabbit anti-TBPH (Pierce), Mouse anti-a-tubulin (Sigma, T6199), Goat anti-rabbit (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 111-035-003), and Goat anti-mouse (Jackson ImmunoResearch, 115-035-003).

Reagents included Restore Western Blot Stripping Buffer (Thermo Scientific, 21059), WesternBright Sirius (Advansta, K-12043-D20), DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen, 69504), Micro BCA Protein Assay kit (Thermo Scientific, 23235), GeneJET Gel Extraction kit (Thermo Scientific, K0691), MinElute Reaction cleanup kit (Qiagen, 28204), pCR8/GW/TOPO Cloning Kit (Invitrogen, K250020), Zero Blunt TOPO PCR Cloning Kit (Invitrogen, 450159), and One shot Top10 chemical competent cells (Invitrogen, C404003).

The experimental organisms were Drosophila melanogaster w118 and specific lines with incorrectly edited hTDP-43, mutated GluRIIA exon 12, ALFA tag-VGAT, 7ALFA tag-Synapsin (pVID), and GluRIIC-Myc (pVID).

The gRNA sequences used were: 5' hTDP-43 (GGATAATGTAACCGCTGTAC), 3' hTDP-43 (GGCCGGCATCCACAAGGGTC), 5' GluRIIA (CTGAGCGAAAGGGGCGAGC), 3' GluRIIA (GACTCTAAAGTCTAGACATG), 5' VGAT (GGTGGGTCATTCTCATTA), 3' VGAT (GCCTGCGGAAGATGGATT), 5' Synapsin (GGGCCCCCTTCTGCCAAAGG), 3' Synapsin (GGGTATGCTTTGGCATTGGC), 5' GluRIIC (GCACTCCAATCTCCAGTGTC), and 3' GluRIIC (GGCACCCTTCCCCCCGCTGG).

The primer sequences used were: TBPH 3' forward (GGAACACCGGTTGGTCGAAC), hTDP-43 5' reverse (TTCTCATCCTCGGTCACGCG), pUC forward (CGCGTAATCTGCTGCTTGCAA), ZsGreen forward (GACAGACAACTGGGAGCCTAGTTG), and dU6:3 Re (TGAGTAGGTGGCGTTTCATTCTACTC).
The recombinant DNA vectors pVID and pScarlessHD-DsRed were obtained from Addgene with identifiers 236635 and 64703, respectively.

The hTDP-43 HGE HDR construct was inserted into pCR4 by Topo cloning, with gRNAs targeting the cpes and bgcn genes cloned in pCDF3 vectors, and the edit was surrounded by approximately 1 kb homology arms.

The ALFA-VGAT tagged HDR construct was inserted into pHSG298 by restriction digestion and ligation, with gRNAs targeting the intronic region between VGAT exon 1 and exon 2 cloned in pCFD4 vectors, and the edit was surrounded by approximately 1 kb homology arms.
For immunoblotting, 20 adult Drosophila heads were lysed in RIPA buffer (140 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100, 0.5 mM EGTA, 10 mM Tris-Cl pH 8, 0.1% SDS) and centrifuged at 12000 x g for 1 minute.

Protein concentration was measured using a Micro BCA Protein Assay kit (Thermo Scientific), and 30 μg of protein was loaded onto a 4-12% Tris-Glycine gel (Invitrogen) after mixing with 4x Laemmli buffer and heating at 85°C for 2 minutes.
Protein bands were dry transferred to a PVDF membrane (iblot transfer, Invitrogen) and blocked for 1 hour in 5% milk blocking solution.

The membrane was incubated at 4°C overnight with primary antibodies: anti-hTDP-43 (H00023435-M01, Novus Biologicals, 1:500), anti-TBPH (custom made, Pierce, 1:500), and anti-α-tubulin (T6199, Sigma, 1:10,000).
Secondary antibodies (goat anti-rabbit 111-035-003 and goat anti-mouse 115-035-003, both Jackson ImmunoResearch, 1:10,000) were diluted in blocking solution and incubated for 1 hour.

Chemiluminescent substrate (WesternBright Sirius, Advansta) was used for imaging, and membranes were stripped for 10 minutes at 37°C with Restore Western Blot Stripping Buffer (Thermo Scientific) before re-blocking for consecutive antibody staining.
Genomic DNA from Drosophila lines was purified using a DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen).

PCR was performed using Platinum SuperFi II DNA polymerase (Invitrogen) with a reverse primer (TTCTCATCCTCGGTCACGCG) in the 5' end of the hTDP-43 gene and a forward primer (GGAACACCGGTTGGTCGAAC) in the 3' end of the TBPH gene.

The PCR product was purified using a GeneJET Gel Extraction Kit (Thermo Scientific) and a MinElute Reaction cleanup kit (Qiagen), then cloned into a pCR8 vector using the pCR8/GW/TOPO TA Cloning Kit (Invitrogen) for sequencing.
The study used the nos promoter to express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells, and the authors note that Cas9 concentration could affect vector template integration.
Western blot analysis identified protein size using the Blue Precision Plus molecular weight marker from Bio-Rad.
Agarose gel images for Figs 2D, 2F, 2H, 3C, 4C, and 5D used the SmartLadder molecular weight marker from Eurogentec to identify DNA amplicon size.
The pVID HDR template vector enables the identification of Drosophila genome edited lines with undesired vector integration events using ZsGreen expression.
The product was cloned into a pCR8 vector using the pCR8/GW/TOPO TA Cloning Kit (Invitrogen) and sequenced.
Genomic DNA was purified using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen) for PCR analysis of vector sequences in the Drosophila genome.

PCR primers targeting the lac promoter and pUC ori in pCR4 or pHSG298 plasmid sequences are forward: CGCGTAATCTGCTGCTTGCAA and reverse: TGTCGTGCCAGCTGCATTAATG, yielding an 817 bp band for pCR4 and a 1001 bp band for pHSG298.

PCR primers targeting the region between the zsGreen CDS and the dU6:3 promoter in the pVID vector are forward: 5'-GACAGACAACTGGGAGCCTAGTTG-3' and reverse: 5'-TGAGTAGGTGGCGTTTCATTCTACTC-3', yielding an 813 bp band.
Fluorescence screening for DsRed and ZsGreen eye fluorescence was performed using a fluorescence stereomicroscope (MC165F Leica) equipped with a GFP and dsRed filter.
Images of the fluorescence screening were taken using a fluorescence CCD camera (DFC3000G, Leica).
The study utilized exclusively the nos promoter to highly express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells, a parameter that may affect vector template integration.
The study utilizes the conditional GABAergic synaptic vesicle marker described by Certel, McCabe, and Stowers (2022).
The study employs the upgraded CRISPR/Cas9 tools for tissue-specific mutagenesis in Drosophila described by Koreman et al. (2021).
The study uses the toolkit for converting Gal4 into LexA and Flippase transgenes in Drosophila described by Karuparti et al. (2023).
The study utilizes P-Mediated Transformation vectors for Drosophila as described by Pirrotta (1988).
The study employs the pipeline for precise and efficient genome editing by sgRNA-Cas9 RNPs in Drosophila described by Nyberg et al. (2020).
The study utilizes fluorescent proteins from nonbioluminescent Anthozoa species as described by Matz et al. (1999).
The study utilizes the CRISPR tool kit for genome editing described by Adli (2018).
The study uses high-copy-number and low-copy-number plasmid vectors for lacZ alpha-complementation and chloramphenicol- or kanamycin-resistance selection described by Takeshita et al. (1987).
The study utilizes the CRISPR-based strategy to insert small and large fragments of DNA using short homology arms described by Kanca et al. (2019).
The study employs multiplexed CRISPR technologies for gene editing and transcriptional regulation described by McCarty et al. (2020).
The study utilizes the Drosophila CRISPR/Cas9 toolkit for conditionally manipulating gene expression in the prothoracic gland described by Huynh et al. (2018).
The study employs tRNA-flanked sgRNAs to augment CRISPR applications in Drosophila as described by Port and Bullock (2016).
The study utilizes the expanded toolkit for Drosophila gene tagging using synthesized homology donor constructs for CRISPR-mediated homologous recombination described by Kanca et al. (2022).
The study employs insulated piggyBac vectors for insect transgenesis described by Sarkar et al. (2006).
The study utilizes the Zoanthus sp. green fluorescent protein (ZsGreen) described by Nakamura et al. (2013).
The study uses the GB2sequin file converter for preparing custom GenBank files for database submission described by Lehwark and Greiner (2019).
The methods section omits the exact ionizable lipid identity and the PEG-to-lipid ratio, preventing the definition of a vehicle control and the replication of the 0.67% bystander editing rate.

The LNP study lacks acquisition parameters for off-target detection, specifically sequencing depth and exact CRISPResso2 batch parameters, which prevents verification of whether the reported clean edits are masking low-frequency insertional mutagenesis.

The reported 40% efficiency is a single point estimate lacking a confidence interval, and the analysis is uncorrected for multiple comparisons, creating a data gap that prevents statistical validation of the safety claims.

The exact sample size (n) per group and test statistics are missing from the analysis, which blocks independent statistical verification of the binary safety conclusions drawn from the LNP delivery data.

The study utilized two-tailed unpaired t-tests in GraphPad with data reported as mean ± SEM, but failed to correct for multiple comparisons and omitted reported effect sizes or confidence intervals for the 40% efficiency point estimate.
The animal study was conducted as a single run with n=3 biological replicates per group and two analytical replicates each, creating a sample size too small to detect anything but massive effects.

The reported construct sequences and basic workflow allow reproduction of the design intent, but the lack of specific lipid ratios and raw sequencing files prevents verification of the actual editing outcomes.
The 300-fold efficiency gain is inseparable from the specific SM102 lipid formulation, meaning the biological mechanism of the editor has not been isolated from the delivery vehicle.

The study is unpowered to detect effects other than massive ones due to the use of n=3 biological replicates per group, which blocks the ability to rule out that observed changes are driven by the undefined LNP formulation rather than the editor.

The study's analysis pipeline is not reproducible because raw sequencing reads are missing, preventing verification of the reported 40% efficiency point estimate, 95% confidence intervals, and the statistical treatment of n=3 biological replicates.

The reported mean bystander editing rate of 0.67% and correction rate of 1.25% are statistically uninterpretable due to the absence of raw sequencing data and confidence intervals, blocking any distinction between true off-target events and analytical noise in the Drosophila model.

Adequate safety characterization requires full-genome sequencing depth to distinguish true genomic changes from technical noise, as the current reliance on unverified aggregate metrics lacks the robust baseline needed to judge the 0.67% bystander editing rate.

The 40% editing efficiency claim is an unverified point estimate lacking confidence intervals and per-cell distribution data, which prevents quantifying the risk of unintended edits or distinguishing uniform biological effects from a small fraction of highly edited cells.

Reproduction is blocked by the absence of verified safety data and specific formulation details, which prevents confirmation that the editing outcome is driven by the therapeutic agent rather than the lipid container.

A properly powered, side-by-side study with a fully defined, matched vehicle control is necessary to isolate the biological effect from the delivery mechanism's contribution and distinguish the editor's true activity from background noise or vehicle effects.

documents: The claim that lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encapsulating ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) result in editing-efficiency enhancements larger than 300-fold without detectable off-target edits may not hold if the specific ionizable lipid SM102 and optimized DMG-PEG 2000 concentration are not used, as the study relies on these specific chemically defined formulations for stability and delivery.

The assertion that delivering ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) is safer than using viruses encoding Cas9 and guide RNA is limited by the finding that transient RNP activity does not typically lead to optimal editing outcomes, suggesting that safety advantages may be offset by significantly lower efficacy in standard delivery scenarios.

The potential application of genome editing for the treatment or prevention of common diseases with multifactorial or polygenic causes, such as malignancies or cardiovascular disorders, remains speculative and exceeds the current evidence, which is primarily focused on monogenic diseases.

CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing creates a heterogeneous pool of outcomes including random indels, cytotoxicity, p53 pathway activation, and large chromosomal rearrangements, which limits its reliability for treating multifactorial diseases.

The efficiency of precise repair via homology-directed repair is low compared with non-homologous end joining, particularly in post-mitotic cells such as neurons, which are major cell types of interest for therapeutic applications.

Bystander editing by base editors can lead to unintended genomic changes that hamper therapeutic efficacy, and the potential off-target effects of prime editors have not yet been carefully explored or documented.

Prolonged expression of base and prime editors via viral vectors increases the risk of off-target editing at less-favored genomic sites and increases bystander editing, contradicting the goal of precise, transient gene modification.
There is a non-zero risk of viral genome integration even when non-integrating viral vectors are used, and this risk may be worsened by the deployment of Cas9 nucleases and nickases.

Alternative delivery mechanisms for CRISPR/Cas9, such as virus-like particles, mRNA lipid nanoparticles, and direct ribonucleoprotein delivery, require further refinement to achieve the necessary transient action and rapid degradation.

The hypothesis that insights from Cre recombinase delivery would inform the design of vehicles for ABE8e and PE2 is limited by the distinct physicochemical properties, such as size and charge, between Cre and Cas9-based proteins.

The finding that ABE8e RNP is more stable than ABE8e protein alone is conditional on the single guide RNA being refolded by heating and slow cooling, and further stabilized by the presence of 10% (w/v) sucrose.

The observation that CPP5 did not enhance Cre delivery in the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cell line contrasts with the results in ROSA mT/mG fibroblasts, where only the ANTP peptide modestly improved delivery, indicating that delivery efficiency is context-dependent on the cell type.

The claim that purified RNP offers the most transient and chemically defined delivery modality for CRISPR/Cas9 is limited by the fact that the study's efficacy data is derived from a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration, which may not accurately predict the duration or safety of activity in human clinical applications.

The assertion that virus-like particles (VLPs) offer advantageous activity kinetics similar to RNP is weakened by the unstated limitation that VLPs are not chemically defined, a characteristic that introduces potential confounds regarding manufacturing consistency and clinical application safety.

The reported restoration of visual function in a mouse model using purified ABE and PE RNPs encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles is a finding that may not hold in human patients, as the study lacks real-world human data to validate the efficacy and safety of this specific chemically defined formulation.

The expectation that direct delivery of base- and prime-editor RNPs will create a more defined and clinically relevant formulation is an aspirational claim that exceeds the current evidence, as the study only demonstrates proof-of-concept in a mouse model rather than establishing clinical relevance in humans.

The in vivo efficacy of the CPP5-fusion peptide for delivering Cre recombinase into photoreceptors contradicts its lack of effectiveness in vitro, indicating that the in vitro screening conditions fail to capture the biological factors required for successful delivery in this specific cell type.

The deproteinization of liver tissues via incubation at 99°C for 5 minutes may not fully preserve the integrity of all metabolites or may alter the distribution of labile compounds, potentially affecting the accuracy of the measured concentrations for glycogen, G6P, glucose, and lactate.

The study's statistical conclusions are limited by the fact that the animal study was performed only once, meaning the reported p-values lack the robustness of replicated trials and may not hold under repeated experimental conditions. The findings are further constrained by the use of two-tailed unpaired T tests, which may be less powerful than alternative statistical methods for detecting subtle differences in this specific experimental design.

The generalizability of the findings is restricted because all experiments used the huR83C mouse homozygous for the pathogenic variant G6PC1-R83C, meaning the results may not apply to other GSD-Ia variants or human patients with different genetic backgrounds. The inclusion of untreated huR83C mice as controls in the 3-week study is confounded by their low 3-week survival rate of 39%, which may skew the comparison against treated groups and limit the interpretation of long-term efficacy.

The reported 0.67% bystander editing rate is uninterpretable as a safety metric because the omission of 95% confidence intervals prevents the determination of whether this figure represents a robust precision signal or merely an outlier within the small sample size.

The assertion that the method offers superior safety margins compared to double-strand break approaches is unsupported because the lack of uncertainty quantification on the bystander editing rate prevents a valid statistical comparison of precision between the two mechanisms.

The reported 0.67% bystander editing rate is not reproducible or verifiable without the raw sequencing files and specific bioinformatics parameters from the CRISPResso2 batch analysis, leaving the calculation open to confounding by undefined vehicle variables.

The reported 0.67% bystander rate and overall precision are not robust conclusions because the missing raw sequencing data and unspecified MiSeq Reporter version prevent verification that the demultiplexing software did not introduce the variance, rendering the result methodologically ambiguous.

The standard CRISPResso2 analysis parameters (Q>30, -w 20 -wc-10) do not isolate the delivery variable due to the undefined lipid ratios in the LNP formulation, so the study fails to prove that the medicine itself caused the change rather than the delivery vehicle.

The finding that the CRISPR/Cas9 HDR template vector frequently inserts into the Drosophila melanogaster genome is limited to the specific conventional methods and genomic locations tested, meaning the frequency and occurrence of this undesired event may not hold when using alternative editing strategies, different vector designs, or in other species.

The claim that HDR-based genome-edited animals must be carefully screened to avoid misleading interpretations is a precautionary recommendation that assumes the observed vector integration is a pervasive confound, yet it does not rule out alternative explanations for the observed editing outcomes or establish that this specific vector integration is the sole source of potential misinterpretation in all experimental contexts.

The observation that repair templates integrate into the genome at unintended locations in Drosophila is limited to specific experimental contexts, and the claim that this is a systematic issue may not hold if the frequency or mechanism varies across different species or genetic backgrounds not tested in this study.

The finding that animals carrying unwanted vector template genomic insertions can pass undetected through standard screening procedures assumes that the standard screening methods used are representative of all current practices, and this limitation may not apply if alternative, more sensitive detection methods are employed.

The double-stranded DNA breaks created by guide RNAs and Cas9 in mouse embryonic stem cells, hematopoietic progenitors, human differentiated cell lines, and mouse zygotes carry the potential to induce large deletions or rearrangements of the genomes, representing a significant limitation to the precision of the editing process.

The frequency of undesired mutagenic insertion of the HDR donor plasmid template vector into the Drosophila genome is described as 'alarmingly high' and 'highly frequent,' indicating that standard screening methods may fail to detect these events, which can obscure and confound the analysis of genome-edited animals.

Previous studies identified analogous gene editing problems but did not fully reveal the frequency of these undesired events, suggesting that prior conclusions regarding the safety or accuracy of HDR-directed genome editing in Drosophila may be invalid due to unaccounted for mutagenesis.

The observation that pHSG298 vector sequences were incorporated into the genome in 66.6% of VGAT-edited Drosophila lines suggests that the high rate of unwanted vector integration is not specific to the original gRNAs or the large editing event, but may be a general limitation of the HDR protocol.

The conclusion that the choice of HDR donor vector is not critical relies on a small sample size of only fifteen recovered animals, which limits the statistical power to distinguish between the performance of pHSG298 and pCR4 vectors.

The finding of digressive template vector genomic incorporation in an independent edit of the endogenous Drosophila VGAT gene indicates that this confound may persist across different target genes and gRNA designs, challenging the reproducibility of clean HDR outcomes.

The study reports a high rate of undesired insertional mutagenesis, with 4 out of 22 humanised hTDP-43 Drosophila lines (18%) exhibiting incorrect insertion of the template vector backbone, which limits the reliability of the 'all-in-one' single vector HDR approach.

The identification of correctly edited humanised hTDP-43 Drosophila relies on DsRed eye expression, a selection method that may not distinguish between precise ORF replacement and the insertion of the entire vector backbone, thereby confounding the assessment of editing fidelity.

The use of gRNAs targeting sequences in the TBPH neighbouring genes bgcn and cpes to induce Cas9-dependent double-strand breaks introduces a confound where off-target effects or complex rearrangements in these adjacent regions could contribute to the observed genomic instability and incorrect template integration.

The study found that 18% of the generated Drosophila lines expressed both Drosophila TBPH and human hTDP-43, indicating that the CRISPR-Cas9 editing event failed to knock out the endogenous gene in a significant subset of animals.

The authors conclude that the entire pCR4 HDR editing template plasmid vector inserted into the genome at the site of the designed double-strand break, a conclusion that relies on the assumption that the observed PAM sequence modifications are the sole cause of the insertion rather than a secondary effect of the repair process.

The finding that the undesired template vector insertion is inherited stably across multiple generations is consistent with germline genome insertion, but this observation does not rule out other mechanisms of stable inheritance or epigenetic silencing that might affect the phenotype in subsequent generations.

The pVID vector relies on the assumption that the ZsGreen1 expression under the eye P3 promoter is exclusively indicative of vector backbone incorporation, a condition that may not hold if the promoter exhibits leaky expression or if the fluorescent protein is expressed through alternative, non-insertional mechanisms.

The use of Mini-white as a negative selection marker is limited by its prior evaluation as a template vector negative selection marker, which may not fully account for confounds such as background fluorescence or selection pressure artifacts that could lead to false positives in identifying vector insertional mutagenic events.

The conclusion that pVID allows successful identification and exclusion of undesired vector insertion events is based on small sample sizes (8 lines for Synapsin and 6 lines for GluRIIC), limiting the statistical power to generalize the method's reliability across broader experimental contexts.

The finding that ZsGreen expression perfectly correlates with vector backbone insertion (8/8 and 5/5) may not hold if the ZsGreen cassette is lost through subsequent mutations or if the insertion occurs in a genomic context that silences the 3xP3 eye promoter.

The claim that DsRed-only lines lack vector sequences relies on PCR detection limits; low-level or truncated vector integrations that do not amplify with the specific primers used could be missed, meaning the exclusion of undesired events is not absolute.

The high frequency of anomalous template donor vector insertion observed in the GluRIIA editing experiment suggests that the HDR-based genome editing strategy is unreliable for generating precise single-nucleotide mutations, as 11 out of 12 recovered lines contained the entire pCR4 vector backbone rather than the intended edit.

The finding that 11 incorrectly edited lines contained both unmutated and modified GluRIIA nucleotides indicates a confound where the selection for DsRed expression may have biased the recovery of lines with undesired vector incorporation, challenging the assumption that heterozygous selection prevents such artifacts.

The observation of vector backbone insertion in 11 out of 12 lines implies that the specific experimental conditions, including the use of a pCR4 plasmid with a DsRed cassette and two gRNAs targeting exon 12, are prone to generating mosaic or chimeric genomes that exceed the intended scope of the genetic modification.

The finding that pVID vectors allow the successful identification and exclusion of undesired mutagenic HDR vector insertion events is limited to templates containing a visible marker, as HDR donor vectors without such markers integrate into the genome at high frequencies but are much harder to detect.

The conclusion that the precise sequence of the HDR vector does not influence genome integration is based on a limited observation of only three vector backbones (pCR4, pHSG298, and pVID), which may not generalize to all possible vector designs.

The high frequency of undesired vector insertion (54%) observed in Drosophila germline genome editing relies on specific experimental conditions, including the use of conventional ~1 kb flanking homology arms and specific germline Cas9 expressing animals, meaning the results may not hold for alternative HDR designs or different host organisms.

The gRNAs for the hTDP-43 HDR construct targeted neighboring genes cpes and bgcn with the unstated limitation that this strategy risks off-target effects or unintended disruption of these adjacent genes, despite the stated intent to preserve their amino acid sequences.

The ALFA-VGAT tagged HDR construct relied on a DsRed selection cassette for identification, which introduces a confound where the observed phenotype may be attributable to the presence of the DsRed protein rather than the ALFA tag or the specific genomic insertion.

The use of a single computational tool, CRISPR Optimal Target Finder, to select all gRNAs represents a methodological limitation that may not account for all potential off-target sites or chromatin accessibility issues in the Drosophila genome.

The study's findings regarding HDR vector insertion are limited to experiments using Cas9 expressed under the nos promoter in Drosophila germ cells, and it remains untested whether different Cas9 promoters or expression levels would alter the frequency of undesired backbone vector integration.

The hypothesis that single-guide RNA strategies might reduce undesired HDR donor vector insertion is explicitly stated as untested by the authors, meaning the evidence does not support the claim that this method avoids the confound of vector integration.

The authors acknowledge that other unexamined factors, such as the linearization of the HDR vector template, may enable undesired vector backbone insertion, suggesting that the observed integration events are not fully explained by gRNA efficiency alone.

The requirement to generate many additional lines to select for desired edits due to common HDR template vector insertion represents a significant practical limitation and labor cost that undermines the efficiency of the proposed CRISPR/Cas9-based HDR genome editing approach.

The reliance on the DsRed selection cassette for identifying edited cells in the VGAT and GluRIIA constructs introduces a potential confound, as the presence of the fluorescent marker does not guarantee the successful integration of the specific ALFA tag or exon 12 sequence.

The use of homology arms of only 600-700 bp for the Synapsin and GluRIIC edits represents a limitation compared to the ~1 kb arms used for other constructs, which may reduce the efficiency or fidelity of the homology-directed repair process.

The generation of Drosophila melanogaster lines depends on the successful co-expression of Cas9 under the germ cell specific nos promoter and the injected HDR construct, meaning that any variability in the promoter's activity or the injection efficiency could limit the proportion of viable transgenic offspring.

The use of the nos promoter to express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells presents a limitation because the resulting Cas9 concentration could influence the integration of the vector template, potentially confounding the observed results.

The finding that pVID vector backbone sequences integrate into the Drosophila genome during homology-directed repair is a specific failure mode that may not hold under conditions where Cas9 concentration is lower or where alternative repair pathways are favored.

The study's findings on template vector integration are limited to Drosophila melanogaster germline genome editing and may not apply to other model organisms or cell lines where similar procedures could produce the same undesired outcome.

Because all five analyzed Drosophila lines used two gRNAs and a removable DsRed selection cassette, the observed vector integration may be specific to these experimental conditions and might not hold for lines produced with different numbers of gRNAs or different selection markers.

The exclusive use of the nos promoter to express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells introduces a confound, as the Cas9 concentration itself could influence vector template integration, meaning the results might not hold under different expression levels.

Attributing the observed 40% on-target editing rate or 0.67% residue to the LNP vehicle alone is an unsupported assumption rather than a finding, as the absence of a solvent-only control prevents the isolation of the delivery mechanism from the editor's activity within the acquisition pipeline.

The assertion that the delivery bottleneck, rather than the editor's intrinsic activity, was the primary historical barrier is overstated because the experimental design fails to decouple the mechanism from the delivery vehicle, leaving open the possibility that the observed effects are driven by the formulation's internalization efficiency rather than the editor's biological function.

The claim that the gene-editing tool is safe is unsupported because the potential for the delivery container to cause unwanted changes has not been ruled out, creating a confound that prevents definitive safety conclusions for human use.

Speculating that the missing confidence intervals on the 40% rate reflect strategic intent is an alternative explanation that exceeds the evidence, as statistical reporting practices are independent of employment status and the data gap is better characterized as a methodological deficiency.

The assertion that the LNP work solves the delivery bottleneck is overstated because the missing formulation variables mean the 40% efficiency and 0.67% bystander rates remain confounded, failing to isolate the vehicle's contribution from the editor's activity and leaving the safety profile unresolved.

The claim that the in vivo LNP delivery bottleneck is solved is undermined by the absence of covariate adjustment for baseline mutation rates, which leaves the undefined control formulation as the primary alternative explanation for the observed changes rather than the editor itself.

The claim of a 300-fold efficiency gain for the gene editor is currently inseparable from the specific SM102 lipid formulation, meaning the observed results may be an artifact of lipid-membrane interaction rather than the biological mechanism of the editor itself.

The undefined control formulation, specifically the missing ionizable lipid and PEG ratios, renders the vehicle control indistinguishable from the treatment group, creating a confound that prevents decoupling the editing efficiency from the LNP delivery vehicle.

The omission of specific ionizable lipid identity and lipid-to-RNP weight ratios makes the acquisition pipeline non-reproducible, preventing verification of whether the reported outcomes are driven by the editing machinery or by lipid-membrane interaction artifacts.

The absence of raw sequencing files prevents verification of the reported 40% efficiency point estimate and 95% confidence intervals, leaving it unconfirmed whether the effect sizes are statistically valid or if multiple comparisons were uncorrected in the n=3 biological replicate dataset.

The aggregate off-target metrics reported in the text cannot be confirmed as genuine biological signals rather than analytical artifacts, as the absence of raw sequencing reads and specific guide design parameters prevents an independent analyst from re-running the pipeline to verify that the precision is not a result of specific analysis settings.

The absence of per-cell distribution data prevents distinguishing a uniform biological effect from a small fraction of highly edited cells, so the therapy cannot be considered safe based on aggregate metrics alone.

The high editing efficiency achieved by the lipid delivery vehicle does not confirm treatment safety because the lack of verified safety data and specific formulation details prevents confirmation that the medicine, rather than the lipid container, is driving the observed results.

Replication is hindered by the disagreement on raw data availability and the lack of exact SM102 ratio controls, leaving researchers comparing aggregate metrics against undefined baselines without the specific inputs needed to isolate the biological effect from the delivery mechanism.

Felgner ${ }^{(1)}{ }^{4} \&$ Krzysztof Palczewski ${ }^{(1)}{ }^{1,3,16,17}$ Delivering ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) for in vivo genome editing is safer than using viruses encoding for Cas9 and its respective guide RNA. However, transient RNP activity does not typically lead to optimal editing outcomes. Here we show that the efficiency of delivering RNPs can be enhanced by cell-penetrating peptides (covalently fused to the protein or as excipients) and that lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encapsulating RNPs can be optimized for enhanced RNP stability, delivery efficiency and editing potency. Specifically, after screening for suitable ionizable cationic lipids and by optimizing the concentration of the synthetic lipid DMG-PEG 2000, we show that the encapsulation, via microfluidic mixing, of adenine base editor and prime editor RNPs within LNPs using the ionizable lipid SM102 can result in in vivo editing-efficiency enhancements larger than 300-fold (with respect to the delivery of the naked RNP) without detectable off-target edits. We believe that chemically defined LNP formulations optimized for RNP-encapsulation stability and delivery efficiency will lead to safer genome editing.

Monogenic diseases arise from genetic mutations that lead to aberrant or absent gene expression, and many lack appropriate therapies. Advances in molecular biology have enabled several treatment approaches to address this unmet medical need and correct the molecular basis of inherited diseases. Gene augmentation therapy, for example, delivers a wild-type (WT) copy of a mutated gene via a viral vector to supplement expression ${ }^{1}$. However, gene augmentation is limited by several major shortcomings, including potential loss of expression over long periods, lack of endogenous gene regulation, the inability to package large transgenes ${ }^{2}$ and low efficacy when treating mutations that act in a dominant manner ${ }^{3,4}$. An alternative approach to gene augmentation is genome editing. By correcting the genomic mutation in situ, a one-time treatment could be curative for the lifetime of the patient ${ }^{5,6}$. Of the gene editing techniques, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR/Cas9) editing has shown great promise and has advanced to clinical trials ${ }^{7}$. While these early trials have focused on treating monogenic diseases, it is possible to envision the application of genome editing for the
treatment or prevention of common diseases with multifactorial or polygenic causes, such as malignancies ${ }^{8,9}$, cardiovascular disorders ${ }^{10}$ or neurodegenerative diseases ${ }^{11}$.

The CRISPR/Cas9 system used in gene editing trials consists of a Cas9 nuclease that is targeted to a genomic site by a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM) and guide RNA that focuses the binding of Cas9 on a 20-bp-long DNA protospacer ${ }^{12}$. While CRISPR/ Cas9 is easily programmed by the substitution of the guide RNA, the double-stranded DNA cleavage mediated by the nuclease can lead to a heterogeneous pool of editing outcomes, namely random insertions and deletions (indels) by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), as well as cytotoxicity, p53 pathway activation, and large chromosomal irregularities and rearrangements ${ }^{7}$.Moreover, the efficiency of precise repair via homology-directed repair with a donor DNA template is low compared with NHEJ, especially in post-mitotic cells ${ }^{13}$, including major cell types of interest such as neurons.

of precise repair via homology-directed repair with a donor DNA template is low compared with NHEJ, especially in post-mitotic cells ${ }^{13}$, including major cell types of interest such as neurons. Two alternatives to genome editing with CRISPR/Cas9 nucleases are base and prime editors, which fuse a DNA effector domain to a partially inactivated Cas9 domain, termed a Cas9 nickase ${ }^{14-16}$. These modifications combine the ease of programmability of CRISPR/Cas9 with the precision and direct chemistry of the effector domain of the base or prime editor, while avoiding NHEJ and cytotoxicity caused by double-stranded DNA breaks ${ }^{17}$. Thus, the purity of editing outcomes is much greater for base and prime editors; because the DNA-repair mechanisms that enable base and prime editing are cell-cycle independent, the high editing efficiencies are maintained in post-mitotic cell types when genome editing is performed in vivo ${ }^{18}$. CRISPR/Cas9 strategies, and base and prime editing in particular, are suitable approaches for dominant-negative diseases through correction of the pathogenic allele ${ }^{19,20}$. However, bystander editing by base editors is a concern ${ }^{21}$, as it could lead to unintended changes and hamper the therapeutic efficacy for the patient ${ }^{21}$. As well, the potential off-target effects of prime editors have not yet been carefully explored and documented.

As well, the potential off-target effects of prime editors have not yet been carefully explored and documented. One major hurdle that limits the application of base and prime editors is appropriate and efficient delivery of these editing constructs. The current standard for delivery of gene therapy and gene editing constructs is via viral vectors. However, the net size of the guide RNA constructs along with the base or prime editors exceeds the packaging limits of most commonly used viral vectors, such as lentiviruses (LV) and adeno-associated viruses (AAVs); indeed, base and prime editors delivered by AAV often are split into two viral vectors ${ }^{22}$. In addition, while these viral vectors have been engineered to be less immunogenic than their native counterparts, they still express base and prime editors over a sustained period ${ }^{23}$. Whereas the intended 'on-target' site is favoured thermodynamically to be edited, prolonged expression of base and prime editors leads to an increased risk of off-target editing at less-favoured sites on the genome and transcriptome ${ }^{24}$, either in a Cas9-dependent ${ }^{25}$ or in an effector-dependent manner ${ }^{26,27}$. Prolonged exposure to base editors has been also shown to increase bystander editing ${ }^{28}$. Lastly, there is a non-zero risk of viral genome integration, even when non-integrating viral vectors are used ${ }^{29}$, and this risk could even be worsened by the deployment of Cas9 nucleases and nickases ${ }^{30,31}$. Thus, as sustained expression of CRISPR/Cas9 is unnecessary and only risks unintended editing outcomes, CRISPR/ Cas9 should be delivered in a transient manner and rapidly degraded thereafter. Multiple ways of achieving this transient action have been proposed, such as by virus-like particle (VLP) delivery ${ }^{28,32,33}$, mRNA lipid-nanoparticle (LNP) delivery ${ }^{34}$ and by direct ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, either as naked RNP or as a lipoplex with cationic lipid reagents such as Lipofectamine $2000{ }^{35-38}$. Such a variety of approaches has the potential to fine-tune the duration of activity of CRISPR/Cas9 machinery; however, these alternative delivery mechanisms require further refinement.

Conceptually, delivery of preassembled RNPs offers the most rapid onset and the shortest duration of genome editor activity in the cell. Real-world human data for AAV-mediated delivery of retinal pigment epithelium-specific 65 kDa protein (RPE65) by voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) show that the therapeutic effect may be maintained for 7 years and potentially longer, demonstrating sustained expression of the transgene delivered by AAV ${ }^{39}$. Protein expression after subretinal delivery of mRNA was detected within 4 h and lasted for up to 7 days ${ }^{40}$. In the case of RNP, the purified protein is complexed with synthetic guide RNA before direct delivery into cells, thus bypassing the requirement of transcription (AAV, LV) and translation (AAV, LV, mRNA). VLPs that have RNP encapsulated in a viral shell offer the same advantageous activity kinetics as RNP; however, they are not chemically defined, which may complicate their manufacturing and clinical application. Use of purified RNP thus offers the most transient and chemically defined delivery modality for CRISPR/Cas9.

Previously, we reported the successful correction of the causative mutation in the rd12 mouse model of Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) through delivery of an adenine base editor (ABE) via $\mathrm{LV}^{41}, \mathrm{AAV}^{42}$ and engineered virus-like particles (eVLP) ${ }^{28}$. Likewise, we recently delivered prime editor (PE) via eVLP and achieved effective and precise correction of the rd12 mutation ${ }^{43}$. However, we expect that we can create a more defined, clinically relevant formulation of CRISPR/Cas9-based genome editor through optimization of direct delivery of base- and prime-editor RNPs. Here, following a screening of cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) and commercially available ionizable cationic lipids with acid disassociation constants $\left(\mathrm{p} K_{\mathrm{a}}\right)>6$, we show the restoration of visual function in a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration using purified ABE and PE RNPs encapsulated in lipid nanoparticle LNPs. The potential for therapeutic benefit from administered proteins hinges upon successful delivery across cellular membranes. A number of agents have been demonstrated to enhance intracellular delivery of genome-editing proteins and RNPs, including CPPs. Accordingly, we genetically fused three different CPPs (TAT, CPP5 and ANTP) ${ }^{44-47}$ to the N terminus of Cre recombinase and ABE8e-SpCas9-NG (hereafter referred to as ABE8e), which recognizes the NG PAM (Fig.1a). To facilitate purification, we also fused the 1D4 peptide tag ${ }^{48}$ to the C terminus of ABE8e and the prime editor protein, PE2 (Fig. 1a). Although Cre recombinase and Cas9-based genome-editing proteins possess distinct physicochemical properties, such as size and charge, we hypothesized that insights from the study of intracellular delivery of Cre recombinase would inform the design of delivery vehicles for ABE8e and PE2.

We first purified Cre recombinase to homogeneity, with or without the N-terminal CPP fusion, through nickel metal-affinity chromatography (Ni-NTA) chromatography (Fig. 1b) and size exclusion chromatography (SEC, Fig. 1c), and confirmed the purity of the product through sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) visualized with Coomassie brilliant blue (CBB) (Fig.1d) and anti-Cre western blot (Fig. 1e). ABE8e was similarly purified through affinity chromatography on TALON metal (Fig. 1e) and 1D4 (Fig. 1f) affinity columns and completed with SEC (Fig. 1g); purity was again assessed by SDS-PAGE with CBB staining and anti-Cas9 western blot (Fig. 1h,i). PE2 was purified in a similar manner as ABE8e, with an additional heparin chromatography step after 1D4 immunoaffinity to maximize separation from impurities (Fig. 1j). We noted that ABE8e after immunoaffinity chromatography still contained contaminating nucleic acids and aggregates; these contaminants were removed effectively by SEC (Fig. 1k). We also noted that ABE8e RNP was more stable than ABE8e protein alone, as determined by differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF), especially when the single guide RNA (sgRNA) was refolded by heating and slow cooling (Fig. 1l and Supplementary Fig. 1a-f). The ABE RNP was further stabilized by 10\% (w/v) sucrose. Similar to ABE8e, the PE2 RNP complex with an engineered prime-editing guide RNA (epegRNA) was more stable than PE2 protein alone; however, heat refolding of epegRNA had no additional effect on PE2 RNP stability (Fig. 1m and Supplementary Fig. 1g,h). PE RNP did not require sucrose to remain soluble. For consistency, we heat refolded all sgRNAs and epegRNAs used throughout the study. We also assessed the enzymatic activity of our ABE8e and PE2 RNPs through in vitro activity assays to ensure our proteins maintained activity following purification. ABE8e RNP displayed high levels of activity as assessed by an in vitro deamination assay (Fig. 1n,o), and PE2 RNP similarly displayed high levels of activity as assessed by an in vitro reverse-transcriptase extension assay (Fig.1p,q).

CPPs enable efficient delivery of Cre in vitro and in vivo. We first assessed the delivery of Cre recombinase into the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cultured cell line (colour switching, 'CS') for a rapid and convenient fluorescent readout of intracellular protein delivery. The CS reporter cell line expresses green fluorescent protein (GFP) constitutively, while a stop codon upstream of red fluorescent protein (RFP) gene prevents its expression. Upon delivery of Cre, floxed GFP-STOP is excised, enabling RFP expression in place of GFP (Fig. 2a). As a positive control, we delivered Cre recombinase as a lipoplex with Lipofectamine 3000 to confirm the specificity of this cell line, reaching up to 40\% conversion of the cells (Fig. 2b). Cre recombinase alone induced low but detectable (up to 4.4\%) colour switching from GFP to RFP, indicating an ability of unmodified Cre recombinase to cross cell membranes (Fig. 2b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2a,b). TAT- and ANTP-CPPs resulted in enhancement of Cre delivery (up to 28\% and 45\%, respectively), while the CPP5-CPP did not (Fig. 2b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2a,b). We also delivered Cre as a non-covalent complex with CPP peptide 6×His-CM18-PTD4 (ref. 49), which increased the delivery of Cre to ~6\% and synergistically enhanced the delivery efficiency of CPP-fused Cre proteins (Fig. 2b,d, and Supplementary Figs. 3a,b and 4a,b). Next, we delivered Cre into ROSA mT/mG mice, a global fluorescent reporter strain for monitoring Cre recombinase activity ${ }^{50}$. All cells from the ROSA mT/mG mouse constitutively express membrane-targeted tdTomato from the Rosa26 locus, while a polyadenylation stop signal prevents the expression of enhanced GFP (eGFP). When Cre recombinase is introduced to the cells, the tdTomato and stop signals are excised, enabling eGFP expression (Fig. 2e). We isolated and cultured primary ROSA mT/mG fibroblasts and demonstrated that Cre recombinase delivered alone resulted in low tdTomato to eGFP conversion, while Cre protein delivered by Lipofectamine 3000 resulted in higher conversion (Fig. 2f,g). In contrast to the results with the CS line, only the fused ANTP peptide modestly improved delivery of Cre recombinase to the ROSA mT/mG fibroblasts (Fig. 2f,g). When injected subretinally into ROSA mT/mG mice to evaluate in vivo activity (Fig. 2h), the positive controls, AAV1-CMV-Cre and eVLPs packaging Cre protein, mediated efficient tdTomato to eGFP conversion mainly in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), with occasional and scarce eGFP observed in photoreceptors, as detected by two-photon excitation (Fig. 2i,j). Scale ## Discussion Genome-editing technologies have opened new avenues in gene therapy, offering potential strategies for addressing both genetic and non-genetic diseases ${ }^{6,59,60}$. Simultaneously, the rapid advances in genome editing have illuminated the critical necessity for precise, safe and efficient delivery systems. Traditionally, vectors including AAV and LV have been the standard approaches in this domain. However, a growing body of evidence highlights intrinsic limitations associated with these vectors. For AAV vectors, one limitation is their constrained packaging capacity. AAVs can typically accommodate genomes ~4.7 thousand base pairs long, which can be restrictive, especially when attempting to deliver larger genome-editing constructs such as base editing and prime editing systems ${ }^{61-63}$. This limitation necessitates either the truncation of essential elements, less active homologues, or the use of dual-vector strategies, which can reduce efficiency and increase complexity. Lentiviral vectors, while accommodating larger genetic payloads, have concerns related to their integration into the host genome ${ }^{64}$. Such integrations, although ensuring long-term expression, can disrupt endogenous genes or regulatory elements, leading to potential genotoxicity ${ }^{65-67}$. Unintended insertions can also potentially activate oncogenes or deactivate tumour suppressor genes, escalating the risk of malignancies ${ }^{68,69}$. Moreover, both AAV and lentiviral vectors can induce immune responses ${ }^{70-74}$. The pre-existing immunity to certain AAV serotypes in the population can render AAV-mediated therapies less effective or even elicit adverse immune reactions and prevent redosing ${ }^{72}$. Similarly, lentiviral vectors can trigger cellular immune responses against transduced cells, impacting the longevity and efficacy of the therapeutic intervention. These challenges underscore the necessity to explore alternative delivery systems that can bypass the constraints and risks associated with AAV and LV. Consequently, non-viral delivery methods such as LNPs, silica nanocapsules, eVLPs and RNP delivery have been developed ${ }^{28,35,40,75-81}$. A major advantage of the approach we propose here is the pharmacologically defined formulation of the RNP LNPs, which offer the most transient exposure to genome-editing agents. One of the primary concerns centres on the low concentration of the active macromolecule. Furthermore, the lipid content, which exceeds the weight of the ribonucleoprotein complex by approximately eight times, could pose potential translational challenges in non-human primates or humans, and optimization of the LNP to increase payload delivery without inducing immune response may be required. Overall, optimizing the formulation of LNPs and their characteristics is of paramount importance for enhancing delivery efficiency, especially for challenging target tissues such as the RPE. The RPE has specific structural and physiological attributes that can impact the effectiveness of LNP-mediated delivery. Reducing the size of LNPs has been highlighted as a potential strategy to enhance their uptake by cells. Smaller nanoparticles, typically below 100 nm in diameter, have been shown to be more readily internalized by cells, possibly due to more efficient endocytosis ${ }^{86}$. For the RPE, with its tight junctions and unique phagocytic role, smaller LNPs may offer better uptake and retention to maximize LNP delivery. Enhancing the functionality of LNPs is another potential approach ${ }^{79}$. Incorporating specific ligands or targeting moieties that recognize and bind to receptors on the RPE cells could improve LNP uptake ${ }^{8}$. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of peptides and small molecules that target RPE-specific receptors and increase the internalization of nanoparticles ${ }^{77,88}$. By tailoring the surface properties and composition of LNPs, it could be feasible to exploit the unique biology of the RPE to enhance delivery.

Despite the challenges with the LNP delivery system, our study presents encouraging functional outcomes. While the observed editing efficiency of Rpe65 in rd12 mice was lower than previously reported, a noteworthy restoration of retinal function was evident, as demonstrated by the ERG recordings. Several factors potentially underlie this functional improvement despite the modest genomic correction. A mechanism to consider is the interplay between mRNA transcribed from the corrected Rpe65 allele and that from the mutant Rpe65 allele harbouring a nonsense mutation. It is well established that mRNA molecules containing premature termination codons are often subjected to nonsense-mediated decay, a surveillance pathway that degrades aberrant mRNA transcripts ${ }^{89}$. Thus, mRNA transcribed from the mutant Rpe65 allele could be selectively targeted and degraded by the nonsense-mediated decay pathway, leading to its reduced levels in the RPE. Concurrently, mRNA derived from the corrected Rpe65 allele would remain stable and accumulate, effectively compensating for the diminished mutant transcript levels. However, additional experiments are needed to correlate functional Rpe65 mRNA levels with the zygosity of corrected alleles of Rpe65 in rd12 mice.

Supporting evidence from our previous investigation provides additional insight into the functional implications of our current findings. In a previous study, we characterized a novel animal model, the RPE65-P2A-CreERT2 knock-in mouse. Remarkably, the homozygous knock-in mice, despite expressing RPE65 at levels amounting to only 1-5\% of their WT counterparts, exhibited ERG responses that were nearly indistinguishable from the WT mice ${ }^{90}$. The editing in our current study also resulted in the partial restoration of vision-dependent outcomes, such as the pupillary light reflex and V1 and SC responses, which are all dependent on visual input to the brain. This observation suggests that achieving high levels of RPE65 correction and expression would not be required for fully restoring retinal function, but a low yet stable level of RPE65 could suffice to produce clinically relevant outcomes. In essence, while the genomic-correction efficiencies mediated by ABE or PE LNP could be further optimized, restoration of retinal function could be achieved at low editing rates. The nuanced interplay between genomic editing, mRNA stability and functional restoration provides a compelling rationale for achieving even modest genomic corrections with strategically targeted editors, as they could bring about meaningful therapeutic benefits.

Clarifying these mechanisms is crucial for enhancing delivery efficiency. The discrepancies in the delivery efficiencies of Cre, ABE and PE within our study suggests that optimizing the size of the encapsulated protein, the overall diameter of the LNP, the length of the guide RNA and the surface charge of the protein are crucial factors for improving delivery efficiency. We and others previously showed the potential of RNP delivery via eVLP, lipoplex or RNP with Lipofectamine-type cationic lipids. Here we have described chemically defined and adjustable LNPs that are highly reproducible and stable. Although the RNP LNPs will require additional optimization, including fully quantitative characterization of encapsulation efficiency, before advancing to good manufacturing practice production for non-human-primate and human trials, our approach offers major safety and manufacturing advantages. Future endeavours should focus on refining the LNP formulation to enhance delivery and editing efficiency, particularly to target tissues selectively while also seeking a deeper understanding of the functional consequences of genome editing. There is also a need to develop novel ionizable lipids that would efficiently deliver the RNP with reduced risk of inflammation. Chou ${ }^{\boldsymbol{(} \boldsymbol{1})}$ Glycogen storage disease type-la patients, deficient in the G6PC1 gene encoding glucose-6-phosphatase-α, lack blood glucose control, resulting in life-threatening hypoglycemia. Here we show our humanized mouse model, huR83C, carrying the pathogenic G6PC1-R83C variant displays the phenotype of glycogen storage disease type-la and dies prematurely. We evaluate the efficacy of BEAM-301, a formulation of lipid nanoparticles containing a newlyengineered adenine base editor, to correct the G6PC1-R83C variant in huR83C mice and monitor phenotypic correction through one year. BEAM-301 can correct up to ~60\% of the G6PC1-R83C variant in liver cells, restores blood glucose control, improves metabolic abnormalities of the disease, and confers long-term survival to the mice. Interestingly, just ~10\% base correction is therapeutic. The durable pharmacological efficacy of base editing in huR83C mice supports the development of BEAM-301 as a potential therapeutic for homozygous and compound heterozygous glycogen storage disease type-la patients carrying the G6PC1-R83C variant.

Glycogen storage disease type-la (GSD-Ia; MIM232200), also known as von Gierke disease, is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency in glucose-6-phosphatase-α (G6Pase-α or G6PC1) that is expressed primarily in the liver, kidney cortex, and intestine ${ }^{1-3}$. G6Pase- $\alpha$ catalyzes the hydrolysis of glucose-6-phosphate (G6P) to glucose, which is released into the blood to maintain eugly-cemia. A prevalent pathogenic variant identified in Caucasian GSD-la patients is G6PC1-c.247C > T/p.R83C (hereafter referred to as G6PC1-R83C), which accounts for 32\% of sequenced alleles in patients, and results in severe hypoglycemia due to lack of G6Pase- $\alpha$ enzyme activity ${ }^{4}$. Consequently, GSD-Ia patients, including individuals who harbor the G6PC1-R83C variant, manifest a metabolic phenotype of impaired glucose homeostasis, characterized by fasting hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly, nephromegaly, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, lactic acidemia, and growth retardation ${ }^{1-3}$. Current dietary therapies ${ }^{5-7}$ can enable GSD-la patients to maintain a normalized metabolic phenotype but require strict adherence, making it challenging for patients to maintain glycemic control. In addition, dietary therapies do not address the underlying pathological processes and long-term complications, hepatocellular adenoma/carcinoma (HCA/HCC) and renal disease still occur in metabolically compensated patients ${ }^{1-3,8}$. Gene therapies that address liver G6Pase- $\alpha$ deficiency offer an opportunity
to reduce disease burden and improve the quality of life for GSD-la patients.

A phase III clinical trial for GSD-Ia (NCT05139316) using a recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV) vector ${ }^{9-12}$ to deliver a normal G6PC1 gene is currently in progress. While a promising therapy, there is insufficient data to understand if lifelong episomal transgene expression can be maintained at a therapeutic level in humans ${ }^{13,14}$, and many patients have pre-existing antibodies to the rAAV vector ${ }^{15,16}$, making them ineligible for treatment. Conversely, therapeutic gene editing strategies that correct specific disease-causing mutations within the endogenous G6PC1 gene are anticipated to be durable. Two CRISPR/ Cas9-based gene editing strategies have been demonstrated in vivo to correct the GSD-la phenotype in a homozygous knock-in mouse model, G6pc-R83C ${ }^{17,18}$. One was a homology directed repair (HDR) ${ }^{19,20}$ strategy utilizing AAV to deliver the editing reagents to neonatal G6pcR83C mice ${ }^{17}$. The second was a non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) ${ }^{19,20}$ strategy utilizing lipid nanoparticles (LNP) ${ }^{21,22}$ to deliver the editing DNA oligonucleotides to 2- to 4-week-old G6pc-R83C mice ${ }^{18}$. Both studies showed that the edited G6pc-R83C mice survived to adulthood without suffering hypoglycemic seizures. The prevalent pathogenic G6PC1-c.247C > T/p.R83C variant contains a single $\mathrm{G}>\mathrm{A}$ transition mutation on the complementary strand that can be targeted by the adenine base editors (ABEs) that enable the programmable conversion of A•T to G•C in genomic DNA, and in principle could be used to precisely correct this mutation ${ }^{24-29}$. In this study, we evaluate the efficacy of a newly-engineered ABE to correct metabolic defects associated with GSD-Ia in a humanized mouse model. Messenger RNA encoding the ABE and guide RNA targeting the G6PC1-R83C variant were encapsulated in a LNP ${ }^{21,22}$ formulation hereafter referred to as BEAM-301 and delivered via a single systemic administration either in newborn (NB) mice within 48 hours post birth or at 3 weeks (3W) of age. BEAM-301 at both a high dose (301H, 1.5 mg/kg) and a low dose (301 L, 0.75 mg/kg) were evaluated, and the outcomes monitored to 53 weeks of age. We show that the efficiency of correcting the G6PC1-R83C variant correlates with the activity of hepatic G6Pase- $\alpha$ restored in the edited mice. Moreover, the edited mice harboring $\geq 3$ units of hepatic G6Pase- $\alpha$ activity displayed an improved metabolic profile, sustained 24 hours of fasting, and survived long-term (through 1 year). In contrast, untreated littermates expressed negligible hepatic G6Pase- $\alpha$ activity and exhibited fasting hypoglycemia, with a 3-week survival rate of 39\%. Significantly, no decline in hepatic G6Pase- $\alpha$ activity was observed over the 53-week study. In summary, we have developed a base-editing strategy for in vivo correction of a pathogenic G6PC1 variant in the native genetic locus, that may offer a durable and highly efficient therapeutic for patients with GSD-la.

Consistent with this, of the 42 untreated huR83C mice studied, only 16 (39\%) survived to age 3 weeks. ## Base editing strategy for correction of G6PC1-R83C Genetic correction of the pathogenic human G6PC1-R83C (G6PC1-c.247C > T) variant requires the conversion of an A:T base pair to a G:C base pair. To target this allele, a guide RNA was designed with an saCas9 'NNGRRT' protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM), with target adenine (noted at position 16 in Fig. 1a). The base-editor used harbors an saCas9 nickase domain and a TadA deaminase domain engineered to maximize editing of the target adenine and reduce editing of bystander adenines ${ }^{26}$. Base-editing for correction of the G6PC1-R83C allele was first confirmed in vitro using primary human hepatocytes (Supplementary Fig. 2). Subsequently, the guide RNA and messenger RNA encoding the base-editor were co-formulated into an LNP to generate BEAM-301, an investigational base-editing therapy for GSD-la patients who harbor the G6PC1-R83C variant. Editing at the target adenine corrects the c.247C > T/p.R83C variant back to wild-type c.247C/p.R83. There are two neighboring bystander adenine bases at positions 18 and 22 (Fig. 1a). An edit at position 18 introduces a synonymous variant while an edit at position 22 introduces a nonsynonymous p.Y85H variant.

The encoded protein, G6Pase$\alpha$, is embedded within the endoplasmic reticulum membrane of primarily liver and kidney cortex ${ }^{1-3}$. Previous rAAV-mediated G6PC1 gene augmentation studies have shown efficacy in preclinical models of GSD-Ia ${ }^{9-12}$ and have been translated into an ongoing phase III clinical trial (NCT05139316). However, there is insufficient data to determine the long-term durability of an episomal-based gene therapy in the liver ${ }^{13,14}$. Gene editing may offer a more durable therapy. To date, both a CRISPR/Cas9-based HDR strategy ${ }^{17}$ and a CRISPR/Cas9-based NHEJ strategy ${ }^{18}$ have been evaluated in a mouse model of GSD-la carrying a prevalent GSD-la variant, G6PC1-p.R83C. While both strategies were capable of relieving symptoms of the disease, the editing efficiencies of both approaches were less than $2 \%^{17,18}$. In the present study, baseediting was explored as a precise targeting strategy ${ }^{24-29}$ to correct the G6PC1-p.R83C variant. In summary, we have generated a murine model of GSD-la expressing the human G6PC1-R83C transcript and shown that the huR83C mice manifest a phenotype of impaired glucose homeostasis mimicking human GSD-Ia. This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, #### Abstract CRISPR/Cas9 based genome editing employing Homology Directed Repair (HDR) from template vector sequences is a widely used technique to enable precise insertions, deletions or modifications to genes. Here, we describe an undesired and highly frequent editing event when using conventional CRISPR/Cas9 plus HDR methods for Drosophila melanogaster germline genome editing. We find that the template vector employed for HDR repair unwantedly and commonly inserts into the genome. We observe this deviation from the desired edit at multiple genomic locations, with different HDR vectors and with multiple genome editing designs. To avoid these events, we have generated a novel HDR template vector that enables animals with these undesired insertions to be identified and excluded. Our results suggest that HDR based genome edited animals must be carefully screened for unwanted vector template genomic integration in order to avoid misleading interpretations of genome editing outcomes.
