CRISPR gene-editing technology allows researchers to make precise modifications to genomic DNA. In Drosophila, a cornerstone model organism in genetics, we and others use CRISPR to introduce targeted breaks into the genome alongside a molecular template that serves as a blueprint for repair, enabling specific, designed genetic changes to be introduced. During our experiments, we identified a frequent and previously underappreciated problem: the repair template molecule itself was routinely integrating into the genome at unintended locations. This occurred across multiple genes, template designs, and editing strategies, indicating a systematic issue rather than a one-off anomaly. The consequences

The field was revolutionized by the employment of the clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)/Cas9 system, derived from prokaryotic immunity, which enables the precise targeting and subsequent modification of genes [3]. The system forms the basis to create many types of genetic modifications, for example, insertions, deletions, or substitutions in genes of interest, with improved ease, speed, and accuracy [4]. CRISPR/Cas9 based genome editing relies upon guide RNAs (gRNAs) to direct the endonuclease Cas9 protein to a target DNA sequence, leading to the introduction of double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs) [5]. The cell can then repair these DSBs by either nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) or homologydirected repair (HDR). NHEJ ligates nonhomologous DNA ends, which if occurring erroneously, can induce either insertions or deletions (indels) [6]. HDR on the other hand, uses a DNA template from a homologous DNA strand to repair DSBs [7]. Providing an exogenous 'template' sequence for HDR, commonly delivered from a plasmid vector, enables exploitation of the HDR process to create specific genome insertions, deletions or other nucleotide modifications, when these changes are introduced into the exogenous HDR template. The adaptability of the approach has enhanced the popularity of CRISPR/Cas9 as a technique for germline genome editing in model organisms [8] including Drosophila melanogaster [9]. Germline genome editing in Drosophila employing HDR is most frequently carried out by germline injection of a HDR template plasmid, which contains homology arms flanking the desired edited sequence, together with plasmids expressing one or more gRNAs designed to induce DSBs in the targeted locus. To induce recombination, Cas9 is introduced in the germline either via transient expression from a plasmid or using transgenic animals stably expressing Cas9 (Fig 1) [10]. Successfully edited animals can then be identified by molecular screening (e.g., PCR), phenotypic alterations or selectable markers [10]. While there are many advantages to the use of CRISPR/ Cas9 based genome editing compared to other available methods, several studies have also revealed drawbacks of the technique. In mouse embryonic stem cells, hematopoietic progenitors and human differentiated cell lines, the DSBs created by guide RNAs and Cas9 have the potential to induce large deletions or rearrangements of the genomes [11]. Analogous gene editing problems have been previously identified [13-18], however, the frequency of these undesired events was not fully apparent. However, we additionally found that 18\% (4 out of 22) of the lines we generated expressed both Drosophila TBPH and human hTDP-43 (Fig 2B and 2C). To understand how this unwanted outcome could occur we investigated these lines further. We began by designing a forward primer in the Drosophila TBPH gene and a reverse primer for the hTDP-43 gene in an attempt to amplify the region between these genes. Using genomic DNA generated from Drosophila lines expressing both hTDP-43 and TBPH as a template, we amplified a ~10 kb product that was not present in unedited animals or in animals where the editing event had occurred correctly (Fig 2D). We then sequenced this product and discovered that, in addition to including genomic sequences flanking Drosophila TBPH, it also included the entire pCR4 plasmid vector sequence, indicating that the entire pCR4 HDR editing template plasmid vector had inserted into the genome of these animals (Fig 2E). This insertion occurred proximal to Drosophila TBPH in the region between TBPH and the nearby gene bgcn. We examined the precise sequence where both the 5' and 3' gRNAs were designed to target in this sequence. We found that the donor vector had inserted into the genome at the location where a DSB was designed to have been induced by one of the gRNAs. At this location, on both sides of the insertion, the PAM sequence of the target region was modified to match the edited PAM sequence of the template donor plasmid consistent with this being the insertion point of the vector sequence. From this, we conclude that the entire template vector has inserted into the genome at the site where a DSB was designed to be induced by one of the gRNAs. To determine if the HDR donor vector sequence was present in all incorrectly edited animals, we designed primers to amplify the region between the lac promoter and pUC ori sequence of pCR4. Using these primers, we found that 100\% (4 out of 4) of incorrectly edited animals, i.e., where Drosophila TBPH and hTDP-43 were both expressed, had pCR4 sequences inserted into their genome. No product could be amplified from the genomic DNA derived from back-ground control or correctly edited animals (Fig 2F). Thus, in these anomalously edited animals, we observed an undesired incorporation of the entire HDR donor vector into the genome. We also observed that the undesired template vector insertion could be inherited stably in animals across multiple generations consistent with germline genome insertion.

Selection markers are widely used in yeast, mice and Drosophila to detect exogenous sequence insertional events [13-15,33,34]. As we wished to continue to use a DsRed piggyBAC selection cassette [23] to identify successful editing events (and subsequently 'scarlessly' remove it after successful edit identification), we sought to incorporate an additional selection marker into the HDR template backbone to identify and exclude vector insertional mutagenic events from subsequent analysis. Mini-white [35] is a commonly used selectable marker in Drosophila, and in addition to eyes absent selection, has previously been evaluated as a template vector negative selection marker [36]. We decided to design a vector using a completely exogenous gene for negative selection with a bright selection marker that would be easy and quick to score independently of endogenous eye color. We designed a HDR template cloning vector to produce expression of ZsGreen1 [37], a very bright green fluorescent protein, under the eye P3 promoter [38] only if the vector backbone becomes incorporated into the genome. We dubbed this vector pVID - Vector Insertion Detector (Fig 5A).

Here we describe the highly frequent undesired insertion of the donor template vector into the genome in experiments designed to alter genes based upon homology directed repair. We observed this unwanted insertional mutagenesis in five fully independent HDR procedures utilising Drosophila germline genome editing. Looking across the totality of the genome edits described here, an average of $54 \%(\mathrm{n}=71)$ of the edited lines we generated had undesired vector insertion, revealing the high frequency of a phenomenon previously described qualitatively in other reports [17,18]. The procedures we employed to design our HDR edits were not unusual. gRNA sequences were designed using CRISPR Optimal Target Finder based on conventional on-target and off-target selection criteria [22] (Table 1). The germline Cas9 expressing animals we employed are also widely used [26]. Our HDR repair templates utilised conventional design with ~1 kb flanking homology arms together with the sequence to be inserted or edited including mutated PAM sequences [9]. HDR donor vectors that do not include a visible maker also integrate into the genome at high frequencies but are much harder to detect [17]. Integration of the HDR template is a major issue for subsequent analysis of edited animals, potentially giving rise to misleading results. For example, if the genome edit has not occurred as designed but is falsely indicated as correct, by genomic PCR from the integrated vector, results may be misinterpreted. Alternatively, mutagenic integration of the vector sequence may cause phenotypes not attributable to the designed edit. Unexpected insertions have previously been observed during CRISPR/Cas9 based mouse genome editing, at a rate of 10\% when targeting individual genomic sites with more than one gRNA, compared to 4\% when targeting individual genomic sites with a single gRNA [12]. In our experiments, we speculate that one of the gRNAs we designed to target a gene has a lower efficacy leading recombination to only occur at one gRNA site instead of two, causing a single homologous recombination event and insertion of the vector template into the locus. Indeed, it has been reported that gRNAs can have differing levels of efficiency which can affect editing throughput [43,44]. It is possible, but untested by us, that HDR strategies based upon the use of a single guide RNA might reduce undesired HDR donor vector insertion [17,45] though perhaps at the cost of efficiency [46].

t is possible, but untested by us, that HDR strategies based upon the use of a single guide RNA might reduce undesired HDR donor vector insertion [17,45] though perhaps at the cost of efficiency [46]. It is also possible that other factors, besides the efficiency of the gRNAs, enable undesired vector backbone insertion. One possibility is that the HDR vector template becomes linearised at some frequency which could facilitate insertion into the genome. Linearised templates are becoming increasingly employed in the field of CRISPR/Cas9 in several models, due to increased efficiency of editing [45,47,48]. However, it is noteworthy that during HDR germline editing of mice, insertion of linear HDR template sequences has also been observed, not just in one copy but in several head-to-tail copies [49]. These insertions were shown to be produced by both HDR and NHEJ, or in some cases, a combination of both mechanisms. Similar mechanisms could be compatible with the insertion events that we observe. Therefore, both with linear and circular templates, it is important to remain vigilant by including controls for undesired vector template insertions. Consistent in all of our experiments is also the fact that we express Cas9 in the Drosophila germ cells under the nos promoter to enable HDR to occur. It is possible that other Cas9 sources, such as Cas9 driven by a different promoter, or at a lower or higher expression level, could influence the insertion of the backbone vector though very high levels of Cas9 can be toxic [50].

In order to improve efficiency of HDR-mediated genome editing in our laboratory, we now routinely use two selection cassettes, a positive selection (subsequently removable) dsRed cassette to indicate an editing event has occurred and a negative selection ZsGreen cassette to eliminate events where the HDR template vector has inserted into the genome. We would suggest that others using similar approaches might consider the same, which unfortunately, since HDR template vector insertion is as we describe common, requires the generation of many additional lines to select only those that have the desired edit. Ultimately however, it would be desirable to understand more about the factors that lead to undesired HDR vector genomic integration, in order to design strategies to avoid this unwanted, labor adding and detrimental outcome of CRISPR/Cas9 based HDR dependent genome editing. ## Materials and methods All reagents used in this study are described in Table 2. ## Plasmid construction

Images were taken using a fluorescence CCD camera (DFC3000G, Leica). ## Limitations of the study We note that while we observed the insertion of the template vector using three different vector template backbones, there were still similarities between the five different Drosophila lines we analysed in this paper. For example, in all lines, two gRNAs and a removable DsRed selection cassette were employed. In future experiments it would be beneficial to investigate the possible presence of template vector in lines which have been produced by a different number of gRNAs using a different selection marker. We also tested for undesired insertional mutagenesis only during Drosophila melanogaster germline genome editing and not in other model organisms or cell lines where, given similar procedures, this undesired outcome could also potentially occur. In addition, we used exclusively the nos promoter to highly express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells, and it is possible that the Cas9 concentration could affect vector template integration. ## Supporting information

documents: The encapsulation of adenine base editor and prime editor ribonucleoproteins within lipid nanoparticles using the ionizable lipid SM102 resulted in in vivo editing-efficiency enhancements larger than 300-fold relative to the delivery of the naked ribonucleoprotein.
The lipid nanoparticle formulation using the ionizable lipid SM102 achieved the 300-fold enhancement in in vivo editing efficiency without detectable off-target edits.
In the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cell line, Lipofectamine 3000-delivered Cre recombinase achieved up to 40% conversion, while unmodified Cre recombinase induced up to 4.4% color switching from GFP to RFP.

TAT-Cre and ANTP-Cre fusions enhanced Cre recombinase delivery to 28% and 45% respectively in the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cell line, whereas CPP5-Cre did not enhance delivery compared to unmodified Cre recombinase.
Non-covalent complexation of Cre recombinase with the CPP peptide 6×His-CM18-PTD4 increased Cre recombinase delivery to approximately 6% in the HEK293-loxP-GFP-RFP cell line.

In the rd12 reporter cell line, adenine base editing via plasmid transfection of ABE8e with a validated rd12 sgRNA restored eGFP expression, quantified by next-generation sequencing at 22% and by flow cytometry at 32%.
The addition of 10% w/v sucrose to the ABE8e RNP mixture boosted delivery efficiency, which was further enhanced 1.5-fold by the addition of the non-covalent 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide.
The 6×His-CM18-PTD4 peptide modestly improved the delivery efficiency of the PE2 RNP by approximately 1.6-fold when delivered with 10% sucrose, although overall efficiencies remained low.
Fused CPP peptides did not enhance the delivery of ABE or PE in vitro, in contrast to their effect on Cre recombinase delivery.

Real-world human data for voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) show that the therapeutic effect of AAV-mediated delivery of retinal pigment epithelium-specific 65 kDa protein (RPE65) may be maintained for 7 years and potentially longer.
Protein expression after subretinal delivery of mRNA was detected within 4 hours and lasted for up to 7 days.
The study utilized commercially available ionizable cationic lipids with acid disassociation constants (pKa) greater than 6.

Size exclusion chromatography (SEC) of ABE and PE proteins was performed relative to standards consisting of blue dextran (2,000 kDa), thyroglobulin (670 kDa), γ-globulin (158 kDa), ovalbumin (44 kDa), myoglobin (17 kDa), and vitamin B12 (1.35 kDa).
Averaged (n=3) differential scanning fluorimetry (DSF) profiles were generated for ABE with guide RNA in PBS containing 10% (w/v) sucrose and for PE with guide RNA in PBS.

The ABE RNP LNPs exhibited a hydrodynamic diameter between 200 and 250 nm, measured by dynamic light scattering. The lipid mixture utilized a molar ratio of 50:10:38.5:1.5 for ionizable lipid, DSPC, cholesterol, and DMG-PEG 2000, respectively.
Ionizable lipids SM102, CL4H6, and DODMA were selected for their pKa values of 6.68, 6.25, and 6.59, respectively, to ensure protonation at pH 6.0 for ABE RNP incorporation.
SM102 LNPs achieved a conversion efficiency nearing 100% in rd12 reporter cells, with as little as 20 nM ABE RNP (4.5 μg ml⁻¹) eliciting nearly total conversion.

The study reported only aggregate editing efficiency and omitted the distribution of edited alleles across individual cells, preventing determination of whether functional rescue stems from a small fraction of highly edited photoreceptors or broad, low-level editing.

The methods section specified ionizable lipid and PEG ratios for experimental groups but left the vehicle control formulation undefined, creating a critical gap for interpreting the Kruskal-Wallis results.

The cryo-EM imaging characterization is restricted to the 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 SM102 formulation, leaving the particle size distribution for the 1.5% variant and the vehicle control arms entirely uncharacterized. This missing structural data creates a confounding variable where aggregation kinetics differences between the 1.5% batch and the control could independently alter ERG results, independent of gene-editing efficiency.

The reported bystander editing rate of 0.67% is presented without accompanying uncertainty quantification, preventing a statistical comparison of safety margins against the double-strand break approach. This lack of interval estimation means the study cannot currently demonstrate that the method is cleaner than the alternative, limiting the interpretation of the vision restoration signal to preliminary evidence rather than a confirmed therapeutic advance.

Evaluation of guide-RNA-dependent off-target editing in primary human hepatocytes identified only one intronic off-target site, with an integrated risk analysis determining that an edit at this site is unlikely to impact associated gene function.

Systemic infusion of BEAM-301 failed to restore renal G6Pase-alpha expression because LNP targeted delivery and editing largely occur in hepatocytes within the liver, although restoration of hepatic G6Pase-alpha expression in BEAM-301-edited mice improved nephromegaly.
Treated huR83C mice demonstrated durable normal glucose homeostasis out to 53 weeks of age, regardless of whether BEAM-301 was dosed shortly after birth or at 3 weeks of age.
Liver microsomal G6Pase-α background activity in 3-week-old untreated G6pc-/- mice varies from 0.5 to 2.2 units. Untreated G6pc-/- mice cannot survive to 8 weeks of age even under glucose therapy.

In a study of 25 G6pc-/- mice titrated with rAAV-G6PC1 to express <5 units (0.8 to 4.1 units) of hepatic G6Pase-α activity, all subjects survived the 50-75-week study and maintained glucose homeostasis capable of sustaining 24 hours of fasting. Ten of the 25 treated G6pc-/- mice expressed <2 units of hepatic G6Pase-α activity, which is the lower limit of quantification of the G6Pase-α assay.
NB-301H-edited and 3W-301L-edited huR83C mice expressed 2.4 and 2.6 units of hepatic G6Pase-α activity, respectively, and survived to 53 weeks of age while withstanding a fast.

Transient expression assays in COS1 cells showed that the phosphohydrolase activity of the G6Pase-α-V332L variant retained 81% of wild-type G6Pase-α activity. The difference in phosphohydrolase activity between huG6Pase-α-wildtype and huG6Pase-α-V332L was not statistically significant.

The study utilized a mixed C57BL/6/129S4/SvJaeJ (C57BL-50/129-50) background for huR83C mice, achieved by mating heterozygous mice in 100% C57BL background with wild-type mice in 100% 129S4/SvJaeJ background.
Primary human hepatocytes were seeded at a density of 350,000 cells per well in a 24-well plate and incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2.
Lentiviral transduction was performed at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 40 to introduce the G6PC1 c.247C>T mutation into primary human hepatocytes.
MessengerMAX transfection reagent was co-formulated with base editor mRNA and gRNA at a 3:1 ratio to transfect cell cultures, with genomic DNA harvested at 7 days post-transfection.
The ONE-seq library comprised 14,509 sites selected based on mismatch parameters and genomic annotation. The ONE-seq assay was performed using a saturating concentration of ribonucleoprotein.

Digenome-seq was performed on human genomic DNA isolated from the GM11468 human B-lymphocyte cell line, which is heterozygous for the G6PC1 c.247C > T allele, using a saturating concentration of ribonucleoprotein.

Multiplex amplicon sequencing via rhAmpSeq was performed on primary human hepatocytes treated with BEAM-301 at a concentration at or above the EC90 of on-target editing, with untreated donor-matched primary human hepatocytes serving as controls. Sequencing reads were filtered for a minimum base-quality score of 30 and a mapping quality of 10.

An odds ratio quantifying the enrichment of each observed variant in the treated sample relative to the untreated sample was calculated, and a Fisher's exact test was used to assess statistical significance based on an empirically determined threshold.
Genomic DNA samples were normalized to 20 ng/µl, and targeted amplicon sequencing was performed using 25-µl PCR reactions with 0.5 mM primers and 2 µl genomic DNA template.
On-target G6PC1 alleles were defined as the sum of 10G_12G and 12G edits corresponding to the sequences 5'-CCAGTATGGGCGCTGTCCAAA-3' and 5'-CCAGTATGGACGCTGTCCAAA-3', respectively.

Additional baseedited G6PC1 alleles were defined as the sum of 6G, 6G_10G_12G, and 6G_12G edits corresponding to the sequences 5'-CCAGTGTGGACACTGTCCAAA-3', 5'-CCAGTGTGGGCGCTGTCCAAA-3', and 5'-CCAGTGTGGACGCTGTC-CAAA-3', respectively.

Targeted NGS data analysis comprised five steps: Illumina demultiplexing, read trimming and filtering, alignment to the expected amplicon sequence, generation of alignment statistics and quantification of base-edited alleles, and calculation of the frequencies of corrected G6PC1 alleles.

For the autosomal recessive disorder GSD-Ia, the G6PC1 allele frequency represents the combined frequency of heterozygous and homozygous allelic corrections, where a single allele correction in a cell is required to restore wild-type function.

Off-target editing analysis utilized primary human hepatocytes harvested from 3 donor livers, which were plated on BioCoat Rat Collagen I 24-well plates and treated with BEAM-301 for a terminal timepoint of 1 week.
A Fisher's exact test was used to assess statistical significance based on an empirically determined threshold for the treated sample relative to the untreated sample.
Mice were housed in an ambient temperature controlled within 65-75 °F (18-24 °C) and a humidity level between 40-60%.
The size of the mouse litter was usually reduced to 6-8 pups to reduce feeding competition between littermate pups.
Key animal welfare endpoints included a weight loss of > 20%, a body condition score of 1 (out of 5), and a pain score of 3 or 4 (out of 4).

The statistical analyses were two-tailed unpaired T tests performed using GraphPad Prism version 10.2.2, with data presented as Mean values ± SEM and significance denoted by * for p<0.05 and ** for p<0.005.
The animal study was performed once, with each animal infused with editing reagents independently to represent an independent outcome within the experiment.
All experiments used huR83C mice homozygous for the pathogenic variant G6PC1-R83C, with mR83/mR83 (wild-type) and mR83/huR83C (heterozygote) mice included as controls.
In the shorter 3-week study, untreated huR83C mice with a 3-week survival rate of 39% were included as controls.

BEAM-301 was infused into NB huR83C pups via the temporal vein and into 3W huR83C mice via the retro-orbital sinus. Sex-matched mR83 and mR83/huR83C littermates were used as controls for the BEAM-301-dosed huR83C mice.

For the fasting glucose test, BEAM-301-treated huR83C and control mice were fasted for 24 hours with free access to water, and blood glucose was measured at 0 and 24 hours using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System. The mouse BMI was calculated by dividing body weight in grams by the square of body length in centimeters, where body length was measured from the nose tip to the tail base.

For insulin tolerance testing, 301L-treated huR83C and control mice were fasted for 4 hours and received an intraperitoneal injection of 0.25 IU/kg sterile insulin. Blood glucose was measured at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 minutes post-injection using the HemoCue Glucose 201 System.

Phosphohydrolase assays used 50 μl reaction mixtures containing 50 mM sodium cacodylate buffer (pH 6.5), 2 mM EDTA, 10 mM G6P, and 100–200 μg of permeabilized microsomes incubated at 30 °C for 10 min. The background of non-specific phosphatase activity varied from 0.2 to 2 units in the lysates and was subtracted from all data points.

Enzyme histochemical analysis of G6Pase-α was performed on 10 μm thick tissue sections incubated at room temperature for 10 min in a reaction buffer containing 40 mM Tris-maleate (pH 6.5), 10 mM G6P, 300 mM sucrose, and 3.6 mM lead nitrate. The tissue sections were subsequently incubated for 2 min at room temperature in 0.09% ammonium sulfide solution to visualize trapped lead phosphate as brown colored lead sulfide.

Blood samples were transferred into MiniCollect® TUBE 0.8 ml CAT Serum Separator tubes, allowed to coagulate for 20 min, and then centrifuged for 10 min at 2000 × g. The resulting serum was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at -80°C.

The reported 0.67% bystander editing rate is currently unverifiable due to missing raw sequencing files and specific CRISPResso2 batch analysis inputs, preventing an assessment of whether the calculation holds without confounding vehicle variables.

The study's central finding that LNP delivery restores vision is confounded by undefined vehicle controls and a complete absence of uncertainty quantification, leaving safety margins and human translation unestablished.

The CRISPResso2 pipeline uses a quantification window of -w 20 -wc-10 and a minimum quality score of Q>30, but the unspecified demultiplexing software version and undefined lipid ratios in the LNP formulation prevent the isolation of the delivery variable from formulation artifacts.

The reported 300-fold efficiency gain is confounded by the exclusion of low-quality sequencing reads and reliance on a specific ionizable lipid formulation, which fails to isolate the biological mechanism from the LNP delivery vehicle. The alternative hypothesis that the LNP delivery vehicle drives the observed editing rather than the biological mechanism remains untested due to the lack of variable isolation.
The current evidence supports only a proof-of-concept in a mouse model, with no quantitative data provided to validate efficacy beyond this specific animal system.

The 40% on-target editing rate is confounded by the fixed LNP lipid-to-RNP weight ratio of eight-to-one, which lacks a solvent-only control. This specific acquisition parameter introduces a massive confound, meaning the observed editing rate could be an artifact of the formulation's internalization efficiency rather than the editor's intrinsic activity.

The DSBs created by guide RNAs and Cas9 in mouse embryonic stem cells, hematopoietic progenitors, and human differentiated cell lines have the potential to induce large deletions or rearrangements of the genomes.
Undesired large deletions and insertions have been observed during mouse zygote genome editing.
The study observed that HDR vector template insertion occurs to an alarmingly high degree with multiple template vectors in Drosophila.
In a study of 15 genome-edited Drosophila animals, 10 lines (66.6%) showed incorporation of pHSG298 vector sequences, while 5 lines (33.3%) showed no evidence of a donor vector insertional event.

The study reports that 4 out of 22 humanised hTDP-43 Drosophila lines (n=4) resulted in an incorrect insertion of the template vector backbone, compared to 18 lines (n=18) where the TBPH gene was correctly replaced by hTDP-43.

Genomic DNA PCR using a forward primer in the TBPH 3' end and a reverse primer in the hTDP-43 5' end produced a product of approximately 10 kb from incorrectly edited hTDP-43 Drosophila, which was not present in genomic DNA from Drosophila controls or correctly edited lines.
Western blotting identified 18 of 22 Drosophila lines where only hTDP-43 was expressed and Drosophila TBPH was undetectable, a result confirmed by genomic DNA sequencing.

18% (4 out of 22) of the generated Drosophila lines expressed both Drosophila TBPH and human hTDP-43, and PCR amplification using genomic DNA from these lines yielded a ~10 kb product absent in unedited or correctly edited animals.

100% (4 out of 4) of incorrectly edited Drosophila animals, defined as those expressing both Drosophila TBPH and hTDP-43, had pCR4 vector sequences inserted into their genome, with no product amplified from background control or correctly edited animals.

Of the 12 DsRed expressing Drosophila lines recovered from GluRIIA genome editing, 1 line had the correct edit and 11 lines contained unmutated GluRIIA nucleotides alongside the desired modified nucleotides. PCR analysis confirmed that all 11 incorrectly edited lines had pCR4 vector sequences inserted into their genome.

The study observed a high frequency of anomalous template donor vector insertion into the genome as a consequence of HDR-based genome editing, with 11 of 12 independent lines showing incorrect pCR4 vector backbone insertion compared to 1 line with correct exon replacement.

Unexpected insertions during CRISPR/Cas9 based mouse genome editing occurred at a rate of 10% when targeting individual genomic sites with more than one gRNA, compared to 4% when targeting individual genomic sites with a single gRNA.
Insertion of linear HDR template sequences during HDR germline editing of mice was observed in several head-to-tail copies, produced by both HDR and NHEJ mechanisms or a combination of both.
The human hTDP-43 HGE HDR construct in pCR4 and the ALFA-VGAT tagged HDR construct in pHSG298 were each surrounded by approximately 1 kb homology arms.

Of 16 DsRed expressing Drosophila lines recovered, 8 (50%) also had ZsGreen expression, and PCR for pVID vector sequences from genomic DNA derived from these 8 ZsGreen expressing lines found all (8 of 8) had template vector insertion.

PCR for pVID vector sequences from genomic DNA derived from 8 DsRed expressing lines which did not have ZsGreen expression showed no evidence of vector template sequences (8 of 8), and all 8 had the expected Synapsin genome edit.

In a second CRISPR/Cas9 HDR genome editing procedure targeting the GluRIIC gene, 5 of 6 recovered lines had both DsRed and ZsGreen eye expression, and PCR for pVID vector sequences from genomic DNA derived from these 5 ZsGreen expressing lines found all (5 of 5) had HDR template vector insertion.
The 1 of 6 GluRIIC edited lines which only expressed DsRed had no evidence of HDR template vector insertion.
The VGAT exon 1 and exon 2 intronic region edit and the GluRIIA exon 12 edit were each flanked by approximately 1 kb homology arms.
The 7ALFA-Synapsin edit and the GluRIIC edit were each flanked by two 600-700 bp homology arms.
Across five independent homology directed repair procedures in Drosophila germline genome editing, an average of 54% (n=71) of the generated edited lines contained undesired vector insertion events.

The hTDP43 HGE guide RNA sequences GGATAATGTAACCGCTGTACCGG and GGCCGGCATCCACAAGGGTCCGG exhibited 0 off-targets, GC contents of 45% and 70%, efficiency scores of 4.4 and 5.7, homology arm sizes of 1082bp and 1077bp, cutting distances of 1835bp and 1895bp, and an aberrant vector insertion rate of 18%.

The GluRIIA mutation guide RNA sequences GCTGAGCGAAAGGGGCGAGCTGG and GACTCTAAAGTCTAGACATGTGG exhibited 3 and 0 off-targets, GC contents of 70% and 40%, efficiency scores of 5.6 and 4.3, homology arm sizes of 1000bp and 999bp, cutting distances of 295bp and 203bp, and an aberrant vector insertion rate of 91%.

The ALFA-vGat guide RNA sequences GGTGGGTCATTCTCATTATGG and GCCTGCGGAAGATGGATTTGG exhibited 0 off-targets, GC contents of 44% and 56%, efficiency scores of 5.9 and 5.8, homology arm sizes of 897bp and 1328bp, cutting distances of 18bp and 21bp, and an aberrant vector insertion rate of 67%.

The ALFA-Synapsin guide RNA sequences GGGCCCCCTTCTGCCAAAGGGGG and GGGTATGCTTTGGCA/TTGGCAGG exhibited 1 and 3 off-targets, GC contents of 70% and 55%, efficiency scores of 5.3 and 4.5, homology arm sizes of 604bp and 602bp, cutting distances of 391bp and 5bp, and an aberrant vector insertion rate of 50%.
Screening against the vector marker reduced the aberrant vector insertion rate for the ALFA-Synapsin edit to 0%.
PCR primers targeting the lac promoter and pUC ori in the pCR4 or pHSG298 plasmid sequences were designed to yield an 817 bp band for the pCR4 plasmid and a 1001 bp band for the pHSG298 plasmid.
PCR primers targeting the region between the zsGreen CDS and the dU6:3 promoter in the pVID vector were designed to yield an 813 bp band.
The study analyzed five different Drosophila lines, all of which employed two gRNAs and a removable DsRed selection cassette.
The study utilized exclusively the nos promoter to express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells, a factor that could potentially affect vector template integration.
The study utilized the nos promoter to express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells, with a noted threat to validity that Cas9 concentration could affect vector template integration.

Omission of specific lipid identity and exact lipid-to-RNP weight ratio prevents establishing initial mixing conditions necessary to rule out membrane interaction artifacts, rendering the pipeline opaque regarding whether observed effects are genuine or byproducts of the formulation process.

Missing specific lipid identity and exact ratios confound the 40% efficiency and 0.67% bystander rates by preventing isolation of the vehicle's contribution from the editor's activity, leaving the safety profile uncontrolled.

The statistical power of the in vivo LNP delivery experiments is insufficient to detect effects smaller than massive ones, and the 40% efficiency point estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero due to the lack of covariate adjustment for baseline mutation rates.

The claim that long-term genomic stability is unresolved is methodologically invalid because no long-term follow-up data was collected, and the observed off-target integration in the Drosophila model may be a context-specific artifact rather than a universal failure of the CRISPR editor.

The reported 300-fold efficiency gain remains inseparable from the specific SM102 lipid formulation due to missing formulation parameters, preventing verification of whether the RNP or the delivery vehicle is the active driver. This gap invalidates the claim of universal efficacy and leaves the therapeutic advantage unresolved as a potential delivery artifact.

The reported aggregate off-target metrics cannot be independently verified due to the absence of raw sequencing reads and specific guide design parameters. Without access to the full FASTQ files and exact CRISPResso2 parameters, it is impossible to confirm that the reported precision is not an artifact of the analysis settings.

The study reports a mean bystander editing rate of 0.67% and a 1.25% correction rate, but the absence of raw sequencing data and confidence intervals renders these figures statistically uninterpretable, preventing the distinction between true off-target events and analytical noise in the Drosophila model.

The claim that the prime editor platform achieves a 0.67% bystander rate is unsupported by the absence of confidence intervals, meaning the observed precision is statistically indistinguishable from noise in a small sample, and the low-quality read filtering (Q>30) may artificially suppress the detection of off-target events.

The Q>30 quality threshold functions as a censoring mechanism that systematically removes low-quality reads, potentially excluding rare, low-abundance off-target signals and thereby invalidating the claim that the platform is safe based on a dataset with self-removed ambiguous data points.

The reported 0.67% off-target rate cannot be verified as a true biological floor because the study omits sequencing depth and specific CRISPResso2 parameters, preventing the determination of whether the metric is an artifact of an aggressive filtering pipeline that suppresses off-target detection.

The settlement experiment requires a properly powered, side-by-side study with a fully defined, matched vehicle control to isolate the biological effect from the delivery mechanism's contribution, as current data lacks the statistical power and covariate adjustment to distinguish the editor's activity from background noise.

Replication is blocked by the lack of raw FASTQ files and exact SM102 ratio controls in a public repository, leaving independent labs to compare aggregate metrics against undefined baselines without access to the original authors' filtering steps.
