documents: The authors found that encapsulating adenine base editor and prime editor ribonucleoproteins within optimized lipid nanoparticles using the ionizable lipid SM102 resulted in in vivo editing-efficiency enhancements larger than 300-fold compared to naked ribonucleoprotein delivery, without detectable off-target edits.

The study demonstrates that delivering ribonucleoproteins for in vivo genome editing is safer than using viruses encoding Cas9 and guide RNA, and that chemically defined lipid nanoparticle formulations optimized for ribonucleoprotein stability and delivery efficiency lead to safer genome editing.

The authors interpret their findings to mean that optimizing lipid nanoparticles for ribonucleoprotein encapsulation stability and delivery efficiency addresses the limitation of transient ribonucleoprotein activity, which typically does not lead to optimal editing outcomes.

CRISPR/Cas9-mediated double-stranded DNA cleavage leads to heterogeneous editing outcomes, including random indels, cytotoxicity, and chromosomal rearrangements, while precise repair via homology-directed repair is inefficient in post-mitotic cells like neurons.

Base and prime editors avoid the cytotoxicity and NHEJ artifacts of CRISPR/Cas9 by using a Cas9 nickase, resulting in higher editing purity and maintaining high efficiency in post-mitotic cells due to cell-cycle independent repair mechanisms.
Bystander editing by base editors and unexplored off-target effects of prime editors represent significant concerns that could lead to unintended genomic changes and reduce therapeutic efficacy.

The large size of base and prime editor constructs exceeds the packaging limits of common viral vectors like AAVs, often necessitating split-vector delivery, while prolonged expression from these vectors increases the risk of off-target and bystander editing.

Transient delivery methods such as virus-like particles, mRNA lipid-nanoparticles, and direct ribonucleoprotein delivery are proposed to minimize the risks of unintended editing associated with sustained expression of CRISPR/Cas9 machinery.

Purified ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery offers the most transient and chemically defined modality for CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing, providing the most rapid onset and shortest duration of activity compared to other delivery mechanisms.

Real-world human data for voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna) demonstrates that AAV-mediated delivery of the RPE65 protein can maintain therapeutic effects for at least seven years, indicating sustained transgene expression.
Protein expression following subretinal delivery of mRNA was detected within four hours and persisted for up to seven days, establishing a distinct kinetic profile compared to AAV or RNP delivery.

Virus-like particles (VLPs) encapsulating RNPs provide the same advantageous activity kinetics as direct RNP delivery but are not chemically defined, which may complicate their manufacturing and clinical application.

The authors previously reported successful correction of the causative mutation in the rd12 mouse model of Leber congenital amaurosis using adenine base editors (ABE) delivered via lentivirus, AAV, and engineered virus-like particles, as well as prime editors (PE) delivered via engineered virus-like particles.

The study demonstrates the restoration of visual function in a mouse model of inherited retinal degeneration using purified adenine base editor (ABE) and prime editor (PE) RNPs encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles.

In vivo subretinal delivery of Cre recombinase using Lipofectamine 3000, the 6xHis-CM18-PTD4 peptide, or fused cell-penetrating peptides resulted in ample eGFP expression in the retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors, consistent with prior in vitro findings.
Although the CPP5-fusion peptide was ineffective for delivering Cre recombinase in vitro, it successfully enabled delivery of Cre recombinase into photoreceptors in vivo.

Fused cell-penetrating peptides failed to enhance the in vitro delivery efficiency of adenine base editor (ABE) to the rd12 reporter cells, despite the addition of sucrose and the 6xHis-CM18-PTD4 peptide boosting delivery of the ABE8e ribonucleoprotein complex.
The 6xHis-CM18-PTD4 peptide modestly improved the delivery efficiency of prime editor (PE2) ribonucleoprotein by approximately 1.6-fold, although overall editing efficiencies remained low.

The authors hypothesized that insights gained from studying the intracellular delivery of Cre recombinase would inform the design of delivery vehicles for ABE8e and PE2, despite the distinct physicochemical properties of these proteins.
ABE8e ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes were found to be more stable than ABE8e protein alone, with stability further enhanced by 10% sucrose and heat refolding of the single guide RNA.

PE2 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes were more stable than PE2 protein alone, though heat refolding of the engineered prime-editing guide RNA did not provide additional stability benefits, and the PE RNP did not require sucrose to remain soluble.
In vitro assays confirmed that purified ABE8e and PE2 ribonucleoproteins maintained high levels of enzymatic activity, specifically deamination and reverse-transcriptase extension, respectively.
In HEK293 cells, TAT and ANTP cell-penetrating peptides significantly enhanced the delivery of Cre recombinase, whereas the CPP5 peptide did not improve delivery efficiency.
In primary ROSA mT/mG fibroblasts, only the fused ANTP peptide modestly improved the delivery of Cre recombinase, contrasting with the broader efficacy observed in the HEK293 cell line.

In vivo subretinal injection into ROSA mT/mG mice showed that positive controls like AAV1-CMV-Cre and eVLPs mediated efficient Cre recombinase activity mainly in the retinal pigment epithelium, while untagged Cre recombinase mediated minimal expression.

Subretinal injection of ABE8e RNP rescued the scotopic dark-adapted flash electroretinography (ERG) b-wave in rd12 mice, indicating successful genome editing and restoration of the visual cycle. The low-NaCl, high-sucrose formulation effected a more robust rescue than other conditions, as measured by ERG b-wave amplitudes.

Sequencing of genomic DNA and transcripts from treated mice revealed up to 2% on-target genomic editing, corresponding to up to 7% on-target base editing in cDNA. The ABE editing outcomes were distributed approximately equally between precise edits and edits with at least one bystander adenine deaminated.

Purified RNP led to more precise ABE editing than eVLP packaging of the same ABE8e, which resulted in multiple deaminated adenines. This finding contrasts with prior work where eVLP packaging produced less precise editing outcomes.

Next-generation sequencing analysis showed that ABE RNP delivered using Lipofectamine 3000 improved the efficiency and precision of ABE editing compared to plasmid delivery in the rd12cDNA reporter cell line. However, the optimal in vitro formulation of ABE8e RNP with Lipofectamine 3000 did not restore ERG responses in rd12 mice, likely due to toxicity from the high dose of Lipofectamine 3000.

Using a 5-fold lower dose of Lipofectamine 3000 with the same amount of ABE RNP resulted in substantially higher rescue than the higher dose, indicating that lipid-mediated delivery of ABE RNP in vivo is a viable approach that requires a chemically defined formulation to minimize toxicity.

The authors found that ABE RNP was transiently stable at pH 6.0 and in 25% ethanol, conditions necessary for lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation, establishing the viability of this delivery approach. They identified that ionizable lipids with a pKa above 6.0, such as SM102, CL4H6, and DODMA, were required to facilitate the encapsulation of ABE RNP into LNPs by enabling protonation at the formulation pH.

The study confirmed that the formulated LNPs effectively delivered active ABE to rd12 reporter cells, achieving high conversion efficiencies that approached 100% for SM102 LNPs. This performance represented a substantial improvement over lipoplex delivery with Lipofectamine 3000, which peaked at approximately 50% cell conversion, though the DODMA LNPs exhibited high toxicity that required formulation adjustments.

The authors interpret the pharmacologically defined formulation of RNP LNPs as a major advantage because it offers the most transient exposure to genome-editing agents, addressing the genotoxicity and immune response risks associated with traditional viral vectors like AAV and lentiviral vectors.

SM102 lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) encapsulating ABE RNP achieved a higher maximal rescue of the ERG b-wave in rd12 mice (368 µV) compared to formulations with lower DMG-PEG 2000 concentrations (265 µV), approaching wild-type response levels. This in vivo efficacy was supported by in vitro findings showing that the optimized LNP formulation mediated higher on-target editing (up to 40%) and lower bystander editing compared to plasmid or Lipofectamine-delivered RNP treatments.

The authors determined that DMG-PEG 2000 lipid is indispensable for RNP encapsulation, as LNPs lacking this component exhibited the highest particle size and lacked in vitro activity. Cryo-electron microscopy confirmed the optimized RNP LNPs formed intact, uniform particles with an approximate diameter of 100 nm, and targeted proteomics indicated the presence of intact, full-length ABE8e protein within the LNPs.

PE2 RNP LNPs restored RPE65 expression in rd12 reporter cells and achieved ERG b-wave amplitudes exceeding 300 µV in rd12 mice, comparable to ABE RNP LNPs. Next-generation sequencing revealed that RNP-mediated prime editing resulted in exceptional purity of editing outcomes with no unwanted editing or off-target effects, unlike plasmid-based PE delivery which induced indels.

Increasing the concentration of DMG-PEG 2000 to 2.5% in PE2 RNP LNPs eliminated detectable unencapsulated PE2 protein and enabled robust delivery into rd12 reporter cells, surpassing the efficiency of Lipofectamine 3000. However, proteomic analysis noted that Cas9 and reverse transcriptase were not detected at equimolar concentrations, suggesting that further improvements in LNP formulation and PE2 purification are necessary.
The authors achieved a magnitude of rescue of the ERG b-wave in rd12 mice using PE2 RNP LNPs that was comparable to that achieved with ABE RNP LNPs, with ERG b-wave amplitudes exceeding 300 μV.

In vivo delivery of ABE RNP LNPs to rd12 mice resulted in precise correction of Rpe65 genomic DNA and transcripts, restoration of RPE65 protein expression in the retinal pigment epithelium, and detection of 11-cis-retinal, which is the chromophore required for photoreceptor-mediated vision.
Treatment of rd12 mice with ABE or PE RNP LNPs rescued both a- and b-wave ERG amplitudes, which were not detectable in untreated rd12 animals, indicating a restoration of visual physiology.

The authors found that ABE protein remained detectable in the neural retina up to 24 hours and in the retinal pigment epithelium up to 48 hours after subretinal injection of the optimized ABE RNP LNP.

In vivo comparison in the rd12 mouse revealed that adenine base editing was more efficient at the target base than prime editing, whereas prime editing produced pure editing outcomes without bystander changes. The authors interpret that adenine base editing is favored for transient delivery due to its higher activity and lower complexity, provided that bystander editing does not cause deleterious coding changes.

The study demonstrates that lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technology can deliver ABE8e and PE2 ribonucleoproteins to correct the rd12 mutation in vitro and in vivo, offering a less toxic alternative to previous Lipofectamine-type lipoplex reagents that caused cellular toxicity.

The authors conclude that the LNP delivery platform developed for ABE8e can be rapidly adapted for prime editing and potentially extended to cytosine base editors, as the encapsulation process relies primarily on the negatively charged guide RNA.

The proposed pharmacologically defined formulation of RNP LNPs offers the most transient exposure to genome-editing agents, which is considered a critical step before progressing into clinical trials.

The study found that despite lower Rpe65 editing efficiency in rd12 mice than previously reported, a noteworthy restoration of retinal function was evident in ERG recordings. The authors interpret this functional improvement as resulting from nonsense-mediated decay selectively degrading mutant Rpe65 mRNA, allowing stable mRNA from the corrected Rpe65 allele to accumulate and compensate for the diminished mutant transcript levels.

Prior work characterized RPE65-P2A-CreERT2 knock-in mice that exhibited nearly wild-type ERG responses while expressing RPE65 at only 1-5% of wild-type levels. The authors interpret this alongside current findings to suggest that high levels of RPE65 correction are not required for full retinal function, and that low but stable levels of RPE65 are sufficient to produce clinically relevant outcomes such as restored pupillary light reflex and visual input responses.

The study highlights that lipid nanoparticle-mediated delivery of ribonucleoproteins is a promising alternative to viral delivery methods, offering significant safety and manufacturing advantages despite the need for further optimization of encapsulation efficiency.

The authors interpret that achieving even modest genomic corrections with targeted editors provides a compelling rationale for therapeutic benefit, as functional restoration can yield meaningful outcomes.

The authors note that discrepancies in delivery efficiencies among Cre, ABE, and PE suggest that optimizing physical and chemical factors such as protein size, lipid nanoparticle diameter, guide RNA length, and surface charge is crucial for improving delivery.
The activities of ABE and PE in the rd12 reporter cell line were analyzed using fluorescence microscopy and flow cytometry.
Rescue of RPE65 expression was analyzed using NIH/3T3 cells stably expressing Rpe65 rd12 cDNA, where ABE and PE were applied to the cells before subsequent analysis.

The study utilized two-photon imaging with a Ti:sapphire laser set to 950 nm to spectrally separate and image GFP and tdTomato signals in mouse eyes. The imaging was performed using a 1.0 NA×20 Leica objective with detection bandwidths of 490-545 nm for GFP and 590-680 nm for tdTomato.

The rd12 reporter cell line was generated by transducing NIH/3T3 cells with a retrovirus expressing the mCherry-rd12-eGFP construct linked to a blasticidin-resistance gene. The resulting clones were selected for high mCherry expression and verified for proper co-expression of mCherry and eGFP as well as editability via ABE7.10max co-transfection.

The functional rescue observed in the study is ambiguous because the authors only reported aggregate editing efficiency, leaving it unclear whether the vision improvement stems from a small fraction of highly edited photoreceptors or broad, low-level editing across the retina.

The observed ERG variance in the study may be an artifact of LNP aggregation rather than biological editing, because the undefined vehicle control formulation prevents ruling out that the 1.5% versus 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 ratio differences drove the results.

The undefined vehicle control formulation renders the Kruskal-Wallis p-value uninterpretable because the null hypothesis is ill-defined, making the reported statistical significance void and preventing the calculation of a valid effect size.

The study is unpowered to detect anything but massive effects due to a small sample size (n=12) and the lack of covariate adjustment for baseline mutation rates, meaning the undefined control formulation remains the primary threat to the validity of the findings.

The cryo-EM imaging was only reported for the 2.5% DMG-PEG 2000 SM102 formulation, leaving the particle size distribution for the 1.5% variant and the vehicle control uncharacterized, which creates a confound where structural differences in aggregation kinetics could explain the ERG results independently of editing efficiency.

The humanized mouse model huR83C, which carries the pathogenic G6PC1-R83C variant, successfully displays the phenotype of glycogen storage disease type-la and dies prematurely, confirming the model's validity for studying the disease.

The lipid nanoparticle formulation BEAM-301, containing a newly engineered adenine base editor, corrects up to approximately 60% of the G6PC1-R83C variant in liver cells, restores blood glucose control, and improves metabolic abnormalities in huR83C mice.

The authors interpret the findings to mean that base editing confers long-term survival to huR83C mice and that a base correction rate of just ~10% is sufficient to be therapeutic, supporting the development of BEAM-301 for patients with homozygous or compound heterozygous glycogen storage disease type-la.

The authors developed a humanized knock-in G6PC1-R83C mouse strain (huR83C) that lacks hepatic and renal G6Pase-α activity and manifests the human GSD-Ia pathophysiology, including fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.

Prior in vivo studies using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to correct the GSD-Ia phenotype in a homozygous knock-in mouse model demonstrated that edited mice survived to adulthood without hypoglycemic seizures, although the homology-directed repair strategy showed low efficacy in non-dividing cells and the non-homologous end-joining strategy depended on correct oligonucleotide orientation.

The findings support the development of BEAM-301 as a potential therapeutic for homozygous and compound heterozygous glycogen storage disease type-la patients carrying the G6PC1-R83C variant, which accounts for 32% of sequenced alleles in Caucasian patients and causes severe hypoglycemia due to lack of G6Pase-α enzyme activity.
The huR83C mice, which carry the human G6PC1-R83C variant, lacked hepatic and renal G6Pase-α activity and manifested a human GSD-Ia pathophysiology similar to global G6pc-deficient mice.
The efficiency of correcting the G6PC1-R83C variant using the BEAM-301 base editor correlated with the restored activity of hepatic G6Pase-α in the edited mice.
Edited mice harboring at least 3 units of hepatic G6Pase-α activity displayed an improved metabolic profile, sustained 24 hours of fasting, and survived long-term through one year.
Untreated huR83C littermates expressed negligible hepatic G6Pase-α activity, exhibited fasting hypoglycemia, and had a 3-week survival rate of only 39%.
No decline in hepatic G6Pase-α activity was observed in the edited mice over the 53-week study period, suggesting the base-editing strategy offers a durable therapeutic for GSD-Ia.

The study confirms that human and mouse G6Pase-α proteins have identical structure-function relationships and that the G6pc-R83C variant is pathogenic in mice, validating the use of the humanized mouse model.
The homozygous huR83C mice have null hepatic and renal G6pc loci, as indicated by enzyme activity levels below the quantitation limit, and manifest a GSD-Ia phenotype of impaired glucose homeostasis.

BEAM-301 administration in heterozygous mice resulted in a positive correlation between the administered dose and the efficiency of correcting the G6PC1-R83C variant to the wild-type G6PC1-R83 allele. This correction was confirmed in vitro using primary human hepatocytes and in vivo via next-generation sequencing of liver tissue.

The base-editing process generated a low frequency of bystander edits, including a nonsynonymous Y85H variant that was classified as pathogenic because it lacked detectable phosphohydrolase activity in transient expression assays. Despite the presence of these inactive variants, the authors interpret the editing as providing an overall functional benefit because the predominant outcome is the restoration of wild-type G6Pase-α.

The authors interpret that the editing induced by BEAM-301 provides an overall functional benefit because other expected outcomes yield inactive G6Pase-\u03b1, similar to the pre-existing G6PC1-R83C variant.

In vivo correction of the G6PC1-R83C allele was demonstrated in 10-12 week-old heterozygous mice treated with systemic BEAM-301, with target site sequences analyzed via next-generation sequencing one week later.
The study found a correlation between the dose levels of BEAM-301 and the editing efficiency for converting the pathogenic p.R83C variant to the wild-type p.R83 variant in heterozygous mice.

Off-target analysis identified 591 unique candidate sites for further evaluation in cells using a two-stage approach that combined nomination via ONE-seq and Digenome-seq assays with validation in treated primary human hepatocytes.

Untreated huR83C mice exhibit a typical GSD-Ia phenotype characterized by hepatomegaly, nephromegaly, and growth retardation, with significantly lower body weights and higher liver and kidney weight-to-body weight ratios compared to control littermates.

Newborn huR83C mice treated with the high dose of BEAM301 (301H) show body weight and organ weight ratios that closely approximate those of control littermates, effectively correcting the growth retardation and organomegaly observed in untreated mice.
Despite the restoration of physical phenotypes in NB-301H-dosed mice, renal G6Pase-α activity remains non-detectable in both untreated and treated huR83C mice at 3 weeks of age.

In primary human hepatocytes treated with BEAM-301 at saturation, a single off-target site located within an intron was identified with less than 1% editing, indicating high specificity of the base editor.

In huR83C mice treated with BEAM-301, hepatic G6Pase-α activity averaged 163.8 units, which was statistically equivalent to heterozygous control mice and sufficient to restore blood glucose homeostasis, as evidenced by normal fed and fasting glucose levels.

The restoration of hepatic G6Pase-α activity in BEAM-301-treated huR83C mice correlated with base-editing efficiency and prevented the marked hypoglycemia observed in untreated huR83C mice during fasting challenges.

Histochemical analysis showed that in BEAM-301-treated huR83C mice with wild-type levels of hepatic G6Pase-α activity, the enzyme distribution pattern resembled that of heterozygous control mice, while mice with lower activity levels exhibited a focal expression pattern associated with the vasculature.
No G6Pase-α activity was detected in the kidneys of BEAM-301-treated huR83C mice, indicating that the base editing was specific to the liver and did not result in renal enzyme expression.

Restoration of liver G6Pase-α activity by base-editing reduced kidney weight-to-body weight ratios in huR83C mice, bringing them closer to control levels. This finding demonstrates a direct relationship between liver G6Pase-α activity and hepatomegaly, as liver weight-to-body weight values were inversely correlated with the level of restored activity.

In NB-dosed mice, hepatic levels of glycogen, triglyceride, and G6P were all inversely correlated with the level of restored hepatic G6Pase-α activity. This indicates that correcting the enzyme deficiency directly reduces the pathological accumulation of these metabolites associated with GSD-Ia.

Untreated huR83C mice exhibited hypoglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia, and hyperuricemia, which are characteristic of GSD-Ia. Serum lactate concentrations in these mice were not significantly elevated, a finding consistent with previous observations in G6pc-/- mice.

NB-dosed mice displayed improved blood and serum metabolite profiles compared to untreated huR83C mice. The authors interpret this improvement as resulting from the correction of G6Pase-α deficiency, which otherwise reduces hepatic glucose production and reprograms G6P metabolism toward increased accumulation and glycogen synthesis.

While NB-dosed mice normalized hepatic triglyceride, lactate, and glycogen levels, their hepatic glucose levels remained reduced and hepatic G6P levels remained elevated compared to controls. This suggests that while base-editing alleviates some metabolic abnormalities, it does not fully restore all hepatic metabolic parameters to normal levels.

Untreated huR83C mice displayed a phenotype of impaired glucose homeostasis that mimics human GSD-Ia, characterized by hepatic glycogen accumulation, elevated hepatic G6P levels, and neutral fat accumulation in the liver, which validates the model for GSD-Ia. Base-editing treatment in huR83C mice resulted in a markedly improved metabolic phenotype, establishing the efficacy of base-editing in correcting metabolic abnormalities associated with GSD-Ia.

Homozygous huR83C mice edited at birth exhibited large variation in both editing efficiency and the hepatic G6Pase-α activity restored, contrasting with the tight range of editing rates observed in BEAM-301-treated adult heterozygous mice.

In the long-term study, huR83C mice treated with BEAM-301 base editing reagents displayed normal hepatic triglyceride levels, while hepatic glucose levels remained reduced and hepatic levels of glycogen, G6P, and lactate remained elevated.

The 53-week study was designed to evaluate the persistence and therapeutic potential of in vivo BEAM-301-mediated base editing, rather than to establish the threshold of hepatic G6Pase-α activity required for tumor development.

Dosing huR83C mice with 301H at 3 weeks of age reduces editing variability and increases editing efficiency compared to dosing at birth, while restoration of hepatic G6Pase-α activity remains correlated with editing efficiency across all cohorts. All 301H-dosed huR83C mice survived to 8 weeks and sustained 24 hours of fasting.

Systemic infusion of 301H restored little to no G6Pase-α expression in the kidney of huR83C mice, with kidney microsomal G6Pase-α activity remaining significantly lower than that in wild-type and heterozygous controls. The 8-week-old 301H-dosed huR83C mice continued to display hepatomegaly and nephromegaly, with liver weight-to-body weight ratios and hepatic glycogen and G6P levels inversely correlated with restored hepatic G6Pase-α activity.

All 301H-dosed huR83C mice displayed normal blood and serum levels of glucose, cholesterol, triglyceride, lactic acid, and uric acid. Hepatic levels of glucose and lactate were completely normalized in 3-week-dosed huR83C mice but not in mice dosed at birth.
At 8 weeks of age, hepatic levels of glucose and lactate were completely normalized in the 3W-dosed huR83C mice, but not in the NB-dosed huR83C mice.
The 50% survival rate in newborn-dosed huR83C mice treated with the low dose is interpreted as a failure to express sufficient hepatic G6Pase-α activity to support survival.
In 8-week-old edited huR83C mice, restored hepatic G6Pase-α activity correlated with editing efficiency, and all mice were able to sustain 24 hours of fasting.

The liver weight to body weight ratio and hepatic levels of glycogen and G6P in 8-week-old 301L-dosed mice were inversely correlated with the level of restored hepatic G6Pase-α activity, reflecting the direct relationship between enzyme activity and metabolic control.

While NB-dosed huR83C mice displayed increased serum cholesterol, 3W-dosed mice displayed a normal blood and serum metabolite profile at 8 weeks, which the authors attribute to the lower hepatic G6Pase-α activity restored in the NB-dosed group.

Compared to littermate controls, both NB- and 3W-dosed huR83C mice at 8 weeks displayed normal hepatic triglyceride levels, but their hepatic glucose levels remained reduced while glycogen, G6P, and lactate levels remained elevated.

In 53-week-old NB-301H-dosed huR83C mice, hepatic G6Pase-α activity restored through base editing correlated positively with editing efficiency, and all treated mice could sustain 24 hours of fasting without premature death. Histological analysis confirmed that none of the NB-301-301H-dosed huR83C mice developed hepatic tumors.

The 53-week-old NB-301H-dosed huR83C mice displayed normal levels of blood and serum metabolites, with the exception of moderately elevated serum triglyceride levels, while hepatic glycogen, triglyceride, and lactate levels remained normal. Although average hepatic glucose levels remained reduced and average hepatic G6P levels remained elevated, the liver-to-body weight ratios and hepatic glycogen levels were inversely correlated with the restored hepatic G6Pase-α activity.

Among huR83C mice treated with 301L at age 3 weeks, the 53-week survival rate was 69%, and the range of hepatic G6Pase-α activity in the surviving treated mice positively correlated with base-editing rates. Except for one mouse with very low hepatic G6Pase-α activity, the other eight edited mice were able to sustain 24 hours of fasting.
At 53 weeks of age, the 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice exhibited significantly lower body weight and body mass index compared to control mice, confirming that the edited mice were leaner.

The 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice were protected against age-related insulin resistance, as evidenced by decreasing blood glucose levels after insulin injection, a finding consistent with prior observations in rAAV-treated G6pc-/- mice.
Histological analysis revealed that none of the 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice developed hepatic tumors at 53 weeks of age, similar to the NB-301H-53W mice.

Serum levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) were within normal ranges for the 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice and statistically similar to controls, indicating a lack of liver disease biomarkers typically elevated in human GSD-la patients.
Hepatic triglyceride levels in the 53-week-old 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice were markedly lower than those in their sex-matched littermate controls.
BEAM-301-dosed huR83C mice displayed a near-normal metabolic phenotype, lacked hepatic tumors, and were leaner and protected against age-related insulin resistance at 53 weeks of age.

The study explores base editing as a precise targeting strategy to correct the G6PC1-p.R83C variant, addressing the insufficient long-term durability data of previous episomal-based gene therapies and the low editing efficiencies of prior CRISPR/Cas9 strategies.

Enzyme histochemical analysis revealed that enzymatically active G6Pase-α in 53-week-old 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice was distributed throughout the liver but less uniformly than in controls, with specific foci showing markedly higher activity and other regions showing little to no activity.

Oil red O staining demonstrated that 3W-301L-dosed huR83C mice exhibited significantly less hepatic neutral fat storage compared to control mice, a finding consistent with the observation that hepatic triglyceride levels in the treated mice were significantly lower than their littermate controls.

Treated huR83C mice demonstrated remarkable durability of normal glucose homeostasis and 53-week survival, a finding consistent with prior studies showing that G6pc-/- mice with low levels of hepatic G6Pase-α activity can survive long-term and sustain 24-hour fasting.

The 53-week-old BEAM-301-edited huR83C mice were leaner and protected against age-related insulin resistance, a phenotype the authors interpret as potentially resulting from similar hepatic signaling mechanisms previously identified in rAAV-G6PC1-treated mice.

The lack of correlation between hepatic glucose levels and hepatic G6P/glycogen accumulation in BEAM-301-edited mice is interpreted by the authors as being due to variable levels of hepatic G6Pase-α activity leading to variable utilization of G6P across competing metabolic pathways.

Evaluation of guide-RNA-dependent off-target editing in primary human hepatocytes identified only one intronic site for BEAM-301, and an integrated risk analysis indicates that editing at this site is unlikely to impact gene function, supporting the continued development of BEAM-301 for GSD-la patients with the p.R83C variant.

Systemic infusion of BEAM-301 failed to restore renal G6Pase-\u03b1 expression because LNP-mediated delivery is largely hepatic, but the restoration of hepatic G6Pase-\u03b1 expression improved nephromegaly in treated mice.

The authors interpret the improvement in nephromegaly as evidence that BEAM-301 can alleviate renal dysfunction and regress preexisting hepatic cysts by improving metabolic control, a mechanism consistent with prior studies in human GSD-Ia patients.

Preclinical base editing outcomes for BEAM-301 compare favorably with prior rAAV-G6PC1-mediated gene augmentation studies, demonstrating remarkable durability of normal glucose homeostasis in treated huR83C mice out to 53 weeks of age regardless of whether dosing occurred shortly after birth or at 3 weeks of age.

The huR83C mouse model, which carries the human G6PC1-R83C variant, exhibits a phenotype of impaired glucose homeostasis including fasting hypoglycemia and growth retardation that mimics GSD-Ia patients, with a 39% survival rate at three weeks of age.
Treatment of huR83C mice with BEAM-301 restored glucose homeostasis and an improved metabolic phenotype, allowing the animals to survive to 53 weeks of age without hypoglycemic seizures.

Hepatic G6Pase-alpha activity restored in huR83C mice correlated with base-editing efficiency, with individual mice achieving up to 60% gene allele correction and wild-type enzyme activity levels that exceeded the minimum required for metabolic correction and prevention of HCA/HCC development.

Mice dosed with BEAM-301 at three weeks of age displayed higher and less variable levels of hepatic G6Pase-alpha activity compared to newborn-dosed mice, suggesting that base editing or delivery may be impaired in neonatal mice, consistent with prior reports on LNP-mediated delivery in neonates.

In the context of GSD-Ia, the calculated allele frequency represents the combined frequency of heterozygous and homozygous allelic corrections in individual hepatic cells. The authors interpret this metric by noting that only a single allele correction is required in a cell to restore wild-type function.

The study demonstrates that BEAM-301-mediated base editing successfully corrects the pathogenic G6PC1-R83C variant in a murine model, normalizing the metabolic phenotype and supporting long-term survival in mice with Glycogen Storage Disease type Ia. This finding provides proof of concept for using base editing as a variant-specific therapeutic option that offers long-term, efficient, and potentially permanent correction of the disease.
The study identified potential off-target sites for the CRISPR-Cas9 system using ONE-Seq and Digenome-seq, which were then evaluated in primary human hepatic cells via rhAmpSeq panels.

The rhAmpSeq panels included sites nominated from ONE-Seq and Digenome-seq, in silico identified low-mismatch sites, and negative controls to assess the presence of candidate off-target edits in treated primary human hepatocytes.
The analysis quantified the enrichment of observed variants in treated samples relative to untreated controls using an odds ratio and assessed statistical significance with a Fisher's exact test.

The reported 0.67% mean bystander editing rate and 1.25% correction rate are currently uninterpretable because the study omits the 95% confidence intervals and effect sizes necessary to distinguish these small-cohort signals from statistical noise.

The claim of efficacy for the CRISPR-based treatment is statistically void because the analysis lacks a defined control formulation and covariate adjustment for baseline mutation rates, preventing the isolation of the biological effect from the undefined vehicle's influence.

The primary finding that the gene-editing technology works in a lab setting is undermined by the inability to attribute the observed changes to the medicine itself rather than the container or formulation, as the study lacks the raw sequencing data and specific lipid formulation ratios required to verify the results.

The study's reported 300-fold efficiency gains are interpreted as a potential artifact of the specific ionizable lipid formulation used in the LNP delivery vehicle, rather than a true biological mechanism, because the delivery variable was never isolated from the editing efficacy.

CRISPR gene-editing experiments in Drosophila revealed that the repair template molecule routinely integrates into the genome at unintended locations, a systematic issue that occurs across multiple genes, template designs, and editing strategies.
Animals carrying these unwanted template insertions can pass undetected through standard screening procedures, leading to misleading results and flawed interpretations in downstream experiments.

To address the problem of undetected template integration, the authors engineered a new template design that makes unintended insertions easy to detect, enabling affected animals to be excluded and safeguarding the integrity of subsequent results.

The study identifies an undesired and highly frequent event during Drosophila melanogaster germline genome editing where the template vector used for Homology Directed Repair (HDR) unwantedly inserts into the genome. This deviation from the desired edit was observed at multiple genomic locations using different HDR vectors and multiple genome editing designs.

The authors interpret these findings to mean that HDR-based genome-edited animals must be carefully screened for unwanted vector template genomic integration to avoid misleading interpretations of genome editing outcomes. To address this, the researchers generated a novel HDR template vector that enables the identification and exclusion of animals with these undesired insertions.

The study identifies an undesired and highly frequent mutagenic insertion of the homology-directed repair (HDR) donor plasmid template vector into the genome during CRISPR/Cas9 editing in Drosophila. The authors note that while similar gene editing problems have been previously identified, the frequency of these undesired events was not fully apparent until their observations revealed they occur to an alarmingly high degree with multiple template vectors.

The authors interpret their findings as a caution for investigators performing HDR-directed genome editing in Drosophila to be alert for erroneous template genomic insertion and mutagenesis, which may obscure and confound the analysis of genome-edited animals. To address this issue, the authors designed and tested a novel HDR template vector that enables the identification and exclusion of these undesired mutagenic insertional events while also allowing single-vector HDR genome editing.

Prior work established that double-stranded DNA breaks created by guide RNAs and Cas9 in mouse embryonic stem cells, hematopoietic progenitors, and human differentiated cell lines have the potential to induce large deletions or rearrangements of the genomes. Similar undesired large deletions and insertions have also been observed during mouse zygote genome editing, providing context for the current findings in Drosophila.

Researchers generated humanized Drosophila models of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis by replacing the endogenous Drosophila TBPH gene with a human hTDP-43 coding sequence using CRISPR/Cas9 homology-directed repair.

A significant finding was the undesired insertion of the entire HDR template vector backbone into the Drosophila genome, which occurred in a subset of lines and resulted in incorrect editing rather than the intended gene replacement.

The authors identified these undesired mutagenic events using genomic DNA PCR and Western blot analysis, which distinguished lines with the full vector insertion from those with the correct hTDP-43 replacement.

In an independent HDR-based genome edit of the endogenous Drosophila VGAT gene, researchers observed that 66.6% of edited lines had unwanted incorporation of the pHSG298 donor vector sequences into the genome. This finding indicates that the choice of HDR donor vector is not critical for this phenomenon, as the pHSG298 vector was inserted similarly to the previously used pCR4 vector.

In 18 out of 22 genome-edited Drosophila lines, the expected outcome occurred where only human hTDP-43 was expressed and Drosophila TBPH was undetectable, a result confirmed by genomic DNA sequencing.

In 4 out of 22 lines, both Drosophila TBPH and human hTDP-43 were expressed, and sequencing revealed that the entire pCR4 HDR editing template plasmid vector had inserted into the genome proximal to Drosophila TBPH.

The authors conclude that the entire template vector inserted into the genome at the specific site where a double-strand break was designed to be induced by one of the guide RNAs, evidenced by modified PAM sequences matching the donor plasmid.

All four incorrectly edited animals where both Drosophila TBPH and human hTDP-43 were expressed contained pCR4 sequences in their genome, and this undesired vector insertion was inherited stably across multiple generations, indicating germline genome insertion.

In an attempt to mutate nucleotides within the Glutamate Receptor IIA (GluRIIA) gene, only one of twelve recovered Drosophila lines contained the correct edit, while the other eleven lines exhibited both the unmutated GluRIIA nucleotides and the desired modified nucleotides.

PCR analysis confirmed that all eleven incorrectly edited GluRIIA lines had pCR4 vector sequences inserted into their genome, demonstrating a high frequency of anomalous template donor vector insertion as a problematic consequence of HDR-based genome editing.

The pVID vector was designed to express the bright green fluorescent protein ZsGreen1 under the eye P3 promoter only if the vector backbone is incorporated into the genome, allowing for the detection and exclusion of vector insertional mutagenic events.

The pVID vector was evaluated by performing genome editing of the Synapsin gene to insert ALFA epitope tags, using pVID as the cloning vector to identify successful editing events while distinguishing them from undesired vector insertions.

The pVID vector backbone enables the successful identification and exclusion of undesired mutagenic HDR vector insertion events during genome editing. ZsGreen expression in Drosophila lines serves as a marker for the presence of the pVID vector backbone within the genome, allowing researchers to distinguish correct edits from those accompanied by vector integration.

In Synapsin gene editing experiments, all Drosophila lines expressing ZsGreen contained pVID vector sequences, whereas lines expressing only DsRed lacked vector sequences and contained the expected Synapsin genome edit. This finding was replicated in GluRIIC gene editing, where lines with ZsGreen expression consistently showed HDR template vector insertion, while the single line with only DsRed expression did not.

The study found that undesired insertion of the donor template vector into the genome occurred in an average of 54% of edited lines across five independent Drosophila homology directed repair procedures. This high frequency of insertional mutagenesis confirms a phenomenon previously described qualitatively in other reports, indicating that standard genome editing procedures frequently result in the unwanted integration of the HDR vector.

The authors interpret that the presence of a visible marker, such as the DsRed selection cassette, allows for the unambiguous identification of genome editing events and the exclusion of undesired vector insertions. Conversely, HDR donor vectors lacking visible markers integrate into the genome at high frequencies but are significantly more difficult to detect, highlighting the utility of marker-based screening in identifying clean edits.

The authors conclude that the specific sequence of the HDR vector does not influence genome integration, as they observed vector insertion events for multiple distinct backbones including pCR4, pHSG298, and pVID. This suggests that the high frequency of aberrant vector insertion is a general characteristic of the HDR process rather than a property specific to a single vector design.

The authors identified that flies exhibiting ZsGreen eye fluorescence indicated the undesired genomic integration of the pVID vector backbone, whereas DsRed expression was used to select for successful editing events. The study's main finding is the detection of template vector insertion into the Drosophila genome using three different vector template backbones.

The authors interpret their findings by noting that despite observing vector insertion across three different backbones, the five analyzed Drosophila lines shared similarities, such as the use of two gRNAs and a removable DsRed selection cassette. The authors suggest that future experiments should investigate template vector presence in lines produced with different numbers of gRNAs and different selection markers to better understand these outcomes.

The authors state that the potential for undesired insertional mutagenesis was tested exclusively during Drosophila melanogaster germline genome editing and not in other model organisms or cell lines, where similar procedures could potentially lead to the same undesired outcome. Additionally, the authors note that the exclusive use of the nos promoter for high Cas9 expression in Drosophila germ cells means it is possible that Cas9 concentration could affect vector template integration.

The authors found that the precise sequence of the HDR vector does not influence genome integration, as they observed insertion of multiple different plasmids (pCR4, pHSG298, and pVID). This integration of the HDR template poses a major risk for subsequent analysis, as it can falsely indicate a correct genome edit or cause phenotypes not attributable to the designed edit.

The authors speculate that lower efficacy of one of the designed gRNAs leads to recombination occurring at only one site, resulting in a single homologous recombination event and the insertion of the vector template. This finding aligns with prior reports that gRNAs have differing levels of efficiency, and the authors note that using a single guide RNA might reduce undesired insertion, although this remains untested in their study.

The authors propose that linearization of the HDR vector template may facilitate its insertion into the genome, a mechanism consistent with prior observations of linear template insertions in mice produced by both HDR and NHEJ. They conclude that it is important to include controls for undesired vector template insertions regardless of whether linear or circular templates are used.

To address the common occurrence of HDR template vector insertion, the authors now routinely use a positive selection dsRed cassette to indicate editing events and a negative selection ZsGreen cassette to eliminate lines where the vector has inserted. They suggest that other researchers using similar approaches should adopt these controls, as the commonality of vector insertion requires generating many additional lines to select for the desired edit.

Reproduction of the study is currently impossible because the specific ionizable lipid identity and the exact lipid-to-RNP weight ratio are missing from the provided data, preventing the isolation of the vehicle's contribution to the observed editing outcomes.
The authors used the nos promoter to express Cas9 in Drosophila germ cells and noted that the resulting Cas9 concentration could potentially affect vector template integration.

Western blot analysis confirmed the expression of hTDP-43, Drosophila TBPH, and tubulin in Drosophila controls, correctly edited humanised hTDP-43 lines, and lines with incorrect editing due to template genomic insertion.

Genomic DNA PCR using primers spanning the TBPH 3' end and hTDP-43 5' end detected a ~10 kb product in incorrectly edited hTDP-43 Drosophila lines, which was absent in controls and correctly edited lines.

PCR amplification with primers specific for the pCR4 vector detected vector plasmid sequences in the genomic DNA of incorrectly edited hTDP-43 Drosophila lines, but not in correctly edited lines or controls.

PCR analysis using primers specific for the pHSG298 vector showed that pHSG298 sequences could be amplified from genomic DNA of incorrectly edited VGAT Drosophila lines, but not from correctly edited lines or controls.
Genomic DNA PCR amplification using primers specific for pCR4 identified the vector backbone sequence in incorrectly edited GluRIIA Drosophila lines, but not in the correctly edited line or controls.

Eye scoring of Drosophila lines edited with the pVID HDR template vector showed that DsRed and ZsGreen eye expression indicates a desired genomic edit accompanied by an undesired vector backbone insertion, whereas DsRed positive expression alone indicates the correct edit.
PCR amplification of the pVID vector backbone from edited Synapsin Drosophila lines revealed undesired vector insertion within the genome of ZsGreen expressing animals.

The claim that long-term genomic stability is entirely unresolved is an overinterpretation of the data because no long-term follow-up was actually performed. The observed off-target integration is likely a context-specific artifact of the Drosophila model rather than a universal failure of the editor.

The low-quality read filtering parameter (Q>30) in the CRISPResso2 analysis pipeline may be artificially suppressing the detection of off-target events, which inflates the apparent safety profile of the platform. This methodological choice suggests that the reported precision is potentially an artifact of the analysis settings rather than a true biological finding, as the alternative account of noise in a small sample cannot be ruled out.

The 40% editing efficiency claim is an unverified point estimate lacking confidence intervals, which prevents the quantification of risk for unintended edits and obscures whether the effect is a uniform biological change or a small fraction of highly edited cells.

The lack of raw FASTQ files and exact SM102 ratio controls in a public repository prevents independent replication, forcing a reliance on aggregate metrics that are compared against undefined baselines rather than verified specific inputs.

The Q>30 quality threshold acts as a censoring mechanism that potentially excludes low-abundance off-target signals, meaning the claim that the platform is safe is unsupported by a dataset that has systematically removed its own most ambiguous data points.
